texcoco.t: The Acolhua capital on the eastern shore of Lake Texcoco, a partner in the Aztec Triple Alliance and famed as a centre of law, poetry and learning.
texcoco.o: Texcoco became the capital of the Acolhua, a Chichimec-descended people of the eastern [[e:valley-of-mexico|Valley of Mexico]], in the 14th century. In 1418 the [[s:tepanec-empire|Tepanec Empire]] killed its ruler Ixtlilxochitl I and occupied it, forcing his son [[e:nezahualcoyotl|Nezahualcoyotl]] into exile.
texcoco.r: Allied with [[e:tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]], [[e:nezahualcoyotl|Nezahualcoyotl]] regained Texcoco in 1428-31 and made it a co-leader of the Aztec [[e:aztec-empire|Triple Alliance]]. He built palaces, gardens and the Texcotzinco hill retreat, organised legal councils, and was celebrated as a poet-king. His son Nezahualpilli was famed as a judge and astrologer. Texcoco ruled many towns of the eastern valley.
texcoco.e: [[e:mexica|Mexica]] interference in Texcoco's succession after 1515 divided it, and one faction under Ixtlilxochitl II aided [[e:hernan-cortes|Cortés]], who built his brigantines there in 1521. Its last independent king Cacamatzin died in Spanish custody in 1520.

tanjungpura-kingdom.t: An old kingdom of southwest Borneo, named in Majapahit's records and later continued as the Matan Sultanate until 1950.
tanjungpura-kingdom.o: Tanjungpura on the southwest coast of [[e:borneo|Borneo]], near modern Ketapang, appears in the Javanese Nagarakretagama of 1365 as one of [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit's]] dependencies, and Javanese sources use the name for much of Borneo. Local tradition links its rulers with Javanese princes. Its capital moved several times along the coast and rivers.
tanjungpura-kingdom.r: The kingdom exported diamonds, gold and forest products. Its rulers accepted [[e:islam|Islam]] in the 17th century and the state became known as Matan. Branch courts at Sukadana and Simpang grew up nearby, and the region came under the influence of Banten and later the [[e:dutch|Dutch]].
tanjungpura-kingdom.e: The [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] and then the colonial government gradually reduced the rulers to subordinates. Matan's royal family suffered heavily in the Japanese killings in West [[e:borneo|Borneo]] in 1944, and the state was absorbed into the [[s:indonesia|Republic of Indonesia]] in 1950.

twenty-ninth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: A Delta dynasty from Mendes that kept Egypt independent of Persia in the early 4th century BCE through Greek alliances.
twenty-ninth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Around 399 to 398 BCE Nepherites I, a general from Mendes in the central Delta, overthrew Amyrtaeus of the [[s:twenty-eighth-dynasty-of-egypt|Twenty-eighth Dynasty of Egypt]] and founded a new line. He sent grain and ships to [[s:sparta|Sparta]], then at war with [[e:persia|Persia]], and built at [[e:karnak|Karnak]] and Mendes.
twenty-ninth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The dynasty's strongest king, Hakor (Achoris), ruled for about thirteen years. He allied with Evagoras of [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]] and [[s:athens|Athens]], hired Greek [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] under the Athenian Chabrias and repelled a Persian attack around 385 to 383 BCE. He was an active builder, restoring temples across [[e:egypt|Egypt]]. Rivalry between family branches weakened the throne, with short reigns by Psammuthes and Nepherites II.
twenty-ninth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: In 380 BCE Nectanebo I, a general from Sebennytos, deposed Nepherites II and founded the [[s:thirtieth-dynasty-of-egypt|Thirtieth Dynasty of Egypt]]. The remains of a royal tomb at Mendes, probably that of Nepherites I, have been excavated, and Hakor's building works were often reinscribed by his successors.

toltec-state.t: The Early Postclassic power centred on Tula in Hidalgo, remembered by the Aztecs as the model of civilisation, artistry and legitimate kingship.
toltec-state.o: Tula, or Tollan, grew in the 9th century in the valley of the Tula river in Hidalgo, settled by migrants from the north and from the [[e:valley-of-mexico|Valley of Mexico]]. By about 900 it had become the largest city of central [[s:mexico|Mexico]], with a population of perhaps 40,000 or more.
toltec-state.r: Tula Grande, the ceremonial core, held Pyramid B crowned by colossal stone warrior figures (the Atlanteans), colonnaded halls, ballcourts and a skull rack. Its art stressed military orders, feathered serpents and sacrifice. Obsidian from Pachuca was a key resource. Later Aztec traditions told of the priest-king Ce Acatl Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl and the last ruler Huemac, but these accounts are legendary.
toltec-state.e: Tula was burnt and its rule collapsed around 1150, and its people dispersed. Later dynasties such as [[s:culhuacan|Culhuacan]] and the [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] claimed Toltec descent to legitimise their power, making 'Toltec' a byword for skilled craftsmen.

tu-i-tonga-empire.t: The line of sacred Tongan paramount kings who, from Muʻa on Tongatapu, built a seaborne network of power and prestige reaching Uvea, Samoa and Fiji.
tu-i-tonga-empire.o: Tongan tradition traces the line to ʻAhoʻeitu, son of the sky god Tangaloa and a mortal woman, who became the first Tuʻi [[s:kingdom-of-tonga|Tonga]] around 950. Early rulers lived on Tongatapu, and by the 12th or 13th century the royal centre had moved to Muʻa on the lagoon shore, where the great stone-faced tombs (langi) of later kings still stand.
tu-i-tonga-empire.r: The Tuʻi [[s:kingdom-of-tonga|Tonga]] was a sacred figure, owed the first fruits of the yearly ʻinasi offering. Around 1200 Tuʻitātui is credited with building the Haʻamonga ʻa Maui trilithon. Double-hulled canoes carried chiefs, marriages and tribute across a wide arc, with Tongan influence felt in Uvea, Futuna, parts of Samoa and the Lau islands of Fiji. In the 15th century, after royal assassinations, everyday power passed to a junior line, the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua, and later to the Tuʻi Kanokupolu.
tu-i-tonga-empire.e: Civil wars in the late 18th and early 19th centuries ended with Tāufaʻāhau, the Tuʻi Kanokupolu, uniting the islands as King George Tupou I and founding the [[s:kingdom-of-tonga|Kingdom of Tonga]] in 1845. The last Tuʻi Tonga, Laufilitonga, died in 1865 and the title was not renewed.

twenty-second-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The Libyan pharaohs of Bubastis, founded by Sheshonq I, the biblical Shishak, whose realm gradually split into rival kingdoms.
twenty-second-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Sheshonq I, Great Chief of the Ma and descendant of [[s:meshwesh|Meshwesh]] settlers at Bubastis, succeeded the [[s:twenty-first-dynasty-of-egypt|Twenty-first Dynasty of Egypt]] around 943 BCE. He reunited the country by appointing his sons to key posts, including the high priesthood of [[e:amun|Amun]] at [[s:thebes|Thebes]].
twenty-second-dynasty-of-egypt.r: Sheshonq I campaigned in [[e:palestine|Palestine]] around 925 BCE, recorded on the Bubastite Portal at [[e:karnak|Karnak]] and in the Bible as the attack of Shishak on [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]]. Osorkon I and Osorkon II endowed temples lavishly, and Osorkon II rebuilt at Bubastis. Royal princes held regional commands, so the state became a network of Libyan family fiefs. Under Takelot II, [[s:thebes|Thebes]] rebelled against Prince Osorkon, as his chronicle at Karnak records.
twenty-second-dynasty-of-egypt.e: From about 837 BCE rival kings appeared, including the [[s:twenty-third-dynasty-of-egypt|Twenty-third Dynasty of Egypt]], and the realm fragmented. [[e:piye|Piye's]] invasion around 728 BCE reduced the dynasty to a minor Delta kingship, and its last kings disappeared under the [[s:kushite-empire|Kushite Empire]] around 720 BCE.

taifa-of-beja-and-evora.t: A short-lived state of the Banu Wazir in the Alentejo, one of the regimes that rose on the ruins of Almoravid power in the 1140s.
taifa-of-beja-and-evora.o: In 1144 Sidray ibn [[e:wazir|Wazir]], a commander of a local family, took Beja and Évora in the revolt against the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]]. At first an ally of Ibn Qasi of the [[s:second-taifa-of-mertola|Second Taifa of Mértola]], he soon broke with him, while his relatives held the [[s:second-taifa-of-badajoz|Second Taifa of Badajoz]].
taifa-of-beja-and-evora.r: The territory covered the wheat lands of the Alentejo between the [[e:tagus|Tagus]] and the Algarve, a frontier exposed to raids from the [[s:kingdom-of-portugal|Kingdom of Portugal]]. Sidray ruled as a military strongman and became one of the leading figures of the western revolt.
taifa-of-beja-and-evora.e: Around 1150 Sidray submitted to the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]], who kept him as a governor. Évora was captured for Portugal in 1165 by Gerald the Fearless, and Beja was taken definitively in 1234.

thanjavur-maratha-kingdom.t: A Maratha kingdom in the Tamil Kaveri delta, founded by Shivaji's half-brother and celebrated for the Saraswati Mahal library and Tanjore painting.
thanjavur-maratha-kingdom.o: In 1674 Venkoji (Ekoji I), half-brother of [[e:shivaji|Shivaji]] and a general of the Bijapur sultanate, seized Thanjavur from its Nayak rulers and founded a Bhonsle dynasty there. It thus became a Marathi-speaking court ruling a Tamil land.
thanjavur-maratha-kingdom.r: The Rajas ruled the rich [[e:rice|rice]] lands of the Kaveri delta, surviving pressure from the [[e:mughal-empire|Mughals]], Carnatic Nawabs and Mysore. Serfoji II, whose administration was largely ceded to the British in 1799, expanded the Saraswati Mahal library and patronised Carnatic music, Tanjore painting and [[e:printing-press|printing]].
thanjavur-maratha-kingdom.e: When [[e:shivaji|Shivaji]] II died in 1855 without a male heir, the British annexed Thanjavur under the doctrine of lapse. The palace, library and the painting style it fostered survive in Thanjavur.

trinovantes.t: Essex people whose alliance with Julius Caesar made them Rome's first British treaty partners, and who later rose with Boudica against Camulodunum.
trinovantes.o: The Trinovantes first appear in Caesar's account of 54 BCE, when their prince Mandubracius, whose father had been killed by Cassivellaunus, fled to Caesar in Gaul. Caesar restored him and forbade Cassivellaunus to harm them, making the Trinovantes the earliest British people bound to [[e:rome|Rome]] by agreement.
trinovantes.r: Their land in [[s:kingdom-of-essex|Essex]] and southern Suffolk was rich farmland with close links to the Continent. Rulers such as Addedomarus and Dubnovellaunus issued gold coins, and Camulodunum grew into a vast oppidum defended by long dykes, with burials like the Lexden tumulus holding Roman luxury goods. Around 10 CE the Catuvellaunian king Cunobelinus took Camulodunum and made it his capital.
trinovantes.e: After the Claudian invasion of 43, Camulodunum became the first capital of [[s:roman-britain|Roman Britain]] and from 49 a colony of veterans who seized Trinovantian land. Resentment led the Trinovantes to join Boudica of the [[s:iceni|Iceni]] in 60 or 61, when Camulodunum was burned. Afterwards they formed a civitas in the Roman province.

tangier-international-zone.t: Tangier under joint international administration from 1924 to 1956, a free port famous for banking, smuggling, espionage and expatriate writers.
tangier-international-zone.o: Because of Tangier's strategic position on the [[e:strait-of-gibraltar|Strait of Gibraltar]], [[e:france|France]], [[e:spain|Spain]] and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] agreed at [[e:paris|Paris]] in 1923 that the city and its surroundings would be neither French nor Spanish but internationalised. The statute took effect in 1924; [[e:italy|Italy]] joined in 1928, and other powers including Portugal, [[s:kingdom-of-belgium|Belgium]], the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]] and the [[s:united-states|United States]] took part.
tangier-international-zone.r: A committee of control of foreign consuls and an international legislative assembly governed, while the sultan was represented by a mendoub. Low taxes, free currency exchange and a free port attracted banks, traders, smugglers and spies. [[e:spain|Spain]] occupied the zone during the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]], from 1940 to 1945, after which international rule was restored.
tangier-international-zone.e: After Moroccan independence, an international conference ended the special status in October 1956, and Tangier was reintegrated into the [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Kingdom of Morocco]], keeping a free-port charter for a few years.

taiping-heavenly-kingdom.t: A Christian-inspired rebel state that ruled much of southern China from Nanjing for over a decade, in a civil war that cost perhaps twenty million lives.
taiping-heavenly-kingdom.o: Hong Xiuquan, a Hakka from Guangdong who repeatedly failed the civil service examinations, came to believe from visions and Christian tracts that he was the younger brother of Jesus. His God Worshipping Society gathered followers in Guangxi, and in 1851 he proclaimed the [[e:taiping-rebellion|Taiping]] Heavenly Kingdom. His armies marched north and in 1853 took Nanjing, renamed Tianjing.
taiping-heavenly-kingdom.r: The [[e:taiping-rebellion|Taiping]] banned opium, foot-binding, idolatry and prostitution, segregated men and women in the early years and proposed common ownership of land, though this was hardly applied. Hong governed through 'kings' such as Yang Xiuqing until a bloody purge in 1856. Hong Rengan later proposed Western-style railways and banks.
taiping-heavenly-kingdom.e: Provincial armies such as [[e:zeng-guofan|Zeng Guofan's]] [[e:xiang-army|Xiang Army]] and [[e:li-hongzhang|Li Hongzhang's]] [[e:huai-army|Huai Army]], aided by Western-officered troops, gradually recovered the [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]] valley. Hong Xiuquan died in 1864, and Nanjing fell weeks later. The war devastated the lower Yangtze and weakened the [[s:qing-empire|Qing Empire]] for good.

tiwanaku.t: A highland civilisation near Lake Titicaca whose monumental city and religious art dominated the southern Andes for half a millennium before the Incas.
tiwanaku.o: Tiwanaku began as a village south of Lake Titicaca in present-day [[s:republic-of-bolivia|Bolivia]] in the last centuries BCE and grew into a major ceremonial city by about 500 CE, filling the space left by [[s:pukara|Pukará]]. At 3,850 metres, it is one of the highest cities ever built.
tiwanaku.r: Tiwanaku was ruled by an elite closely tied to religion, centred on monuments such as the Akapana pyramid, the Kalasasaya platform with the Gateway of the Sun, and the Semi-Subterranean Temple. Raised-field farming by the lake, llama caravans and colonies in warmer valleys such as Moquegua supplied the city. Its Staff God imagery spread across the southern [[s:andecavi|Andes]]. At its height the city may have held 20,000 people or more.
tiwanaku.e: Tiwanaku collapsed around 1000 to 1100, probably after a long drought undermined lake-shore agriculture. The region broke up into Aymara kingdoms such as the [[s:lupaca-kingdom|Lupaca Kingdom]] and [[s:colla-kingdom|Colla Kingdom]]. The [[e:inca-empire|Incas]] later regarded Titicaca as their place of origin. Tiwanaku became a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 2000.

taifa-of-valencia.t: A rich taifa on the Valencian huerta, governed by Amirid heirs and later by Toledo, whose fall ended with El Cid's conquest of the city in 1094.
taifa-of-valencia.o: In 1010-1011 the [[e:freedmen|freedmen]] Mubarak and Muzaffar took control of [[e:valencia|Valencia]] as the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]] disintegrated. In 1021 the city recognised Abd [[e:al-aziz|al-Aziz]] ibn Abi [[e:amir|Amir]], a grandson of the regent al-Mansur, whose family ruled until 1065.
taifa-of-valencia.r: [[e:valencia|Valencia]] drew wealth from irrigated [[e:huerta|huerta]] farming, [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:silk|silk]] and its port. Abd [[e:al-aziz|al-Aziz]] (1021-1061) was a capable ruler who also controlled Almería for a time. In 1065 [[e:idris-i-al-mamun|al-Mamun]] of the [[s:taifa-of-toledo|Taifa of Toledo]] annexed the city, and after [[e:toledo|Toledo]] fell in 1085 [[e:alfonso-vi-of-castile|Alfonso VI]] installed the deposed al-Qadir in Valencia as a Castilian client.
taifa-of-valencia.e: In 1092 the qadi Ibn Jahhaf killed al-Qadir and appealed to the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]]. Rodrigo Díaz, El Cid, besieged the city and took it in June 1094, creating the [[s:lordship-of-valencia|Lordship of Valencia]].

ternate-sultanate.t: The clove sultanate of the North Moluccas, which drove out the Portuguese in 1575 and dominated the eastern spice islands for a century.
ternate-sultanate.o: Ternate, a small volcanic island off Halmahera, was one of the few places in the world where [[e:cloves|cloves]] grew. Its kings, part of the Moloku Kie Raha alliance with [[s:tidore-sultanate|Tidore]], Bacan and [[s:jailolo-sultanate|Jailolo]], grew rich supplying Javanese and Malay traders. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Zainal Abidin, who had studied [[e:islam|Islam]] at Giri in [[e:java|Java]], formally adopted Islam in the late 15th century.
ternate-sultanate.r: The Portuguese built a fort on Ternate in 1522. In 1570 they murdered [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Hairun, and his son Babullah besieged the fort until the Portuguese left in 1575. Babullah then claimed authority over 72 islands from [[e:sulawesi|Sulawesi]] to [[s:territory-of-papua|Papua]], and received Francis Drake in 1579. Ternate's power rested on clove revenues and war fleets of kora-kora [[e:galley|galleys]].
ternate-sultanate.e: From 1607 Ternate allied with the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] against [[e:spain|Spain]], but gradually became its [[e:vassal|vassal]], accepting the destruction of clove trees outside Ambon. The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] deposed and exiled [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Muhammad Usman in 1914 after unrest. The sultanate survives today as a cultural institution in North Maluku.

taifa-of-baeza.t: The breakaway realm of the Almohad prince al-Bayyasi, whose alliance with Castile hastened the fall of the upper Guadalquivir.
taifa-of-baeza.o: In 1224, amid a succession crisis in the [[s:almohad-caliphate|Almohad Caliphate]] after the death of [[e:yusuf-ii|Yusuf II]], the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] prince Abd Allah al-Bayyasi, a governor in [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]], proclaimed himself [[e:caliphate|caliph]] at Baeza and sought the support of [[e:ferdinand-iii-of-castile|Ferdinand III of Castile]] against his rivals.
taifa-of-baeza.r: Al-Bayyasi ruled Baeza and nearby towns as a Castilian ally and [[e:vassal|vassal]], handing over castles such as Martos and Andújar in exchange for military help. This open dependence on a Christian king discredited him among Andalusi Muslims.
taifa-of-baeza.e: In 1226 al-Bayyasi was murdered by his own followers near Almodóvar while fleeing [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]]. Baeza soon passed to [[e:ferdinand-iii-of-castile|Ferdinand III]], among the first major towns of the Guadalquivir to fall to the [[s:crown-of-castile|Crown of Castile]].

tashkent-hakimate.t: A short-lived city-state centred on Tashkent, built by Yunus Khoja on the Kazakh trade frontier before Kokand absorbed it.
tashkent-hakimate.o: In the 18th century Tashkent was divided into four quarters under rival leaders and passed under Kazakh and [[e:dzungars|Dzungar]] overlordship. Around 1784 Yunus Khoja, hakim of one quarter, united the city and threw off the authority of the Kazakh khans of the [[s:senior-juz|Senior Juz]].
tashkent-hakimate.r: Yunus Khoja ruled Tashkent as an independent state, extending control over nearby towns and Kazakh pastures and trading with [[e:russia|Russia]], which welcomed the caravans. He built a strong army and fought the [[s:khanate-of-kokand|Khanate of Kokand]], defeating it in 1799 and briefly taking Khujand.
tashkent-hakimate.e: Yunus Khoja died around 1803, and his sons quarrelled. Alim Khan of the [[s:khanate-of-kokand|Khanate of Kokand]] conquered Tashkent in 1808 or 1809, after which it remained a Kokandi city until the Russian conquest of 1865.

tilantongo.t: The most prestigious Mixtec kingdom of the highlands of Oaxaca, seat of the famous ruler Lord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw.
tilantongo.o: Tilantongo, Ñuu Tnoo in Mixtec, emerged as a royal seat in the Mixteca Alta by the 10th century, around 900. Pictorial histories painted on deerskin, such as the Codex Bodley and Codex Zouche-Nuttall, trace its dynasties from that period.
tilantongo.r: Mixtec kingdoms were small city-states ruled by lords and ladies of interlinked noble houses, and Tilantongo was considered the senior line. In the 11th century Lord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw, a lord from Tilantongo, built a wide domain through war and alliance before being sacrificed in 1115. Mixtec artisans were renowned for gold work, turquoise mosaic and painted books.
tilantongo.e: Tilantongo fell under [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] tribute in the late 15th century and came under Spanish rule in the 1520s, when its nobles retained some rights as caciques. Its codices are among the most important surviving pre-Hispanic books.

tartessos.t: A legendary kingdom of the lower Guadalquivir whose silver wealth drew Phoenician and Greek traders, remembered by Herodotus and the Bible.
tartessos.o: Tartessos emerged in the 9th century BCE in the region of Huelva, [[e:seville|Seville]] and Cádiz, where a local [[e:late-bronze-age|Late Bronze Age]] society came into intense contact with Phoenician traders from [[s:gadir|Gadir]]. The [[e:silver|silver]] and [[e:copper|copper]] of the Río Tinto mines fuelled the exchange, and Greek and Biblical sources (as Tarshish) remembered it as a land of fabulous wealth.
tartessos.r: Archaeology shows an elite culture that adopted eastern goods and styles, seen in the gold of the El Carambolo treasure and the palace-sanctuary of Cancho Roano. [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] tells of King Arganthonios, who ruled for decades and welcomed Phocaean [[e:greeks|Greeks]] around 600 BCE. Whether Tartessos was a unified kingdom or a network of chiefdoms is still debated, as is its link to the south-western script.
tartessos.e: Around 500 BCE the Tartessian culture declined, perhaps through falling [[e:silver|silver]] demand, the eclipse of [[s:tyre|Tyre]] and the rise of [[e:carthage|Carthage]]. Its lands passed to the [[s:turdetani|Turdetani]], whom Strabo saw as its heirs, and the name Tartessos became a byword for lost riches.

taifa-of-badajoz.t: The great western taifa of al-Andalus, ruled by the Aftasid dynasty from Badajoz across much of what is now Extremadura and central Portugal.
taifa-of-badajoz.o: After 1009 the freedman Sabur al-Saqlabi took control of the old Lower March around Mérida and [[e:badajoz|Badajoz]]. On his death in 1022 his [[e:vizier|vizier]] Abd Allah ibn al-Aftas, of [[e:berbers|Berber]] descent, seized power and founded the Aftasid dynasty, which soon added [[e:lisbon|Lisbon]], Évora and Santarém.
taifa-of-badajoz.r: The Aftasids governed the largest [[e:taifa|taifa]] in the west, from the Guadiana valley to the [[e:tagus|Tagus]] estuary. Their court was a literary centre: Muhammad al-Muzaffar compiled a vast anthology, and Umar al-Mutawakkil was a noted poet. The state fought [[e:seville|Seville]] over its southern borders and lost Coimbra to Ferdinand I of León in 1064, then paid tribute to [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]].
taifa-of-badajoz.e: In 1093 al-Mutawakkil ceded [[e:lisbon|Lisbon]], Sintra and Santarém to [[e:alfonso-vi-of-castile|Alfonso VI]] in return for protection. The [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] saw this as treason, took [[e:badajoz|Badajoz]] in 1094 and executed him with his sons, ending the dynasty.

thirty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.t: Egypt's brief second period of Persian rule, from Artaxerxes III's reconquest to the arrival of Alexander the Great.
thirty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.o: After failed attempts in 351 BCE, the Persian king [[e:artaxerxes-iii|Artaxerxes III]] invaded [[e:egypt|Egypt]] in 343 BCE, defeating Nectanebo II of the [[s:thirtieth-dynasty-of-egypt|Thirtieth Dynasty of Egypt]] at Pelusium and capturing Memphis. Egypt again became a [[e:satrapy|satrapy]] of the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]], and Manetho counts the Persian kings as the Thirty-first Dynasty.
thirty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.r: Greek writers describe a harsh reconquest, with temple treasures looted and city walls destroyed, though some stories, such as the killing of the Apis bull, may be propaganda. A local rebel, Khababash, briefly held power in the Delta in the late 330s BCE. The [[e:satrapy|satrapy]], ruled from Memphis, had to face unrest while [[e:persia|Persia]] itself suffered the murders of [[e:artaxerxes-iii|Artaxerxes III]] and Arses.
thirty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.e: After the battle of [[e:battle-of-issus|Issus]], the [[e:satrapy|satrap]] Mazaces surrendered [[e:egypt|Egypt]] to [[e:alexander-the-great|Alexander the Great]] without a fight in 332 BCE, and it passed to the [[s:macedonian-empire|Macedonian Empire]] and later the [[s:ptolemaic-empire|Ptolemaic Empire]].

taifa-of-algeciras.t: A Hammudid taifa on the Bay of Algeciras, controlling the crossing of the Strait of Gibraltar until Seville seized it in 1058.
taifa-of-algeciras.o: Algeciras, the main crossing point to [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]], was a Hammudid possession. Around 1035 a branch of the family under Muhammad ibn al-Qasim made the town and its district a separate principality, while his cousins ruled the [[s:taifa-of-malaga|Taifa of Málaga]].
taifa-of-algeciras.r: The state was small but strategic, controlling the port that linked [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]] with [[e:ceuta|Ceuta]] and the [[e:maghreb|Maghreb]]. Its rulers, like the Málaga line, used the caliphal titles of the Hammudids and relied on [[e:berbers|Berber]] troops. Little more is known about its administration.
taifa-of-algeciras.e: Around 1058 al-Mutadid of the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]] besieged Algeciras and forced al-Qasim ibn Muhammad to surrender it. Algeciras was later the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]]' landing place in 1086.

tarhuntassa.t: Tarhuntassa, a Hittite royal city and later a rival appanage kingdom, whose rulers challenged the great kings at Hattusa.
tarhuntassa.o: Around 1280 BCE [[e:muwatalli-ii|Muwatalli II]] moved the Hittite capital, with the gods of [[e:hattusa|Hattusa]], to Tarhuntassa, a city in southern [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]] whose site is still unknown. His son Urhi-Teshub moved the court back, and [[e:hattusili-iii|Hattusili III]] made Tarhuntassa an [[e:appanage|appanage]] kingdom for Muwatalli's other son Kurunta.
tarhuntassa.r: Tarhuntassa ruled the Lower Land towards the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] as a high-ranking [[e:vassal|vassal]]. A treaty between [[e:tudhaliya-iv|Tudhaliya IV]] and Kurunta, on a bronze tablet found at [[e:hattusa|Hattusa]] in 1986, defines its borders and privileges. Seals suggest Kurunta later claimed the title great king.
tarhuntassa.e: Rivalry between Tarhuntassa and [[e:hattusa|Hattusa]] weakened the empire in its last decades. Both collapsed c. 1180 BCE; afterwards a great king Hartapu, known from inscriptions at Kızıldağ, ruled in the region.

tusheet-khanate.t: The central and leading Khalkha khanate of Outer Mongolia, whose khans founded Erdene Zuu monastery and whose family produced the first Jebtsundamba Khutughtu.
tusheet-khanate.o: The Khalkha [[e:mongols|Mongols]] were given by Dayan Khan to his son Geresenje, whose descendants divided them. Abtai, a great-grandson of Dayan Khan, became the leading prince of central Khalkha, met the Third [[e:dalai-lama|Dalai Lama]] in 1586 and received the title Khan; his successors took the title Tüsheet Khan.
tusheet-khanate.r: The khans ruled nomadic subjects along the Orkhon and Tuul valleys through Chinggisid nobles. Abtai Khan founded Erdene Zuu monastery beside the ruins of [[e:karakorum|Karakorum]] around 1585, a centre of Gelug [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] in [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]]. Zanabazar, son of Tüsheet Khan Gombodorj, became the first Jebtsundamba Khutughtu, the head of Mongolian Buddhism, as well as a famous sculptor.
tusheet-khanate.e: Tüsheet Khan Chikhundorj's war with the [[s:zasagt-khanate|Zasagt Khanate]] in 1687 gave the [[e:dzungars|Dzungar]] ruler Galdan a pretext to invade; Khalkha refugees fled south, and in 1691 at Dolon Nor the Khalkha princes submitted to the [[e:kangxi-emperor|Kangxi Emperor]] of the [[s:qing-empire|Qing Empire]], becoming a Qing province.

tavastia.t: Inland Finnish province around the lakes of Häme, brought under Swedish rule by the crusade of Birger Jarl in the mid-13th century.
tavastia.o: Tavastia, or Häme, covers the lake district of southern central [[s:grand-duchy-of-finland|Finland]]. In the late Iron Age its people, the Tavastians, formed one of the main Finnish groups alongside the Finns proper of the south-west and the [[s:karelians|Karelians]] in the east. They are mentioned in Rus' chronicles as the 'Yem', against whom Novgorod campaigned from the 11th century.
tavastia.r: The Tavastians lived from slash-and-burn farming, hunting, fishing and the [[e:fur-trade|fur trade]], which took them far into the northern wilderness. They had no single ruler; local chiefs and kin groups led society. Papal letters of the 1230s complain of Tavastians returning to paganism and attacking Christians.
tavastia.e: A Swedish expedition led by Birger Jarl, known as the Second Swedish [[e:crusade|Crusade]] and traditionally dated 1249, subdued Tavastia and built Häme Castle. The province became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-sweden|Kingdom of Sweden]] and the Diocese of Turku, and remained so until [[s:grand-duchy-of-finland|Finland]] passed to [[e:russia|Russia]] in 1809.

theme-of-sicily.t: Byzantine military province of Sicily, based at Syracuse, which slowly fell to Arab conquest between 827 and 965.
theme-of-sicily.o: [[e:sicily|Sicily]] was part of the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]] after Justinian's reconquest in 535. In the late 7th century it was organised as a theme, a province under a military governor ([[e:strategos|strategos]]) at [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]]. Emperor Constans II had resided at Syracuse from 663 until his murder there in 668.
theme-of-sicily.r: The [[e:strategos|strategos]] commanded the island's forces and also controlled Byzantine Calabria. [[e:sicily|Sicily]] was a rich source of grain and tax revenue, and the [[e:papacy|papacy]] owned large estates there until Leo III confiscated them in the 730s. The island became increasingly Greek-speaking and Greek in its church, receiving monks and refugees from the eastern [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]].
theme-of-sicily.e: In 827 the rebel commander Euphemius invited the [[s:aghlabid-emirate|Aghlabids]] of [[e:ifriqiya|Ifriqiya]], who invaded and took Palermo in 831, [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]] in 878 and Taormina in 902. Rometta, the last Byzantine stronghold, fell in 965, completing the [[s:emirate-of-sicily|Emirate of Sicily]].

terra-mariana.t: Medieval Livonia, the crusader land dedicated to the Virgin Mary that covered most of modern Latvia and Estonia from the 13th century to 1561.
terra-mariana.o: Terra Mariana grew out of the Livonian [[e:crusade|crusade]] led by [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Albert of Riga. In 1207 Albert received his lands as a fief of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]], and [[e:papacy|Pope]] Innocent III dedicated the conquered land to the Virgin Mary, giving it its name. By 1227 the Livonians, Latgalians and Estonians had been conquered.
terra-mariana.r: Terra Mariana was never a single state but a patchwork: the [[s:archbishopric-of-riga|Archbishopric of Riga]], the bishoprics of Dorpat, Ösel-Wiek and Courland, the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]], the Danish [[s:duchy-of-estonia-1219-1346|Duchy of Estonia]] (1219-1346), and powerful towns such as Riga and [[s:reval|Reval]]. A German-speaking elite of clergy, knights and merchants ruled Latvian, Estonian and Liv peasants, and the towns flourished in Hanseatic trade.
terra-mariana.e: The Lutheran [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] spread in the 1520s, and the [[e:livonian-war|Livonian War]], begun by [[e:ivan-iv-of-russia|Ivan IV of Russia]] in 1558, broke the region apart. In 1561 the Treaty of Vilnius dissolved the Order's state, creating the [[s:duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia|Duchy of Courland and Semigallia]] and the [[s:duchy-of-livonia|Duchy of Livonia]] under Poland-[[e:lithuania|Lithuania]], while [[e:sweden|Sweden]] took northern [[s:republic-of-estonia|Estonia]].
terra-mariana.la: Middle Low German, Latin, Latvian, Estonian

twenty-eighth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: A one-king dynasty under Amyrtaeus of Sais, who freed Egypt from Persian rule in 404 BCE.
twenty-eighth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Amyrtaeus, a prince of Sais and probably a grandson of an earlier rebel of the same name, led a revolt against [[s:achaemenid-egypt|Achaemenid Egypt]] when [[e:darius-ii|Darius II]] died in 404 BCE. By about 400 BCE even the Jewish garrison at Elephantine dated its documents by his reign.
twenty-eighth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: Very little is known of his rule. He controlled the Delta and gradually the whole country, and [[e:persia|Persia]], distracted by the revolt of [[e:cyrus-the-younger|Cyrus the Younger]], did not try to recover [[e:egypt|Egypt]].
twenty-eighth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: Around 399 to 398 BCE Amyrtaeus was overthrown by Nepherites I of Mendes, founder of the [[s:twenty-ninth-dynasty-of-egypt|Twenty-ninth Dynasty of Egypt]]; an [[e:aramaic|Aramaic]] [[e:papyrus|papyrus]] suggests he was executed.

tyranny-of-pherae.t: Line of ambitious tyrants in the Thessalian city of Pherae who briefly made Thessaly a great power under Jason before falling to Philip II.
tyranny-of-pherae.o: Pherae, in south-eastern Thessaly near the port of Pagasae, rose against the old aristocratic families of [[s:larissa|Larissa]] and [[s:pharsalus|Pharsalus]]. Around 406 BCE Lycophron of Pherae seized power and tried to dominate all of Thessaly, defeating his rivals in 404 BCE. His successor Jason built a large [[e:mercenary|mercenary]] army and was elected tagos, leader of the Thessalian federation, around 374 BCE.
tyranny-of-pherae.r: The tyrants depended on paid [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]], the port of Pagasae and alliances with outside powers. Jason planned a fleet and even, according to [[e:xenophon|Xenophon]], a campaign against [[e:persia|Persia]], but was assassinated in 370 BCE. Alexander of Pherae (369-358 BCE) was notorious for cruelty and fought [[s:thebes|Thebes]], killing Pelopidas at Cynoscephalae in 364 BCE though losing the battle.
tyranny-of-pherae.e: Alexander was murdered by his wife Thebe and her brothers, who ruled in turn. Their struggle with the [[s:thessalian-league|Thessalian League]] brought in [[e:philip-ii-of-macedon|Philip II of Macedon]], who defeated the Phocian allies of Pherae at the Crocus Field in 352 BCE and expelled the tyrants. Thessaly then came under Macedonian control.

taexali.t: People of north-east Scotland recorded by Ptolemy, who named the headland of Kinnaird Head after them and listed their town Devana.
taexali.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Taexali in the north-east of [[e:scotland|Scotland]], in modern Aberdeenshire, with a headland, Taexalorum Promontorium, usually identified as Kinnaird Head, and a settlement called Devana, perhaps near the Dee or the Don. They grew from local Iron Age farming communities of the lowlands between the Dee and the Deveron.
taexali.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. The region is rich in hillforts, souterrains and recumbent stone circles from earlier ages, and Roman marching camps, such as those at Raedykes and Normandykes, show that Roman armies under Agricola and later Severus passed through their lands. Mixed farming on fertile lowland soils supported a relatively dense population.
taexali.e: The Taexali disappear from the record after Ptolemy. Their territory later formed part of the [[s:kingdom-of-the-picts|Kingdom of the Picts]], whose symbol stones are especially numerous in Aberdeenshire.

trucial-states.t: The British-protected sheikhdoms of the lower Gulf coast, bound by maritime truces from 1820 and united as the UAE in 1971.
trucial-states.o: After expeditions against the [[s:sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah|Qawasim]] of the Sheikhdom of [[e:ras|Ras]] al-Khaimah, [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] imposed the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 on the rulers of the coast. The Perpetual Maritime Truce of 1853 banned warfare at sea, giving the Trucial States, or Trucial Coast, their name, and exclusive agreements in 1892 gave [[e:britain|Britain]] control of their foreign relations.
trucial-states.r: Each sheikh governed his own territory; [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] managed defence and foreign affairs through a political agent, based at [[s:sheikhdom-of-sharjah|Sharjah]] and from 1954 at [[s:sheikhdom-of-dubai|Dubai]]. Members were [[s:sheikhdom-of-abu-dhabi|Abu Dhabi]], Dubai, Sharjah, [[s:sheikhdom-of-ajman|Ajman]], [[s:sheikhdom-of-umm-al-quwain|Umm al-Quwain]], [[s:sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah|Ras al-Khaimah]], later [[s:sheikhdom-of-fujairah|Fujairah]] and briefly [[s:sheikhdom-of-kalba|Kalba]]. A Trucial States Council from 1952 and the Trucial [[e:oman|Oman]] Scouts provided common institutions, and oil from 1962 transformed Abu Dhabi.
trucial-states.e: In 1968 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] announced its withdrawal from east of Suez. After negotiations, six sheikhdoms formed the [[s:united-arab-emirates|United Arab Emirates]] on 2 December 1971, and [[s:sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah|Ras al-Khaimah]] joined in 1972.

tibetan-empire.t: The empire of the Yarlung kings that united the Tibetan plateau, rivalled Tang China for the Silk Road and brought Buddhism and writing to Tibet.
tibetan-empire.o: Clan chiefs of the Yarlung valley, led by Namri Songtsen, united much of central [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]] in the early 7th century. His son Songtsen Gampo made Lhasa his capital, absorbed [[s:zhangzhung|Zhangzhung]] in the west and married princesses from [[e:tang-dynasty|Tang China]] and, by tradition, [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Nepal]], establishing the empire as a major Asian power.
tibetan-empire.r: The emperor (tsenpo) ruled through powerful noble clans and ministers; a [[e:census|census]] and military districts underpinned a formidable cavalry army. Writing in a script based on Indian models is credited to Songtsen Gampo's reign. [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]] conquered the [[s:tuyuhun|Tuyuhun]] in 663, contested the [[e:tarim-basin|Tarim Basin]] with [[e:tang-dynasty|Tang China]], briefly occupied [[e:changan|Chang'an]] in 763 and held Dunhuang. Trisong Detsen made [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] the state religion and founded Samye monastery.
tibetan-empire.e: After the treaty with [[s:later-tang|Tang]] of 821 to 822, recorded on a pillar in Lhasa, court conflict over [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] grew. The emperor Langdarma was assassinated, traditionally in 842, and a succession dispute broke the empire apart, beginning the Era of Fragmentation. Its kings and script remained foundations of Tibetan identity.

tundama.t: A Muisca lordship around modern Duitama whose ruler led the last organised resistance of the Muisca against the Spanish.
tundama.o: Tundama was a territory of the [[s:muisca-confederation|Muisca Confederation]] in the north of the high plateau, around modern Duitama in Boyacá. It was ruled by a chief also called Tundama and stood among the lordships independent of the zaque of the [[s:zacazgo-of-hunza|Zacazgo of Hunza]].
tundama.r: Tundama was a chiefdom of farming communities growing [[e:maize|maize]], [[e:potato|potatoes]] and quinoa around lakes and marshes. Its chiefs allied with neighbouring [[s:iraca|Iraca]] and fought both the zaque and the zipa. Little is known of its internal organisation beyond Spanish accounts of the conquest.
tundama.e: In 1539 the Spanish under Baltasar Maldonado defeated Tundama at the Battle of Bonza after fierce resistance, and the chief was later killed. Duitama became a town in the [[s:new-kingdom-of-granada|New Kingdom of Granada]], and the chief is remembered as a hero of indigenous resistance.

terengganu-sultanate.t: East-coast Malay sultanate founded by a Johor prince, long a tributary of Siam, and today a state of Malaysia.
terengganu-sultanate.o: The Terengganu Inscription Stone of the early 14th century shows [[e:islam|Islam]] there centuries earlier, but the present sultanate was founded in 1708 by Tun Zainal Abidin, a son of the [[s:johor-sultanate|Johor Sultanate]]'s Bendahara family, who became [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Zainal Abidin I. Terengganu later sent the bunga mas, gold and [[e:silver|silver]] trees, as tribute to Siam.
terengganu-sultanate.r: The sultans governed a coastal society of fishermen, boat builders, weavers and traders in [[e:pepper|pepper]] and gold. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Baginda Omar in the 19th century strengthened royal power and encouraged crafts such as brocade weaving. Islamic scholarship flourished, and the court resisted foreign advisers longer than most Malay states.
terengganu-sultanate.e: The Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909 transferred Terengganu to British protection; it accepted a British adviser in 1919 and joined the [[s:unfederated-malay-states|Unfederated Malay States]]. After Japanese and Thai occupation it entered the [[s:federation-of-malaya|Federation of Malaya]] and became a state of [[s:malaysia|Malaysia]], its sultan one of the nine rulers who elect the king.

tuyuhun.t: A kingdom founded by Xianbei migrants on the Qinghai plateau that ruled the Qiang for three centuries and controlled a key trade route until Tibet conquered it.
tuyuhun.o: Tuyuhun, an elder son of the Murong [[s:xianbei|Xianbei]] chief, quarrelled with his brother and led his followers west in the late 3rd century, eventually settling around Qinghai Lake. His grandson Yeyan named the people after him around 329, establishing a state that ruled the local Qiang herders.
tuyuhun.r: The Tuyuhun lived as herders famed for their horses, the Qinghai 'dragon colts', and dwelt in tents, though they built a walled capital at Fuqi west of Qinghai Lake. They controlled the Qinghai route linking the southern Chinese dynasties with [[e:central-asia|Central Asia]], and [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] spread among them. Kualü took the title of [[e:khagan|khagan]] in the 6th century.
tuyuhun.e: [[e:sui-dynasty|Sui]] armies attacked in 609 and the [[s:later-tang|Tang]] general [[e:li-jing|Li Jing]] defeated them in 635, making the kingdom a Tang [[e:vassal|vassal]]. The [[s:tibetan-empire|Tibetan Empire]] conquered it in 663, and the Tang defeat at the Dafei River in 670 ended hopes of restoration. Its last ruler, Murong Nuohebo, fled to Tang territory with his followers.

three-leagues.t: The Alpine republic of the Grisons, a federation of three leagues of communes that ruled the Valtellina and allied with the Swiss for three centuries.
three-leagues.o: The [[s:league-of-gods-house|League of God's House]], the [[s:grey-league|Grey League]] and the [[s:league-of-the-ten-jurisdictions|League of the Ten Jurisdictions]] formed alliances with one another during the 15th century, completed by 1471. Acting together as the Free State of the Three Leagues, they became associates of the [[s:old-swiss-confederacy|Old Swiss Confederacy]] in 1497 and 1498 and fought beside the Swiss in the Swabian War of 1499.
three-leagues.r: [[e:sovereignty|Sovereignty]] lay with the communes, which voted on major decisions, an early form of direct democracy. A common diet met in rotation at Chur, Ilanz and Davos. In 1512 the leagues conquered the Valtellina, Bormio and Chiavenna, which they ruled as subject lands. The Grisons troubles of 1618 to 1639, a civil war entangled with Spanish and French interests, tore the state apart.
three-leagues.e: In 1797 the Valtellina broke away and joined [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] [[s:cisalpine-republic|Cisalpine Republic]]. In 1799 French forces attached the leagues to the [[s:helvetic-republic|Helvetic Republic]], and in 1803 they became the Swiss canton of Graubünden.

tauromenium.t: Greek city on a terrace above the Ionian Sea, founded by survivors of Naxos, famous for its theatre with a view of Etna.
tauromenium.o: After Dionysius I destroyed [[s:naxos|Naxos]] in 403 BCE, its survivors and Sicels settled on Monte Tauro above the old site. In 358 BCE Andromachus, father of the historian Timaeus, refounded the community as a Greek city, Tauromenium.
tauromenium.r: Under Andromachus the city welcomed Timoleon when he landed in [[e:sicily|Sicily]] in 344 BCE to free [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]]. Tauromenium later passed under Agathocles and then Hieron II of Syracuse. Its [[e:theatre|theatre]], built in the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]] and enlarged by the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]], overlooks the coast and Mount Etna. Inscriptions record its magistrates and public finances in detail.
tauromenium.e: When [[e:rome|Rome]] captured [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]] in 212 BCE, Tauromenium came under Roman rule, enjoying the privileged status of an allied city. Octavian later made it a colony after it sided with Sextus Pompeius. It survives as Taormina.

transcaucasian-commissariat.t: The first regional government of Transcaucasia after the October Revolution, which refused to recognise Bolshevik power and paved the way for independence.
transcaucasian-commissariat.o: After the Bolsheviks seized power in [[e:petrograd|Petrograd]] in November 1917, Georgian Mensheviks, Armenian Dashnaks and Azerbaijani Musavatists in Tiflis refused to accept their rule. On 28 November 1917 they formed the Transcaucasian Commissariat as a provisional government for the region, splitting from the [[s:russian-republic|Russian Republic]] in practice.
transcaucasian-commissariat.r: Chaired by the Georgian Menshevik Evgeni Gegechkori, it was a coalition of the three main national parties. It signed the Erzincan [[e:armistice-of-11-november-1918|armistice]] with the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] in December 1917 as the Russian army melted away from the [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]] front, and faced rising ethnic violence and food shortages. In February 1918 it convened the Transcaucasian [[e:sejm|Sejm]] from deputies elected to the Russian Constituent Assembly.
transcaucasian-commissariat.e: Under pressure from Ottoman advances and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, the [[e:sejm|Sejm]] declared independence in April 1918, replacing the Commissariat with the [[s:transcaucasian-democratic-federative-republic|Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic]]. Its brief life marked the first step from Russian rule towards the separate republics of [[s:georgia|Georgia]], [[s:armenia|Armenia]] and [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]].

taifa-of-toledo.t: The central taifa of al-Andalus under the Dhul-Nunid dynasty, famous for its scientists and for its fall to Alfonso VI of Castile in 1085.
taifa-of-toledo.o: [[e:toledo|Toledo]], the old Visigothic capital and frontier city of the Middle March, threw off caliphal rule around 1010. Its notables first chose local leaders, then invited the [[e:berbers|Berber]] Banu Dhi al-Nun, lords of Uclés and Huete, whose Ismail al-Zafir established the dynasty in the 1030s.
taifa-of-toledo.r: [[e:idris-i-al-mamun|Al-Mamun]] (1043-1075) made [[e:toledo|Toledo]] one of the most powerful [[e:taifa|taifas]], conquering [[e:valencia|Valencia]] in 1065 and [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]] in 1075. His court sponsored science: the astronomer al-Zarqali produced the Toledan Tables, and Ibn Wafid laid out botanical gardens. A large Mozarab Christian and Jewish population lived in the city, and tribute was paid to León and [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]].
taifa-of-toledo.e: [[e:idris-i-al-mamun|Al-Mamun's]] grandson al-Qadir, unpopular and dependent on [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]], surrendered [[e:toledo|Toledo]] to [[e:alfonso-vi-of-castile|Alfonso VI]] on 25 May 1085. The loss shocked [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]] and led the remaining [[e:taifa|taifas]] to call in the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]]. Toledo became a centre of translation from Arabic into [[e:latin|Latin]].

tomis.t: Milesian colony on the western Black Sea coast, later famous as the place of Ovid's exile and today the Romanian port of Constanta.
tomis.o: Tomis was settled by [[e:greeks|Greeks]] from [[s:miletus|Miletus]] on a peninsula of the western [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] shore, in a region the Greeks called [[s:scythia|Scythia]] Minor, probably in the 6th century BCE. It began as a trading post beside the older colony of [[s:histria|Histria]] and grew slowly into a city with its own territory, trading with the [[s:getae|Getae]] and other Thracian peoples of the Dobruja hinterland.
tomis.r: Like other West Pontic colonies, Tomis was a self-governing polis with a council and assembly and close ties to its mother city [[s:miletus|Miletus]]. Its economy rested on grain, fish and exchange with inland peoples, whose raids were a constant threat. It struck its own coins in the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]], and under Roman rule it headed the league (koinon) of the West Pontic Greek cities.
tomis.e: The Roman general Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus brought the West Pontic cities under Roman control in 72-71 BCE. The poet Ovid, exiled there by Augustus in 8 CE, complained of its cold and its barbarous neighbours. Tomis later became the capital of the Roman province of [[s:scythia|Scythia]] and is today Constanta.

tagalog-republic.t: Revolutionary government of the Katipunan under Andres Bonifacio, the first organised Filipino state against Spanish rule.
tagalog-republic.o: The Katipunan, a [[e:secret-society|secret society]] founded in [[e:manila|Manila]] in 1892, launched the Philippine Revolution in August 1896. Its supreme leader, Andres Bonifacio, styled the movement a nation, the Haring Bayang Katagalugan, using Tagalog in a broad sense to mean all the native people of the islands.
tagalog-republic.r: Government rested on the Katipunan hierarchy, with a supreme council headed by Bonifacio as president and committees in towns. It had its own flag, seals and rituals of initiation, and its ideals of liberty and brotherhood were set out in writings by Emilio Jacinto. Fighting was concentrated in Cavite, [[e:manila|Manila]] and surrounding provinces.
tagalog-republic.e: Rivalry between Katipunan factions in Cavite came to a head at the Tejeros Convention of March 1897, which elected Emilio Aguinaldo president. Bonifacio rejected the result, was arrested and executed in May 1897. Aguinaldo's forces went on to found the [[s:republic-of-biak-na-bato|Republic of Biak-na-Bato]].

tunjur-kingdom.t: A mysterious kingdom that ruled Darfur and Wadai before the Keira sultans, remembered through traditions and the ruins of Ain Farah.
tunjur-kingdom.o: The origins of the [[e:tunjur|Tunjur]] are obscure and debated: traditions variously claim Arab, Nubian or local descent. By around 1400 they had replaced the earlier [[s:daju-kingdom|Daju kingdom]] as the dominant power in the Jebel Marra and northern [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]] region, and their rule extended west into what became [[e:wadai-empire|Wadai]].
tunjur-kingdom.r: Almost nothing is documented about [[e:tunjur|Tunjur]] government. The red-brick ruins of Ain Farah, including what may be a mosque and earlier church-like structures, are attributed to them, suggesting links with the [[e:nile|Nile]] valley. They are traditionally credited with introducing [[e:islam|Islam]] to [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]] and controlling caravan trade between the Nile and the [[e:chad|Chad]] basin.
tunjur-kingdom.e: In the 17th century [[e:tunjur|Tunjur]] rule was overthrown in [[e:wadai-empire|Wadai]] by Abd al-Karim, founder of the [[s:wadai-empire|Wadai Empire]], and in [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]] by the [[e:keira-dynasty|Keira dynasty]] of the [[s:darfur-sultanate|Darfur Sultanate]]. The Tunjur survived as a people in Darfur and [[e:chad|Chad]].

tsangpa-dynasty.t: The kings of Tsang who briefly united central Tibet in the early 17th century, before falling to the Gelug school and its Mongol allies in 1642.
tsangpa-dynasty.o: Zhingshak Tseten Dorje, an official of the [[s:rinpungpa|Rinpungpa]] at Samdrubtse (Shigatse), rebelled and by 1565 had replaced his masters as ruler of Tsang. His descendants expanded steadily, and in 1618 Karma Phuntsok Namgyal conquered Ü, ending the last [[s:phagmodrupa-dynasty|Phagmodrupa dynasty]] influence and ruling most of central [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]].
tsangpa-dynasty.r: The Tsangpa kings, who ruled from the fortress of Samdrubtse, were patrons of the Karma Kagyu and Jonang schools and hostile to the Gelug, whose monasteries had powerful Mongol supporters. They issued a law code and tried to centralise the country. Wars with the new state of [[s:zhabdrung-bhutan|Zhabdrung Bhutan]] to the south were costly.
tsangpa-dynasty.e: Gelug leaders invited the [[s:khoshut-khanate|Khoshut]] [[e:mongols|Mongols]] under Güshi Khan, who defeated the Tsangpa allies and in 1642 took Samdrubtse; the last king, Karma Tenkyong Wangpo, was executed. Güshi Khan handed authority to the Fifth [[e:dalai-lama|Dalai Lama]], founding the [[s:ganden-phodrang|Ganden Phodrang]] and the Khoshut Khanate.

thembu-kingdom.t: The Thembu paramountcy of the eastern Cape, a senior Nguni royal house whose descendants include Nelson Mandela.
thembu-kingdom.o: The Thembu were among the [[e:nguni|Nguni-speaking]] peoples settled between the Kei and Mthatha rivers, with royal genealogies reaching back many generations before written records. By the 18th century the Thembu paramount was recognised as holding senior rank among the southern Nguni, alongside the Xhosa and Mpondo royal houses.
thembu-kingdom.r: The king ruled through councils of chiefs and counsellors, with [[e:cattle|cattle]] as the measure of wealth and the basis of marriage alliances. Royal houses were divided into the Great House and the Right-Hand House, a pattern shared with the [[s:xhosa-kingdom|Xhosa Kingdom]]. Under Ngubengcuka in the early 19th century the Thembu sought alliances with the [[s:cape-colony|Cape Colony]] against raiders displaced by the wars of that era.
thembu-kingdom.e: Missionary influence and Cape magistrates spread through Thembuland from the mid-19th century, and after conflicts under Ngangelizwe the territory was annexed to the [[s:cape-colony|Cape Colony]] by 1885. The royal house continues, and Nelson Mandela was a descendant of Ngubengcuka.

turgesh-khaganate.t: A Turkic khaganate of the Chu and Ili valleys that led the steppe resistance to the Arab conquest of Transoxiana.
turgesh-khaganate.o: The Turgesh were one of the tribes of the [[s:western-turkic-khaganate|On Oq]] confederation of the [[e:western-turkic-khaganate|Western Turkic Khaganate]]. Their chief Wuzhile took Suyab around 699 as the Western Turkic state collapsed, and his son Saqal succeeded him before being killed by the [[s:second-turkic-khaganate|Second Turkic Khaganate]] in 711.
turgesh-khaganate.r: Under Suluk, who rose around 716, the Turgesh became a major power, allied with the [[s:tibetan-empire|Tibetan Empire]] and the Sogdian princes against the [[e:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyads]]. Arab sources call him Abu Muzahim, 'the one who jostles'. He routed an Arab army on the 'Day of Thirst' in 724, inflicted heavy losses on another at the Battle of the Defile in 731, and sustained a court at Suyab and Talas on Sogdian trade.
turgesh-khaganate.e: Suluk was murdered in 738 after a defeat at Kharistan, and civil war between the Yellow and Black Turgesh factions followed. [[e:tang-dynasty|Tang China]] intervened, and by 766 the [[s:karluk-yabgu|Karluk Yabgu]] had taken Suyab and the Turgesh lands.

tres-zapotes.t: A long-lived Olmec and Epi-Olmec centre in the Tuxtla region, whose Stela C bears one of the oldest Long Count calendar dates in the Americas.
tres-zapotes.o: Tres Zapotes grew on the western edge of the Tuxtla Mountains in southern Veracruz around 900 BCE, during the Olmec period. Unlike [[s:san-lorenzo|San Lorenzo]] and [[s:la-venta|La Venta]], it survived the wider Olmec decline after 400 BCE and continued as a regional centre for centuries.
tres-zapotes.r: The site has two colossal heads from its Olmec phase. In the following Epi-Olmec period, power seems to have been shared among several groups whose plazas were spread across the settlement rather than held by a single ruler. Stela C carries a Long Count date equivalent to 32 BCE, and the site illuminates the transition from Olmec to later writing and calendar traditions.
tres-zapotes.e: Tres Zapotes declined by about 300 CE, though the area remained inhabited. Its inscriptions are key evidence that the Long Count and early writing developed in the Gulf Coast before their flowering among the Maya.

turdetani.t: The heirs of Tartessos in the lower Guadalquivir, praised by Strabo as the most cultured of the Iberians, with written laws in verse.
turdetani.o: The Turdetani appear after the decline of [[s:tartessos|Tartessos]] around 500 BCE, occupying the same rich lower Guadalquivir valley in modern [[e:seville|Seville]], Huelva and Cádiz. Ancient writers saw them as the successors of the Tartessians.
turdetani.r: They lived in many towns ruled by local kings and aristocracies. Strabo called them the wisest of the Iberians, said to have laws in verse and an ancient literature. Their land produced grain, [[e:olive-oil|olive oil]] and wine and held the [[e:silver|silver]] and [[e:copper|copper]] of the Sierra Morena and Río Tinto. They were heavily influenced by [[s:gadir|Gadir]] and the other Phoenician cities, and later by [[e:carthage|Carthage]].
turdetani.e: Under [[s:barcid-iberia|Barcid Iberia]] they supplied [[e:silver|silver]] and troops. After 206 BCE [[e:rome|Rome]] took control; Culchas, who ruled 28 towns, first aided Rome and then joined the revolt of 197 BCE. Defeated, they became the core of [[s:hispania-ulterior|Hispania Ulterior]] and later [[s:hispania-baetica|Baetica]].
