tuwana.t: Tuwana, a Neo-Hittite kingdom around Tyana in southern Cappadocia, whose king Warpalawa is carved on the Ivriz rock relief.
tuwana.o: Tuwana lay in the plain south of modern Niğde, in the region the [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyrians]] called [[s:tabal|Tabal]]. It emerged as a separate kingdom in the 8th century BCE around the old city of Tuwanuwa, later Greek Tyana.
tuwana.r: King Warpalawa ruled with Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions and is shown on the rock relief at Ivriz before the storm god Tarhunza, who holds grapes and ears of wheat, symbols of the land's fertility. He paid tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] in 738 BCE.
tuwana.e: After Warpalawa, Tuwana fades from the record during the rise of [[s:kingdom-of-phrygia|Phrygia]] and the Cimmerian invasions of the 7th century BCE. Tyana remained an important city in [[s:kingdom-of-cappadocia|Cappadocia]].

transitional-government-of-ethiopia.t: The interim government formed by the victorious EPRDF in 1991, which accepted Eritrean independence and introduced Ethiopia's ethnic federal system.
transitional-government-of-ethiopia.o: After the fall of the [[s:peoples-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia]] in May 1991, the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) convened a conference in July 1991 that adopted a Transitional Charter. Meles Zenawi, leader of the [[s:tigray|Tigray]] People's Liberation Front, became president of the Transitional Government.
transitional-government-of-ethiopia.r: The charter recognised the right of [[e:ethiopia|Ethiopia's]] nations and peoples to self-determination, up to secession, and the country was reorganised into regions largely along ethnic lines. The [[e:oromo|Oromo]] Liberation Front initially joined the government but withdrew in 1992. The new government accepted the independence referendum in [[s:state-of-eritrea|Eritrea]], which led to the creation of the State of [[e:eritrea|Eritrea]] in 1993. The economy was opened to markets.
transitional-government-of-ethiopia.e: A constituent assembly adopted a new constitution in December 1994, and after elections in 1995 the [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia]] was proclaimed, with Meles Zenawi as prime minister.

trust-territory-of-the-pacific-islands.t: A United Nations strategic trust territory in Micronesia administered by the United States, scene of nuclear tests, which split into four modern states.
trust-territory-of-the-pacific-islands.o: American forces captured [[e:japan|Japan's]] [[s:south-seas-mandate|South Seas Mandate]] during the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]]. In 1947 the [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] placed the Marshall, Caroline and Northern Mariana Islands under American administration as the only strategic trust territory, giving the [[s:united-states|United States]] the right to fortify them.
trust-territory-of-the-pacific-islands.r: The US Navy governed until 1951, then the [[e:departement|Department]] of the Interior, with headquarters moved to Saipan in 1962. From 1946 to 1958 the [[s:united-states|United States]] conducted 67 nuclear tests at Bikini and Enewetak, including the Castle Bravo explosion of 1954, which contaminated Rongelap. Development was neglected until the 1960s. A Congress of Micronesia, created in 1965, became the forum for negotiating the islands' future.
trust-territory-of-the-pacific-islands.e: The districts chose separate paths: the Northern Mariana Islands became a US commonwealth, while the Marshall Islands and the Federated States of Micronesia gained independence in free association in 1986. Palau's compact took effect in 1994, ending the trusteeship.

tay-son-dynasty.t: A peasant-rooted Vietnamese dynasty of three brothers who toppled both the Nguyen and Trinh lords and routed a Qing invasion at Dong Da in 1789.
tay-son-dynasty.o: In 1771 the brothers Nguyen Nhac, Nguyen Hue and Nguyen Lu of Tay Son village in Binh Dinh rose against the [[s:nguyen-lords|Nguyen lords]], attracting peasants, merchants and highland peoples with promises to redistribute wealth. In 1778 Nguyen Nhac proclaimed himself emperor at Do Ban, near the old [[e:cham|Cham]] capital of Vijaya.
tay-son-dynasty.r: Nguyen Hue defeated a Siamese army at Rach Gam-Xoai Mut in 1785 and overthrew the [[s:trinh-lords|Trinh lords]] in 1786. When the Qing invaded to restore the [[s:later-le-dynasty|Later Le dynasty]], he declared himself emperor Quang Trung and destroyed them at Dong Da in 1789. He promoted chu nom as an official script, reformed land registers and planned a capital at Phu Xuan.
tay-son-dynasty.e: Quang Trung's death in 1792 left the throne to his young son Canh Thinh, and the brothers' realms quarrelled. Nguyen Anh, backed by French volunteers and southern supporters, captured Phu Xuan in 1801 and Thang Long in 1802, founding the [[s:nguyen-dynasty|Nguyen dynasty]].

taifa-of-tavira.t: A brief independent lordship at Tavira in the eastern Algarve, one of the many local regimes of the 1140s revolt against the Almoravids.
taifa-of-tavira.o: In 1145, as the Muridun revolt led by Ibn Qasi spread through the Algarve and Almoravid authority collapsed, local leaders took control of Tavira, a port on the Gilão river, and held it independently.
taifa-of-tavira.r: Known only from brief mentions in Arabic chronicles, the state consisted of the town and its coastal district, with fishing, salt and trade along the Algarve coast. Its rulers were drawn into the shifting alliances among the [[s:second-taifa-of-mertola|Second Taifa of Mértola]], the [[s:second-taifa-of-silves|Second Taifa of Silves]] and the [[s:taifa-of-beja-and-evora|Taifa of Beja and Évora]].
taifa-of-tavira.e: Around 1150 Tavira accepted [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] rule along with the rest of the western Algarve. It was conquered by the [[s:kingdom-of-portugal|Kingdom of Portugal]] in 1242.

tepanec-empire.t: The dominant power of the Valley of Mexico before the Aztecs, ruled from Azcapotzalco, which the Mexica overthrew in 1428.
tepanec-empire.o: The [[e:tepanecs|Tepanecs]] settled on the western shore of [[e:lake-texcoco|Lake Texcoco]], with their capital at [[e:azcapotzalco|Azcapotzalco]], in the 13th century. Under [[e:tezozomoc|Tezozomoc]], who ruled from about 1367 to 1426, they expanded across the [[e:valley-of-mexico|Valley of Mexico]], using the [[e:mexica|Mexica]] of [[e:tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] and [[s:tlatelolco|Tlatelolco]] as tributary allies and [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]].
tepanec-empire.r: The [[e:tepanecs|Tepanec]] realm was a tributary state: subject altepetl kept their rulers but owed tribute and military service. [[e:tezozomoc|Tezozomoc]] conquered [[s:culhuacan|Culhuacan]], Xaltocan and in 1418 [[s:texcoco|Texcoco]], and placed relatives on several thrones, including [[s:tlatelolco|Tlatelolco]]. [[e:azcapotzalco|Azcapotzalco]] was a large city and an important slave market.
tepanec-empire.e: After [[e:tezozomoc|Tezozomoc's]] death, his son [[e:maxtla|Maxtla]] seized power and turned on the [[e:mexica|Mexica]]. [[e:tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] under [[e:itzcoatl|Itzcoatl]], allied with [[e:nezahualcoyotl|Nezahualcoyotl]] of [[s:texcoco|Texcoco]] and [[s:tlacopan|Tlacopan]], destroyed [[e:azcapotzalco|Azcapotzalco]] in 1428. The victors formed the [[e:aztec-empire|Triple Alliance]] of the [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]].

trapezus.t: Trapezus, a Greek colony on the south-eastern Black Sea coast that became Trebizond, where Xenophon's Ten Thousand reached the sea.
trapezus.o: Colonists from [[s:sinope|Sinope]] founded Trapezus on a table-shaped headland, from which its name comes, traditionally in 756 BCE. It controlled a harbour and the route inland to the Armenian highlands, among the Colchian and Pontic peoples of the coast.
trapezus.r: Trapezus was a Greek city governed by its citizens, paying tribute to [[s:sinope|Sinope]] and later recognising Persian overlordship. In 400 BCE the Ten Thousand Greek [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] described by [[e:xenophon|Xenophon]] arrived here after their march, and the city hosted them for a month. It traded [[e:timber|timber]], metals and hazelnuts.
trapezus.e: Trapezus was absorbed by the [[s:kingdom-of-pontus|Kingdom of Pontus]] in the 2nd century BCE and passed to the Roman world after [[e:pompey|Pompey]] defeated Mithridates VI in 63 BCE. It later became [[s:empire-of-trebizond|Trebizond]], capital of the Empire of Trebizond.

texuandri.t: People of the sandy heathlands of the Kempen and Brabant whose land, Toxandria, became the first Roman foothold of the Salian Franks.
texuandri.o: Known chiefly from Pliny, who lists them among the peoples of Gallia Belgica, the Texuandri lived in the region between the Meuse and the Scheldt, in the modern Belgian Kempen and [[e:dutch|Dutch]] North [[s:duchy-of-brabant|Brabant]]. They may have been a subdivision of the [[s:tungri|Tungri]].
texuandri.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Their land was thinly settled, with scattered farms on poor sandy soils, and inscriptions record Texuandrian soldiers serving in the Roman army, including in [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]].
texuandri.e: In the 3rd and 4th centuries the area was disrupted by Frankish raids. In 358 the future emperor Julian accepted the submission of the [[s:salian-franks|Salian Franks]], who had already settled in Toxandria, and let them stay as Roman allies, and the region became the cradle of Frankish power in the [[e:low-countries|Low Countries]].

taifa-of-albarracin.t: A mountain taifa in the Sierra de Albarracín ruled for nearly a century by the Berber Banu Razin, one of the longest-lived small states of al-Andalus.
taifa-of-albarracin.o: The Banu Razin, a [[e:berbers|Berber]] family of the Hawwara who had held the district of al-Sahla since the 8th century, declared independence around 1012 under Hudhayl ibn Khalaf ibn Razin as the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]] broke apart.
taifa-of-albarracin.r: Albarracín was a rugged frontier lordship of castles, pasture and [[e:timber|timber]] between the [[e:taifa|taifas]] of [[e:toledo|Toledo]], [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]] and [[e:valencia|Valencia]]. Its survival owed much to the long reign of Abd al-Malik ibn Hudhayl (c. 1045-1103), who paid tribute to [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]] and to El Cid when necessary. The town's walls and its compact old quarter date in part from this period.
taifa-of-albarracin.e: The [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] annexed Albarracín in 1104, soon after the death of Abd al-Malik. In 1170 the Navarrese noble Pedro Ruiz de Azagra received the town, founding the semi-independent [[s:lordship-of-albarracin|Lordship of Albarracín]].

thebes.t: Leading city of Boeotia whose generals Epaminondas and Pelopidas broke Spartan power at Leuctra in 371 BCE and briefly made Thebes the first power of Greece.
thebes.o: Thebes grew from the Mycenaean palace town on the [[s:mycenaean-kingdom-of-thebes|Kadmeia]], surviving the collapse c. 1200 BCE. In the Archaic period it became the chief city of Boeotia and, from the late 6th century BCE, the head of the [[s:boeotian-league|Boeotian League]], competing with Orchomenus and [[s:plataea|Plataea]] for leadership.
thebes.r: Thebes was ruled mostly by landowning oligarchies. It sided with [[e:persia|Persia]] in 480 BCE and was punished after [[s:plataea|Plataea]], then backed [[s:sparta|Sparta]] in the [[e:peloponnesian-war|Peloponnesian War]]. [[e:sparta|Sparta]] seized the [[s:mycenaean-kingdom-of-thebes|Kadmeia]] in 382 BCE, but Pelopidas liberated it in 379 BCE. With the Sacred Band and Epaminondas's deep [[e:phalanx|phalanx]], Thebes won at Leuctra, freed [[s:messene|Messenia]] and founded [[s:megalopolis|Megalopolis]].
thebes.e: After Epaminondas died at [[s:mantinea|Mantinea]] in 362 BCE, Theban power faded. Defeated with [[s:athens|Athens]] at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, Thebes revolted and was razed by Alexander in 335 BCE. [[e:cassander|Cassander]] rebuilt it in 316 BCE, and it passed under [[e:rome|Rome]] in 146 BCE.

tabal.t: Tabal, a group of Neo-Hittite kingdoms on the central Anatolian plateau, caught between Assyria, Phrygia and Urartu.
tabal.o: Tabal emerged after the Hittite collapse in the region of later [[s:kingdom-of-cappadocia|Cappadocia]], south of the Kızılırmak. From the 9th century BCE Assyrian texts mention the kings of Tabal, sometimes as many as twenty-four, but at times one ruler dominated, such as Tuwati and his son Wasusarma.
tabal.r: Its rulers wrote Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions, often styling themselves great king, and drew wealth from [[e:silver|silver]] mines and the trade routes of the plateau. The [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyrians]] demanded tribute and tried to secure loyalty through marriage alliances with local kings.
tabal.e: [[e:sargon-ii|Sargon II]] gave his daughter to Ambaris of Bit-Burutash, but deposed him in 713 BCE for plotting with [[s:kingdom-of-phrygia|Phrygia]] and [[s:kingdom-of-urartu|Urartu]]. Tabal was later overrun by Cimmerian invaders in the 7th century BCE and disappears around 650 BCE.

tori-fatehpur-state.t: A small Bundela jagir of Bundelkhand, one of the minor estates recognised by the British in the early 19th century.
tori-fatehpur-state.o: Tori Fatehpur was a small estate in [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]], held by a Bundela or allied [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] family. The register dates it to 1690, but its founding is known mainly from local tradition.
tori-fatehpur-state.r: The jagirdar ruled a handful of villages. After the British established supremacy in [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]], the estate was recognised by sanad and supervised through the Bundelkhand Agency of Central [[e:india|India]]. Little else is recorded.
tori-fatehpur-state.e: Tori Fatehpur joined [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] in 1948 and Uttar Pradesh in 1950. Its lands lie in [[s:jhansi-state|Jhansi]] district.

tanganyika-territory.t: The British-ruled mandate that replaced German East Africa on the mainland of Tanzania and became independent under Julius Nyerere in 1961.
tanganyika-territory.o: British forces conquered most of [[s:german-east-africa|German East Africa]] in the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]]. In 1920 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] set up a civil administration, and in 1922 the [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] confirmed [[s:tanganyika|Tanganyika]] as a British mandate, with its capital at Dar es Salaam. After the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]] it became a UN trust territory.
tanganyika-territory.r: Governor Donald Cameron introduced [[e:indirect-rule|indirect rule]] through chiefs and native authorities from 1925. The economy rested on sisal, [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] and [[e:cotton|cotton]], with settler estates in the north. After 1945 the [[e:groundnut|Groundnut]] Scheme, a vast plan to grow [[e:peanut|peanuts]], collapsed at great cost. [[e:swahili|Swahili]] spread as a common language, aiding national politics. TANU, founded in 1954 by Julius Nyerere, won the elections of 1958 to 1960.
tanganyika-territory.e: [[s:tanganyika|Tanganyika]] became independent on 9 December 1961 under Nyerere and a republic a year later. In 1964 it united with [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]] to form [[s:tanzania|Tanzania]].

tidore-sultanate.t: The clove sultanate of the North Moluccas, rival of Ternate and ally of Spain, which claimed authority over much of western New Guinea.
tidore-sultanate.o: Tidore, a volcanic island just south of [[s:ternate-sultanate|Ternate]], was one of the four Moluccan kingdoms known as the Moloku Kie Raha. Its rulers adopted [[e:islam|Islam]] in the late 15th century. In 1521 the surviving ships of Ferdinand Magellan's expedition loaded [[e:cloves|cloves]] at Tidore, beginning a long alliance with [[e:spain|Spain]] against Ternate and the Portuguese.
tidore-sultanate.r: Tidore's wealth came from [[e:cloves|cloves]], and its sultans claimed overlordship of southern Halmahera, the Raja Ampat islands and coasts of New [[e:guinea|Guinea]], which sent tribute. Under [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Saifuddin in the late 17th century it accepted the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]]. Prince Nuku led a long revolt from 1780 and, with British help, briefly restored independence in 1801.
tidore-sultanate.e: Tidore became a [[e:dutch|Dutch]] dependency in the 19th century. After [[e:indonesian-independence|Indonesian independence]] [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Zainal Abidin Syah supported [[e:indonesia|Indonesia's]] claim to West New [[e:guinea|Guinea]] and became its first governor. The sultanate survives as a cultural institution.

tripolitania.t: The late Roman and Byzantine province of western Libya, named after its three cities of Leptis Magna, Oea and Sabratha.
tripolitania.o: Around 303 [[e:diocletian|Diocletian]] separated the eastern part of [[s:africa-proconsularis|Africa Proconsularis]] to form the province of Tripolitania, the 'land of three cities': [[s:leptis-magna|Leptis Magna]], Oea ([[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]]) and Sabratha. Its capital was [[e:leptis-magna|Leptis Magna]], and the province stretched from the Gulf of Gabès to the Gulf of Sirte.
tripolitania.r: The coastal cities lived from [[e:olive-oil|olive oil]], trade and the [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] to the [[s:sultanate-of-fezzan|Fezzan]], while the hinterland was guarded by the frontier zone of the limes Tripolitanus, with fortified farms (gsur) in the wadis. Raids by the [[s:austuriani|Austuriani]] in the 360s, and the corruption of the military count Romanus, are described by Ammianus Marcellinus. Cities shrank as the economy declined.
tripolitania.e: The [[s:vandal-kingdom|Vandal Kingdom]] took the province in 455, and the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]] recovered it in 533, rebuilding walls at Leptis and Sabratha. After wars with the [[s:laguatan|Laguatan]], Arab forces under [[e:amr-ibn-al-as|Amr ibn al-As]] took [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]] in 643 for the [[s:rashidun-caliphate|Rashidun Caliphate]].

takeda-clan-domain.t: The mountain domain of the Takeda of Kai, whose lord Takeda Shingen was one of the most feared commanders of Japan's Sengoku era.
takeda-clan-domain.o: Takeda Nobutora unified the province of Kai after years of fighting local rivals and in 1519 founded a new seat at Tsutsujigasaki, around which the town of Kofu grew. In 1541 his son Harunobu, later known as Shingen, exiled him and took over.
takeda-clan-domain.r: Shingen conquered Shinano and parts of Suruga, Kozuke and Totomi, fighting Uesugi Kenshin five times at Kawanakajima. He built flood-control dykes, the Shingen-zutsumi, developed gold mines and issued a house code. His cavalry and organised [[e:vassal|vassal]] bands made Kai a military power, and he crushed [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] at Mikatagahara in 1573.
takeda-clan-domain.e: Shingen died in 1573. His son Katsuyori lost much of his army to Oda and Tokugawa [[e:musket|musketeers]] at Nagashino in 1575; in 1582 their forces invaded, [[e:vassal|vassals]] defected, and Katsuyori killed himself at Tenmokuzan.

taifa-of-crevillent.t: A small Muslim lordship near Elche whose ra'is ruled under Christian overlords for some 75 years after the fall of Murcia.
taifa-of-crevillent.o: Around 1243, when the [[s:third-taifa-of-murcia|Third Taifa of Murcia]] accepted Castilian overlordship by the Treaty of Alcaraz, the Banu Hudayr family kept control of Crevillent and its district as autonomous Muslim lords, or ra'is.
taifa-of-crevillent.r: Known only from scattered documents, the lordship was a Muslim enclave of irrigated farmland under Christian protection, first of the [[s:crown-of-castile|Crown of Castile]] and, after the Treaty of Torrellas of 1304, of the [[s:crown-of-aragon|Crown of Aragon]]. It survived the Mudéjar revolt of 1264-1266 and kept contacts with the [[s:emirate-of-granada|Emirate of Granada]].
taifa-of-crevillent.e: Around 1318 the last ra'is left for [[e:granada|Granada]], and Crevillent was absorbed into the [[s:kingdom-of-valencia|Kingdom of Valencia]]. Its Muslim population remained as Mudéjares until the expulsion of the [[e:moriscos|Moriscos]] in 1609.

third-taifa-of-malaga.t: Málaga under its qadi Ibn Hassun, who ruled the city independently after the Almoravid collapse until the Almohads forced him out.
third-taifa-of-malaga.o: In 1145, as Andalusi cities expelled their Almoravid garrisons, the people of Málaga accepted the authority of their qadi, Abu al-Hakam ibn Hassun, a member of a local family of jurists.
third-taifa-of-malaga.r: Like other [[e:qadi|qadis]] of the second [[e:taifa|taifa]] period, Ibn Hassun ruled on the strength of his religious office and local support. He governed a prosperous port, but had little military power and faced pressure from Almoravid loyalists, from the [[s:taifa-of-jaen|Taifa of Jaén]] and from the advancing [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]].
third-taifa-of-malaga.e: In 1153 the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]] took Málaga, and Ibn Hassun is reported to have killed himself rather than be captured. The city remained under Almohad and then Nasrid rule until 1487.

turks-and-caicos-islands.t: Low-lying islands southeast of the Bahamas, once a centre of salt raking, now a British Overseas Territory dependent on tourism and finance.
turks-and-caicos-islands.o: Bermudian salt rakers worked the Turks Islands from the 1680s, and Loyalists from the American colonies planted [[e:cotton|cotton]] on the Caicos after 1783. The islands were administered from the [[s:bahamas|Bahamas]] from 1799, but salt merchants on Grand Turk resented Nassau's taxes. In 1848 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] made them a separate colony with their own president and council under the oversight of [[e:jamaica|Jamaica's]] governor.
turks-and-caicos-islands.r: The economy rested almost entirely on salt, raked from shallow pans by enslaved and then free labourers and exported to [[e:north-america|North America]]. The tiny colony struggled to pay its way, and in 1873 it was annexed to [[s:jamaica|Jamaica]] as a dependency, with a commissioner at Cockburn Town on Grand Turk. A US missile tracking station later operated on Grand Turk, and John Glenn landed nearby in 1962.
turks-and-caicos-islands.e: When [[s:jamaica|Jamaica]] became independent in 1962, the islands became a separate crown colony, sharing the Bahamas' governor until 1973. They remain a British Overseas Territory; [[e:london|London]] suspended self-government from 2009 to 2012 after corruption findings. Tourism on Providenciales is now the main industry.

talysh-khanate.t: A Caspian khanate in the subtropical lowlands and forests of Talysh, divided between Russia and Persia in 1828.
talysh-khanate.o: Around 1747, after [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah's]] death, Jamal al-Din Khan, called Qara Khan, made the Talysh district an independent khanate, with its capital first at Astara and then Lankaran on the Caspian shore. His family claimed descent from the [[e:safavid-empire|Safavids]]. The district had earlier been governed for the shahs by local Talysh chiefs.
talysh-khanate.r: The khans ruled Talysh-speaking and Azerbaijani villages in fertile lowlands and forested mountains, producing [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:silk|silk]] and fish for Caspian trade. Their small state survived by balancing the [[s:quba-khanate|Quba Khanate]], [[s:qajar-iran|Qajar Iran]] and [[e:russia|Russia]]. Mir Mustafa Khan, who ruled from 1786, sought Russian protection against the [[e:qajar-dynasty|Qajars]].
talysh-khanate.e: Russian forces stormed Lankaran in 1812, and the Treaty of Gulistan in 1813 confirmed Russian protection. After Persian reoccupation in 1826, the Treaty of Turkmenchay in 1828 split Talysh along the Astara river, and the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] annexed the northern part.

tairona.t: Chiefdoms of Colombia's Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta that built stone-terraced towns such as the Ciudad Perdida and whose descendants still live in the mountains.
tairona.o: Settlement in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta and its [[e:caribbean|Caribbean]] coast developed from around 200 CE, and the Tairona style, with stone architecture, emerged by about 1000 CE. Communities built towns on mountain ridges with terraces, stairways and paved paths.
tairona.r: The Tairona were organised in independent chiefdoms and towns linked by alliances, with priests called mamas holding great authority. Teyuna, known as the Ciudad Perdida or Lost City, had some 170 stone terraces and a network of paved roads. Farming of [[e:maize|maize]], [[e:cassava|cassava]] and fruit on terraces sustained dense populations. Their goldsmiths made fine pendants and nose ornaments in tumbaga, a gold-[[e:copper|copper]] alloy.
tairona.e: Spanish contact began after the foundation of Santa Marta in 1525. The Tairona resisted for decades until a major revolt was crushed around 1600, after which towns such as Teyuna were abandoned. Their descendants, the Kogi, Arhuaco, Wiwa and Kankuamo peoples, still live in the Sierra.

tuscarora-nation.t: An Iroquoian people of North Carolina who, after defeat in the Tuscarora War, moved north to become the sixth nation of the Iroquois Confederacy.
tuscarora-nation.o: The Tuscarora lived on the coastal plain of North [[s:province-of-carolina|Carolina]] along the Roanoke, Tar and Neuse rivers, an Iroquoian-speaking people among Algonquian and Siouan neighbours. Their language and traditions point to an ancient kinship with the [[s:iroquois-confederacy|Haudenosaunee]] to the north. By the 17th century they formed several groups of towns, trading deerskins with English traders from [[e:virginia|Virginia]].
tuscarora-nation.r: Towns were led by their own chiefs, with the southern towns under Hancock and the northern under Tom Blount by 1711. Colonial traders cheated them, slave raiders seized their people, and settlers at New Bern encroached on their land. In 1711 Hancock's towns attacked the settlements and executed the surveyor John Lawson, beginning the Tuscarora War. Colonial forces with Yamasee allies destroyed their stronghold of Neoheroka in 1713.
tuscarora-nation.e: Most Tuscarora moved north and around 1722 were adopted as the sixth nation of the [[s:iroquois-confederacy|Iroquois Confederacy]]. Many sided with the Americans in the Revolution. Today the Tuscarora Nation lives near Lewiston, [[e:new-york|New York]], and at Six Nations of the Grand River in Ontario.

taurida-soviet-socialist-republic.t: A Bolshevik republic in the Crimea in spring 1918, ended within weeks by a German advance and a Crimean Tatar revolt.
taurida-soviet-socialist-republic.o: After the Bolsheviks crushed the [[s:crimean-peoples-republic|Crimean People's Republic]] in January 1918, they proclaimed the Soviet Socialist Republic of Taurida in March 1918 at Simferopol, covering the [[e:crimea|Crimea]] and the neighbouring mainland districts. Anton Slutsky became chairman of its council of people's commissars.
taurida-soviet-socialist-republic.r: The republic was dominated by Bolsheviks and radical sailors from Sevastopol, and its brief rule was marked by requisitions and mass killings of officers and property owners. It nationalised land and property but had little real administration, and it faced hostility from the Crimean [[e:tatars|Tatars]].
taurida-soviet-socialist-republic.e: In April 1918 German troops entered the [[e:crimea|Crimea]], and Crimean [[e:tatars|Tatars]] rose in revolt. Slutsky and other leaders were captured near Alushta and shot. The Germans then set up the [[s:crimean-regional-government|Crimean Regional Government]].

thera.t: Dorian island city on volcanic Santorini, best known as the founder of Cyrene in Libya and for some of the earliest Greek inscriptions.
thera.o: After the [[e:bronze-age|Bronze Age]] eruption destroyed the Minoan town of Akrotiri, Santorini was resettled by Dorians from Laconia in the early Iron Age, led by tradition by Theras. Their town grew on the ridge of Mesa Vouno, on the south-east of the island.
thera.r: Thera was an aristocratic community with Spartan customs, and its rock-cut inscriptions of the 7th century BCE are among the oldest Greek writing. On Delphi's advice, Therans sent settlers under Battus to found [[s:kingdom-of-cyrene|Cyrene]] in [[e:libya|Libya]] c. 631 BCE, as recorded in a later foundation decree. The island paid tribute to [[s:athens|Athens]] in the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]] from the 420s BCE.
thera.e: In the 3rd century BCE Thera became a Ptolemaic naval base, with a garrison and [[e:gymnasium|gymnasium]]. It passed under Roman control by 146 BCE, and its ancient city on Mesa Vouno remained inhabited into Byzantine times.
thera.re: Greek religion; cult of Apollo Karneios

tokugawa-clan-domain.t: The domain built by Tokugawa Ieyasu from his small home province of Mikawa into the largest holding in Japan, the springboard of the Tokugawa shogunate.
tokugawa-clan-domain.o: Matsudaira Motoyasu, later [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]], spent his youth as a hostage of the Imagawa. After Imagawa Yoshimoto's death at Okehazama in 1560 he returned to Okazaki, broke with the Imagawa and allied with [[e:oda-nobunaga|Oda Nobunaga]] in 1562. In 1566 he took the name Tokugawa.
tokugawa-clan-domain.r: [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Ieyasu]] unified Mikawa, crushing an Ikko uprising, and took Totomi, moving to Hamamatsu in 1570. He survived defeat by Takeda Shingen at Mikatagahara in 1573 and gained Suruga, Kai and part of Shinano after 1582. He fought [[e:toyotomi-hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] to a draw at Komaki and Nagakute in 1584, then became his leading [[e:vassal|vassal]], administering through loyal hereditary retainers.
tokugawa-clan-domain.e: In 1590 Hideyoshi transferred [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Ieyasu]] to the former Later Hojo lands in the Kanto, where he made Edo his capital. Victory at [[e:battle-of-sekigahara|Sekigahara]] in 1600 and appointment as [[e:shogun|shogun]] in 1603 turned the domain into the [[e:tokugawa-shogunate|Tokugawa shogunate]].

taifa-of-malaga.t: The Hammudid taifa of Málaga, ruled by a Berberised Arab dynasty that claimed the caliphate of al-Andalus after the Umayyads fell.
taifa-of-malaga.o: The Hammudids, descendants of the [[s:idrisid-dynasty|Idrisids]] of [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]], had briefly held the [[e:caliphate|caliphate]] in [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]] from 1016. Driven from the capital, they made Málaga their base around 1026, when Yahya ibn Ali al-Mutali established his court there while still claiming the title of caliph.
taifa-of-malaga.r: The Hammudids led the [[e:berbers|Berber]] party in the fitna and were recognised as [[e:caliphate|caliphs]] by several Berber [[e:taifa|taifas]], including Ronda and Carmona. Their state, spanning Málaga and at times Algeciras and [[e:ceuta|Ceuta]], was weakened by succession quarrels, and real power often lay with Berber commanders and the [[s:zirid-emirate|Zirids]] of [[e:granada|Granada]].
taifa-of-malaga.e: In 1057 Badis of the [[s:taifa-of-granada|Taifa of Granada]] annexed Málaga, ending the Hammudid line in [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]]. The city was later briefly independent again as the [[s:second-taifa-of-malaga|Second Taifa of Málaga]] under a Zirid prince.

tovata-confederacy.t: A confederation of eastern Fiji built by the Tongan prince Enele Maʻafu, the main rival to Cakobau's power before Fiji was united.
tovata-confederacy.o: Enele Maʻafu, a kinsman of George Tupou I of the [[s:kingdom-of-tonga|Kingdom of Tonga]], came to Fiji in 1847 to oversee the Tongans living there. Through warfare and alliances he became the dominant power in the Lau Islands and parts of Vanua Levu. In 1867 he and the chiefs of Lau, Cakaudrove and Bua formed the Confederation of Lau, known as Tovata, with Lomaloma on Vanua Balavu as its seat.
tovata-confederacy.r: Tovata adopted a written constitution with a council of chiefs and Maʻafu as its leading figure. It promoted [[e:christianity|Christianity]] of the Wesleyan kind, which Tongans had brought to eastern Fiji, and drew revenue from the trade in copra and [[e:cotton|cotton]] with European planters and merchants. Its rivalry with the [[s:kingdom-of-bau|Kingdom of Bau]] under Cakobau shaped Fijian politics.
tovata-confederacy.e: In 1871 Maʻafu agreed to join Cakobau's new [[s:kingdom-of-fiji|Kingdom of Fiji]] and became its [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]] for Lau, ending Tovata. He signed the cession of Fiji to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 1874 and was recognised as Tui Lau, a title that survives.

taifa-of-santa-maria-del-algarve.t: A small taifa at Santa María, today's Faro, ruled by the Arab Banu Harun in the far south of present-day Portugal.
taifa-of-santa-maria-del-algarve.o: Around 1018 Said ibn Harun, of a local Arab family, made himself independent in the coastal town of Santa María de Harun, the later Faro, and its district in the eastern Algarve as caliphal authority disappeared.
taifa-of-santa-maria-del-algarve.r: The state was a small coastal principality of fishing, salt pans and dry farming, with figs, almonds and olives. Its rulers recognised the Hammudid [[e:caliphate|caliphs]] for a time and later sought to balance between the [[s:taifa-of-silves|Taifa of Silves]] and [[e:seville|Seville]]. Little else is recorded about its government.
taifa-of-santa-maria-del-algarve.e: Around 1051 the last ruler, Muhammad ibn Said, surrendered his town to al-Mutadid of the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]]. The town's name later gave rise to Faro, and the Algarve fell to Portugal in 1249.

taurini.t: Alpine people of the upper Po whose chief town Hannibal stormed in 218 BCE and whose name lives on in Turin.
taurini.o: The Taurini lived at the foot of the western [[e:alps|Alps]] where the Dora Riparia meets the Po. Ancient writers called them Ligurian or Celtic; they were probably a Ligurian people with strong Celtic influence. Little is known of their early history.
taurini.r: They are known only from Greek and Roman writers. Their chief town, called Taurasia by Appian, controlled routes from the Alpine passes into the Po plain. In 218 BCE they were at war with the [[s:insubres|Insubres]].
taurini.e: After crossing the [[e:alps|Alps]] in 218 BCE, [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]] took Taurasia in three days when its people refused his alliance, and massacred the defenders. The region later came under [[e:rome|Rome]], and Augustus founded the colony of Augusta Taurinorum on or near the site, the origin of Turin.

tarquinii.t: Etruscan city famed for its painted tombs and remembered by Rome as the home of the Tarquin dynasty.
tarquinii.o: Tarquinii, Etruscan Tarchna, grew on a plateau above the Marta valley near the coast, one of the earliest and largest Villanovan centres of Etruria. In legend it was founded by Tarchon, and the haruspex Tages, who revealed Etruscan religious lore, appeared in its fields. Its port at Gravisca welcomed Greek traders from the 6th century BCE.
tarquinii.r: Aristocratic families dominated the city and are commemorated in the painted chamber tombs of the Monterozzi necropolis, more than 200 of them, showing banquets, dancers, athletes and later underworld scenes. Its magistrates bore the title zilath, and the Spurinna family's elogia record their deeds. Roman tradition said Demaratus of [[s:corinth|Corinth]] settled here and his son became [[e:rome|Rome's]] king Tarquinius Priscus.
tarquinii.e: Tarquinii fought [[e:rome|Rome]] in the 4th century BCE, notoriously sacrificing 307 Roman prisoners in 358 BCE. After further wars it made peace and became a Roman ally around 281 BCE, and later a municipium. Its painted tombs are a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

tsardom-of-russia.t: Russia under its first tsars, from Ivan the Terrible to Peter the Great, which expanded from the Volga to the Pacific.
tsardom-of-russia.o: In January 1547 [[e:ivan-iv-of-russia|Ivan IV]], grand prince of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]], was crowned tsar, a title derived from Caesar that claimed equality with emperors. He conquered the [[s:khanate-of-kazan|Khanate of Kazan]] in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556, opening the [[e:volga|Volga]] to Russian control.
tsardom-of-russia.r: The tsar ruled as an autocrat with the boyar council, the [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox Church]] and a growing service nobility. Ivan's reign brought the [[e:livonian-war|Livonian War]] and the terror of the oprichnina. After the Rurikid line died out in 1598 the Time of Troubles followed, with Polish troops in [[e:moscow|Moscow]], until Michael [[e:russian-empire|Romanov]] was elected in 1613. The law code of 1649 bound peasants as serfs, and explorers reached the Pacific by 1639.
tsardom-of-russia.e: [[e:peter-the-great|Peter I]] modernised the army and state, founded [[e:saint-petersburg|Saint Petersburg]] in 1703 and defeated [[e:sweden|Sweden]] in the [[e:great-northern-war|Great Northern War]]. After the [[e:treaty-of-nystad|Treaty of Nystad]] in 1721 he took the title of emperor, and the tsardom became the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]].

tsu-domain.t: The domain of the Todo family in Ise and Iga, founded by the master castle builder Todo Takatora and famous for switching sides in 1868.
tsu-domain.o: Todo Takatora, who had served many lords before attaching himself to [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]], was transferred from Iyo to Iga and part of Ise in 1608. He rebuilt Tsu castle and Iga Ueno castle and laid out Tsu as a castle town on the road to the Ise shrines.
tsu-domain.r: The domain, eventually some 323,000 koku, was held by Takatora's descendants throughout the [[e:edo-period|Edo period]]. Takatora was trusted by the [[e:shogun|shoguns]] as a builder of castles, including work on Edo and Osaka. Tsu benefited from the pilgrim traffic to Ise, while Iga, administered from Ueno, kept its own traditions.
tsu-domain.e: At the battle of Toba-Fushimi in 1868 Tsu troops, stationed to block the imperial forces, instead turned their guns on the [[e:shogun|shogunate]]'s army, contributing to its defeat. After abolition in 1871 the domain became part of Mie Prefecture.

theodosia.t: Milesian port in south-eastern Crimea that exported grain until it was conquered by the Bosporan Kingdom in the 4th century BCE.
theodosia.o: Theodosia was founded by settlers from [[s:miletus|Miletus]] in the 6th century BCE on a bay of the south-eastern Crimean coast, at modern Feodosia. Its good harbour and fertile hinterland made it an important outlet for grain grown by local peoples.
theodosia.r: Theodosia lived from exporting grain, fish and hides to the [[e:aegean|Aegean]], especially [[s:athens|Athens]]. It long resisted absorption by the neighbouring [[s:bosporan-kingdom|Bosporan Kingdom]], with help from [[s:heraclea-pontica|Heraclea Pontica]]. The Bosporan ruler Satyrus I died while besieging it in 389 BCE.
theodosia.e: Leucon I of the [[s:bosporan-kingdom|Bosporan Kingdom]] captured Theodosia, probably c. 355 BCE, and developed its harbour for the grain trade with [[s:athens|Athens]]. It remained a Bosporan city and centuries later became the Genoese port of [[s:kingdom-of-kaffa|Kaffa]].

templar-cyprus.t: Brief rule of Cyprus by the Knights Templar after they bought the island from Richard the Lionheart, ended by a Cypriot revolt within a year.
templar-cyprus.o: Having conquered [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]] from Isaac Komnenos in 1191, [[e:richard-i-of-england|Richard I]] had no use for governing it during the [[e:third-crusade|Third Crusade]]. He sold the island to the Knights Templar, then led by Grand Master Robert de Sable, for 100,000 bezants, of which 40,000 were paid in advance.
templar-cyprus.r: The order sent only a small force, said to number about twenty knights and some soldiers, under Armand Bouchart to govern from Nicosia. They raised heavy taxes to pay the purchase price, and their harsh rule quickly angered the Greek population, who had already suffered under Isaac.
templar-cyprus.e: At Easter 1192 the Cypriots rose and besieged the Templars in Nicosia. The knights broke out, killing many townspeople, but realised they could not hold the island. They returned it to Richard, who sold it to [[e:guy-of-lusignan|Guy of Lusignan]], founder of the [[s:kingdom-of-cyprus|Kingdom of Cyprus]].

taifa-of-cordoba.t: The former caliphal capital governed as a council-led republic by the Jahwarid family after the caliphate was formally abolished in 1031.
taifa-of-cordoba.o: In 1031 the notables of [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]], exhausted by two decades of civil war, deposed the last Umayyad [[e:caliphate|caliph]], Hisham III, and abolished the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]]. The [[e:vizier|vizier]] Abu al-Hazm ibn Jahwar became head of a government that ruled through a council of leading citizens.
taifa-of-cordoba.r: The Jahwarids presented themselves as administrators rather than kings. Abu al-Hazm restored order and finances, avoided wars and maintained the city's markets and scholarship, though [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]] had lost much of its population and grandeur. The poet Ibn Zaydun served the regime before falling out with it.
taifa-of-cordoba.e: Abd al-Malik ibn Jahwar's rule ended when al-Mutamid of the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]] took [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]] in 1070. [[e:toledo|Toledo]] held it from 1075 until [[e:seville|Seville]] recovered it in 1078. The city later rose again as the [[s:second-taifa-of-cordoba|Second Taifa of Córdoba]].

treveri.t: Powerful people of the Moselle, famed for their cavalry, whose land became the site of Trier, a Roman imperial capital.
treveri.o: The Treveri lived along the Moselle in modern [[s:county-of-luxembourg|Luxembourg]] and Rhineland-Palatinate. They were counted among the [[s:belgae-britain|Belgae]], though [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] says they claimed Germanic descent. Their great oppidum on the Titelberg in Luxembourg was a centre of minting and trade.
treveri.r: Caesar calls their cavalry the best in Gaul. Their nobility split between Indutiomarus, leader of the anti-Roman party, and his son-in-law Cingetorix, who backed Caesar.
treveri.e: Indutiomarus led a revolt in 54 BCE and was killed; Labienus defeated the Treveri in 53 BCE. Around 16 BCE the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] founded Augusta Treverorum ([[e:trier|Trier]]), which became the capital of the [[s:gallic-empire|Gallic Empire]] and of the western [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]] under Constantine.

tokushima-domain.t: The domain of the Hachisuka family in Awa on Shikoku, which grew rich on indigo and gave Japan the Awa Odori dance festival.
tokushima-domain.o: After [[e:toyotomi-hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] conquered Shikoku in 1585, he granted Awa province to his retainer Hachisuka Iemasa, who built Tokushima castle. His son Yoshishige fought for [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] in 1600 and in 1615 the island of Awaji was added, bringing the domain to about 257,000 koku.
tokushima-domain.r: Hachisuka lords ruled for the whole [[e:edo-period|Edo period]]. The domain promoted [[e:indigo|indigo]] cultivation on the Yoshino river plain and controlled its sale, making Awa indigo famous across [[e:japan|Japan]], while salt pans also brought revenue. The Awa Odori summer dance, traditionally linked to the castle's completion, became the domain's signature festival, and puppet [[e:theatre|theatre]] flourished.
tokushima-domain.e: The domain supported the new government in the [[e:meiji-restoration|Meiji Restoration]]. A violent dispute with the Inada family of Awaji in 1870 led to Awaji's transfer, and after abolition in 1871 Awa became Tokushima Prefecture.

tagaung-kingdom.t: The legendary first kingdom of the Burmese chronicles, placed at Tagaung on the upper Irrawaddy and claimed as the ancestral seat of Burmese kingship.
tagaung-kingdom.o: Burmese chronicles, compiled many centuries later, say that Abhiraja, a prince of the [[s:sakya-regime|Sakya]] clan of the Buddha, migrated from [[e:india|India]] and founded Tagaung on the east bank of the Irrawaddy, traditionally dated to the 9th century BCE. Archaeology at the site shows a walled settlement of the early first millennium CE, associated with Pyu-style culture, but nothing confirms the chronicle dates.
tagaung-kingdom.r: Almost nothing reliable is known about its government. The chronicles give a long list of kings descended from Abhiraja and say the realm was overrun by raiders from the north, after which a branch of the royal line moved south to found [[s:sri-ksetra-kingdom|Sri Ksetra]]. Excavated brick walls, burial urns and pottery point to a modest urban centre linked to the Pyu world.
tagaung-kingdom.e: The chronicle account ends with Tagaung's fall and the migration of its princes, a story that later Burmese dynasties used to connect themselves to the Buddha's family. Tagaung survived as a town, and its place in royal genealogy gave it lasting symbolic weight in the [[s:ava-kingdom|Ava Kingdom]] and [[s:konbaung-dynasty|Konbaung dynasty]].

tabasaran-maysumate.t: A small principality of the Tabasaran people in southern Dagestan, in the mountains behind Derbent, ruled by hereditary maysums.
tabasaran-maysumate.o: Tabasaran, a mountainous district west of Derbent, was home to the Tabasaran people, Muslims since the early Islamic centuries. By the 16th century a hereditary ruler with the title maysum governed part of it from Khuchni, while another part was ruled by a qadi; the origins of the dynasty are obscure.
tabasaran-maysumate.r: The maysums ruled villages of farmers and herders through local nobles and customary law, and the district was known for its carpets. Tabasaran was a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]] for much of this period and was drawn into the struggles between the khans of Derbent and Quba, the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] and [[e:russia|Russia]].
tabasaran-maysumate.e: The [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] established a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1806 and annexed Tabasaran in 1813, recognised in the Treaty of Gulistan with [[e:persia|Persia]]. Its lands were later absorbed into Russian administrative districts of [[e:dagestan|Dagestan]].

tibur.t: Latin city above the falls of the Aniene, a member of the Latin League that kept its independence as a Roman ally after 338 BCE.
tibur.o: Tibur, modern Tivoli, stood on a ridge where the Aniene river drops from the hills into the plain east of [[e:rome|Rome]]. Legend claimed Greek founders, three Argive brothers including Tiburtus. Settlement goes back to the early Iron Age, and by the 6th century BCE it was one of the stronger [[e:latin|Latin]] towns.
tibur.r: Tibur controlled the routes from [[e:rome|Rome]] into the central Apennines and quarried travertine. Its great sanctuary of Hercules Victor drew traders and pilgrims. As a member of the [[s:latin-league|Latin League]] it often acted independently of Rome, and in the 360s and 350s BCE it allied with the [[e:gauls|Gauls]] against Rome.
tibur.e: Tibur fought on the [[e:latin|Latin]] side in the Latin War of 340–338 BCE and lost territory, but unlike most Latin towns it kept independence as a Roman ally until citizenship came after the Social War. It became a resort for Roman aristocrats and the site of Hadrian's Villa.

tsardom-of-vidin.t: Western Bulgarian realm of Ivan Sratsimir on the Danube, which split from Tarnovo in 1356 and was the last Bulgarian state to fall to the Ottomans.
tsardom-of-vidin.o: [[e:tsar|Tsar]] Ivan Alexander of the [[s:second-bulgarian-empire|Second Bulgarian Empire]] made his younger son Ivan Shishman heir and gave his eldest, Ivan Sratsimir, the north-western region around Vidin. By 1356 Sratsimir ruled there as a separate tsar, and the two Bulgarian realms became rivals.
tsardom-of-vidin.r: Sratsimir ruled from Vidin's Baba Vida fortress over lands along the [[e:danube|Danube]], minting his own coins and placing his church under the Patriarch of [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] rather than Tarnovo. In 1365 Louis I of [[e:hungary|Hungary]] seized Vidin and held it for four years, trying to convert the population to [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]], until Wallachian and Bulgarian forces restored Sratsimir. Afterwards he became an Ottoman [[e:vassal|vassal]].
tsardom-of-vidin.e: In 1396 Sratsimir opened Vidin to the crusaders of Sigismund of [[e:hungary|Hungary]]. After their defeat at Nicopolis, [[e:bayezid-i|Sultan Bayezid I]] took Vidin and Sratsimir was captured, ending Bulgarian independence until 1878.

third-taifa-of-murcia.t: The realm of Ibn Hud, who briefly united al-Andalus against the Almohads, and of his heirs, who ended as Castilian vassals in Murcia.
third-taifa-of-murcia.o: In 1228 Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Hud, claiming descent from the Hudids of [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]], rose against the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]] in the Ricote valley. He recognised the Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliph]], took the title al-Mutawakkil, and within months most of [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]], including [[e:seville|Seville]], [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]] and [[e:granada|Granada]], accepted his rule.
third-taifa-of-murcia.r: Ibn Hud's popularity rested on rejecting [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] doctrine and promising relief from taxes, but his armies lost to León at Alange in 1230 and [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]] fell to [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]] in 1236. He was murdered in Almería in 1238, and his realm shrank to [[e:murcia|Murcia]]. By the Treaty of Alcaraz of 1243 Murcia became a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] of the [[s:crown-of-castile|Crown of Castile]].
third-taifa-of-murcia.e: The Mudéjar revolt of 1264 drew a Castilian and Aragonese response: James I of [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]] took [[e:murcia|Murcia]] in 1266 for [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]], and the territory became the [[s:kingdom-of-murcia|Kingdom of Murcia]].

taifa-of-arcos.t: A small Berber-ruled taifa centred on the clifftop town of Arcos de la Frontera, one of several absorbed by the expanding Abbadids of Seville.
taifa-of-arcos.o: During the fitna after 1009, [[e:berbers|Berber]] troops who had served the [[e:caliphate|caliphs]] settled in the hill towns of western [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]]. Around 1011 the Banu Khizrun, a [[e:zanata-berbers|Zanata]] Berber family, made Arcos their seat and ruled it as an independent principality.
taifa-of-arcos.r: Arcos was a fortified town controlling the Guadalete valley and routes between [[e:seville|Seville]], Jerez and the Strait. Like the other small [[e:berbers|Berber]] [[e:taifa|taifas]] of the region, it relied on its walls and on alliances with the Hammudids and the [[s:taifa-of-ronda|Taifa of Ronda]] against Seville. Only the outline of its rulers' succession is known.
taifa-of-arcos.e: The Abbadid ruler al-Mutadid of the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]] annexed Arcos in the 1050s or 1060s as he swept up the [[e:berbers|Berber]] principalities of the south-west. [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]] took the town in the 13th century.

tetrarchy-of-galilee-and-peraea.t: Herod Antipas's tetrarchy in Galilee and east of the Jordan, the political setting of the ministries of John the Baptist and Jesus.
tetrarchy-of-galilee-and-peraea.o: After the death of Herod the Great in 4 BCE, Augustus gave his son Herod Antipas two separate territories: [[e:galilee|Galilee]], west of the [[e:sea-of-galilee|Sea of Galilee]], and Peraea, a strip east of the [[s:hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan|Jordan]]. Antipas first rebuilt Sepphoris, wrecked in the unrest after his father's death, as his seat.
tetrarchy-of-galilee-and-peraea.r: Antipas ruled as a Roman client and largely respected Jewish sensibilities, minting coins without images. Around 19 CE he founded Tiberias on the lake shore, named after the emperor, and moved his capital there. The Gospels and Josephus record that he imprisoned and executed John the Baptist, and Luke says Jesus was sent to him during his trial. Fishing, farming and [[e:olive-oil|olive oil]] sustained the economy.
tetrarchy-of-galilee-and-peraea.e: His divorce of a daughter of the Nabataean king Aretas IV to marry Herodias led to a war he lost in 36. Accused of conspiracy by his nephew Agrippa, he was deposed by Caligula in 39 and exiled to Gaul. His lands passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-herod-agrippa|Kingdom of Herod Agrippa]].

transcaucasian-sfsr.t: The Soviet federation of Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan from 1922 to 1936, a founding member of the USSR.
transcaucasian-sfsr.o: In March 1922 the Soviet republics of [[s:georgia|Georgia]], [[s:armenia|Armenia]] and [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]] were joined in a union, which in December 1922 became the Transcaucasian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic with its capital at Tiflis. On 30 December 1922 it was one of the four founding republics of the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]].
transcaucasian-sfsr.r: The federation was driven by [[e:moscow|Moscow's]] wish to control the region's economy, railways and borders and to damp national rivalries. Georgian communists who opposed it lost out to Stalin and Ordzhonikidze in the so-called Georgian Affair. It shared a single government, while the three republics kept their own institutions. Lavrentiy Beria led its Communist Party from 1932.
transcaucasian-sfsr.e: Under the 1936 Soviet constitution the federation was dissolved, and the [[s:georgian-ssr|Georgian SSR]], [[s:armenian-ssr|Armenian SSR]] and [[s:azerbaijan-ssr|Azerbaijan SSR]] became separate union republics of the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]]. Each of the three later became independent within its Soviet borders in 1991.

tahirid-sultanate.t: The last Sunni dynasty of medieval Yemen, successors of the Rasulids, swept away by the Mamluk and Ottoman invasions.
tahirid-sultanate.o: The Banu Tahir were a family from the Rada'a and Juban region who served the [[s:rasulid-dynasty|Rasulid dynasty]]. As Rasulid rule collapsed in the 1440s, the brothers Ali and [[e:amir|Amir]] ibn Tahir seized Aden and Zabid and by 1454 had made themselves sultans of lowland and southern [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]].
tahirid-sultanate.r: The [[s:tahirid-dynasty|Tahirids]] ruled from Rada'a, Juban, Ta'izz and Zabid and inherited the Rasulid tax system and Aden's trade, though with less wealth. They were [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] patrons of learning; [[e:sultan|Sultan]] [[e:amir|Amir]] ibn Abd al-Wahhab built the Amiriya [[e:madrasa|Madrasa]] at Rada'a, completed in 1504, with exceptional painted interiors. They fought the Zaydi [[e:imam|imams]] for the highlands and Sanaa.
tahirid-sultanate.e: In 1515 a [[s:mamluk-sultanate|Mamluk Sultanate]] fleet arrived to fight the Portuguese and turned on the [[s:tahirid-dynasty|Tahirids]]. [[e:amir|Amir]] was killed in 1517, the year the [[e:mamluk|Mamluks]] fell to the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]]. Remnants held out in Aden until 1538, when [[s:yemen-eyalet|Yemen Eyalet]] began.

tonina.t: A warlike Maya kingdom in the Ocosingo valley of Chiapas that captured a king of Palenque and recorded the last known Long Count date of the Classic era.
tonina.o: Toniná, anciently Popo', was built on a terraced hillside in the highlands of [[e:chiapas|Chiapas]]. A dynasty is attested from the 6th century, around 500 CE, and the city grew into a regional power at the western edge of the Maya lowlands.
tonina.r: Toniná's terraced acropolis rises some 70 metres above the valley and carried temples, palaces and ballcourts. Its sculptors favoured statues in the round and images of bound captives. Under K'inich B'aaknal Chaak it waged war on [[s:palenque|Palenque]], and in 711 Toniná captured Palenque's king K'an Joy Chitam II, shown bound on a relief. A stucco frieze depicts the underworld with a skeletal figure holding a severed head.
tonina.e: Toniná outlasted most lowland kingdoms. A monument dated 909 bears the last known Long Count date of the Classic Maya, after which royal rule ended. The site was later reoccupied on a small scale.

trinidad-and-tobago.t: Twin-island Caribbean state, independent since 1962 and a republic since 1976, built on oil and gas and known as the home of Carnival, calypso and steelpan.
trinidad-and-tobago.o: After the [[s:west-indies-federation|West Indies Federation]] collapsed, the [[s:colony-of-trinidad-and-tobago|Colony of Trinidad and Tobago]] became independent on 31 August 1962 under Prime Minister Eric Williams of the People's National Movement, with the British monarch as head of state.
trinidad-and-tobago.r: Williams governed until his death in 1981. The Black Power protests of 1970 and an army mutiny shook his government, but the oil boom of the 1970s brought wealth and nationalisation of the energy sector. A new constitution made the country a republic on 1 August 1976, with a president as head of state. Politics has tended to divide along African and Indian lines, and natural gas and petrochemicals became the backbone of the economy.
trinidad-and-tobago.e: The Jamaat al Muslimeen held the prime minister and parliament hostage in a failed coup attempt in 1990. Basdeo Panday became the first prime minister of Indian descent in 1995 and Kamla Persad-Bissessar the first woman in 2010. The country remains a parliamentary republic.

tanganyika.t: The independent state of mainland Tanzania from 1961 to 1964, led by Julius Nyerere before its union with Zanzibar.
tanganyika.o: [[s:tanganyika-territory|Tanganyika Territory]] became independent on 9 December 1961, with Julius Nyerere, leader of the Tanganyika African National Union (TANU), as prime minister and Elizabeth II as head of state. It was one of the first East African countries to gain independence, achieved peacefully through elections.
tanganyika.r: Nyerere resigned as prime minister in January 1962 to rebuild TANU, handing office to Rashidi Kawawa, and on 9 December 1962 Tanganyika became a republic with Nyerere as executive president. [[e:swahili|Swahili]] was promoted as a national language, chieftaincies were abolished in 1963, and TANU moved towards a one-party state. In January 1964 an army mutiny was put down with British help.
tanganyika.e: After the revolution in [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]], Nyerere and Abeid Karume agreed to unite their countries. On 26 April 1964 Tanganyika and the [[s:peoples-republic-of-zanzibar|People's Republic of Zanzibar]] formed the United Republic, renamed [[s:tanzania|Tanzania]] in October 1964.

teotihuacan.t: The largest city of the early Americas, whose avenues and pyramids in the Valley of Mexico shaped politics, trade and art across Mesoamerica for centuries.
teotihuacan.o: Teotihuacan grew rapidly in the 1st century BCE, drawing in people from the [[e:valley-of-mexico|Valley of Mexico]], partly after the volcanic eruptions that damaged Cuicuilco. By about 250 CE it covered some 20 square kilometres, with perhaps 100,000 inhabitants.
teotihuacan.r: The city was planned on a grid around the Avenue of the Dead, with the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon and the Feathered Serpent Temple. Most residents lived in multi-family apartment compounds, some housing migrants from Oaxaca and the Gulf Coast. No ruler is named in its art, and some scholars propose shared or collective rule. Obsidian working and wide trade spread its influence as far as [[s:tikal|Tikal]] and [[s:kaminaljuyu|Kaminaljuyu]].
teotihuacan.e: Around 550 CE the civic centre was burnt and its power collapsed, perhaps through internal revolt. The population fell sharply. The [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] later revered the ruins as the place where the gods created the present sun.

torks.t: Oghuz Turkic nomads of the southern Russian steppe who fought the Rus' and later served them as frontier guards.
torks.o: The Torks were [[e:oghuz-turks|Oghuz Turks]] who moved west from the Aral and Caspian steppes in the late 10th century, part of the westward migrations that followed the collapse of the [[s:oghuz-yabgu-state|Oghuz Yabgu State]]. Byzantine writers called them Uzes. In 985 they appear as allies of Prince Vladimir of Kiev in his campaign against the [[e:volga|Volga]] [[e:bulgars|Bulgars]].
torks.r: The Torks were pastoral nomads organised in clans under chiefs, with no strong central power. They competed with the [[s:pechenegs|Pechenegs]] for the steppe north of the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] and raided both Rus' and the Byzantine [[e:balkans|Balkans]]; a large Uz horde crossed the [[e:danube|Danube]] in 1064 before being destroyed by disease and Bulgarian attacks.
torks.e: In 1060 a combined Rus' army defeated the Torks, and the arrival of the Cumans soon after forced them from the steppe. Many settled as allies of the Kievan princes along the Ros River, among the Chorni Klobuky, 'Black Hats', who guarded the frontier.

tudmir.t: The autonomous Christian principality of Theodemir in Murcia and Alicante, whose 713 surrender treaty is one of the earliest documents of al-Andalus.
tudmir.o: Theodemir, a Visigothic noble who governed the south-east, resisted the Muslim invaders and then negotiated. In April 713 he signed a treaty with Abd [[e:al-aziz|al-Aziz]] ibn Musa, keeping control of seven towns, including Orihuela, Mula, Lorca and Alicante, in return for submission and tribute.
tudmir.r: The treaty guaranteed the Christians their lives, property and churches as long as they paid an annual tax in coin and in kind, wheat, barley, vinegar, honey and oil, and did not shelter enemies. Theodemir ruled as a client prince, and the region became known in Arabic as Tudmir after him. His successor Athanagild kept the autonomy for a time.
tudmir.e: Arab settlers, especially Syrian troops after 743, moved into the region, eroding Christian autonomy. By the reign of [[e:abd-al-rahman-i|Abd al-Rahman I]] it was absorbed into the [[s:emirate-of-cordoba|Emirate of Córdoba]], and in 825 Abd al-Rahman II founded [[e:murcia|Murcia]] as the capital of the province of Tudmir.

taifa-of-molina.t: An obscure frontier lordship at Molina de Aragón, ruled by the Banu Galbun, whose lord appears as El Cid's friend Abengalbón in the Cantar de mio Cid.
taifa-of-molina.o: The Banu Galbun appear to have taken control of the castle of Molina and its district in the upper Gallo valley around 1012, as the Middle March of [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]] fragmented after the fall of the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]]. Little more is known of its beginnings.
taifa-of-molina.r: Molina was a small border principality between the [[e:taifa|taifas]] of [[e:toledo|Toledo]], [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]] and Albarracín, more a fortified lordship than a full kingdom. It is known mainly from Christian sources and from the epic Cantar de mio Cid, in which its lord Abengalbón is a loyal ally who hosts the Cid's wife and daughters.
taifa-of-molina.e: Molina came under Almoravid control around 1100. In about 1129 [[e:alfonso-i-of-aragon|Alfonso I of Aragon]] took the town, and it was soon granted to the Lara family, becoming the [[s:lordship-of-molina|Lordship of Molina]].

turaida.t: Livonian chiefdom on the lower Gauja, whose leader Caupo became the crusaders' most important native ally and visited the pope in Rome.
turaida.o: Turaida, Thoreida in [[e:latin|Latin]], was a land of the Livonians, a Finnic people, on the lower course of the Gauja river in modern [[s:republic-of-latvia|Latvia]]. Its fortified hill at Turaida controlled river traffic and was the seat of the elder Caupo at the beginning of the 13th century.
turaida.r: The Livs farmed, fished and traded along the Gauja and Daugava. Caupo accepted baptism early, travelled to [[e:rome|Rome]] around 1203 and met [[e:papacy|Pope]] Innocent III, and supported [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Albert of Riga against his own countrymen, who rose against him in 1212. The Livs of Turaida supplied troops to the crusaders' campaigns in [[s:republic-of-estonia|Estonia]].
turaida.e: Caupo was killed at the Battle of St Matthew's Day in 1217. Turaida came under the [[e:bishop|bishop]] of Riga, who built a stone castle there in 1214, and it became part of the [[s:archbishopric-of-riga|Archbishopric of Riga]]. The Livonian language slowly gave way to Latvian.

toyotomi-regime.t: The government of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the commoner-born warlord who completed the unification of Japan and invaded Korea.
toyotomi-regime.o: Hideyoshi, a foot soldier's son who rose in [[e:oda-nobunaga|Oda Nobunaga's]] service, avenged Nobunaga by defeating Akechi Mitsuhide at Yamazaki in 1582 and then beat Shibata Katsuie at Shizugatake in 1583. He began Osaka castle as his base, became imperial regent (kampaku) in 1585 and received the new surname [[e:toyotomi-clan|Toyotomi]] in 1586.
toyotomi-regime.r: Hideyoshi subdued Shikoku, Kyushu and finally the Later Hojo at Odawara in 1590, unifying [[e:japan|Japan]]. He confiscated weapons from farmers in the sword hunt of 1588, surveyed land nationwide and froze the separation of warriors and peasants. He expelled [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] missionaries in 1587 and patronised [[e:tea|tea]] master Sen no Rikyu. His invasions of [[e:korea|Korea]] in 1592 and 1597 ended in failure.
toyotomi-regime.e: On Hideyoshi's death in 1598 a council of five elders governed for his young son Hideyori. [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu's]] victory at [[e:battle-of-sekigahara|Sekigahara]] in 1600 ended [[e:toyotomi-clan|Toyotomi]] power, though Hideyori held Osaka until its fall in 1615.

third-republic-of-venezuela.t: The patriot republic Bolívar rebuilt from Angostura on the Orinoco, which launched the campaigns that freed northern South America.
third-republic-of-venezuela.o: After exile in [[s:jamaica|Jamaica]] and [[s:first-empire-of-haiti|Haiti]], Bolívar returned to [[s:venezuela|Venezuela]] in 1816. In 1817 patriot forces under Manuel Piar and Bolívar captured the Guayana region and its town of Angostura, now Ciudad Bolívar, on the Orinoco, giving the patriots a secure base. The republic was proclaimed there.
third-republic-of-venezuela.r: Bolívar consolidated his authority, ordering Piar's execution in 1817 for insubordination. José Antonio Páez won over the llaneros of the plains, and British and Irish volunteers formed the British [[e:legion|Legion]]. The newspaper Correo del Orinoco spread patriot views from 1818. The Congress of Angostura met in February 1819, when Bolívar delivered his famous address on government.
third-republic-of-venezuela.e: After Bolívar's crossing of the [[s:andecavi|Andes]] and victory at Boyacá in August 1819, the Congress of Angostura proclaimed the union of [[s:venezuela|Venezuela]] and New [[e:granada|Granada]] as [[s:gran-colombia|Gran Colombia]] in December 1819.

takamatsu-domain.t: A domain of Sanuki on Shikoku, ruled by a branch of the Tokugawa family and known for Ritsurin garden and its fine sugar.
takamatsu-domain.o: Ikoma Chikamasa received Sanuki from [[e:toyotomi-hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] in 1587 and in 1588 began Takamatsu castle, a sea castle with moats fed by seawater. The Ikoma kept the province after 1600, but a family dispute led the [[e:shogun|shogunate]] to remove them in 1640.
takamatsu-domain.r: In 1642 Matsudaira Yorishige, a son of the Mito Tokugawa founder, was given eastern Sanuki with 120,000 koku, and his line ruled until the end of the period as close kin of the [[e:shogun|shoguns]]. The domain developed the Ritsurin garden and, under Matsudaira Yoritaka in the late 18th century, promoted salt and fine wasanbon [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]].
takamatsu-domain.e: Takamatsu fought for the [[e:shogun|shogunate]] at Toba-Fushimi in 1868 and was occupied and punished by the new government. After its abolition in 1871 the area became part of Kagawa Prefecture.

tran-dynasty.t: The Vietnamese dynasty that defeated three Mongol invasions in the 13th century under the generalship of Tran Hung Dao.
tran-dynasty.o: The Tran clan, coastal landowners from Nam Dinh, gained control of the late [[s:ly-dynasty|Ly dynasty]] court. In 1225 Tran Thu Do arranged the marriage of the child empress Ly Chieu Hoang to his nephew Tran Canh, who became emperor Tran Thai Tong, and the Tran ruled Dai Viet from Thang Long.
tran-dynasty.r: Tran rulers kept power in the family through intermarriage and a system of senior emperors who abdicated to guide their sons. Princes held large estates worked by bondsmen. The dynasty expanded the Red River dikes, compiled the first national history, and promoted the Truc Lam Zen school founded by Tran Nhan Tong. Writing in chu nom developed.
tran-dynasty.e: [[s:ly-dynasty|Dai Viet]] repelled Mongol invasions in 1258, 1285 and 1287 to 1288, the last ending at Bach Dang. The 14th century brought wars with [[s:champa|Champa]] and weak rulers, and in 1400 the minister Ho Quy Ly deposed the last Tran emperor, founding the [[s:ho-dynasty|Ho dynasty]].

toucouleur-empire.t: The empire created by the jihad of Umar Tall, which conquered Segou and Massina and stretched across the western Sahel until the French conquest.
toucouleur-empire.o: Umar Tall, a Tijani scholar from [[s:imamate-of-futa-toro|Futa Toro]], returned from the pilgrimage to [[e:mecca|Mecca]] with great prestige and in 1849 set up a fortified base at Dinguiraye, on the edge of [[s:imamate-of-futa-jallon|Futa Jallon]]. In 1852 he launched a [[e:jihad|jihad]], conquering the [[s:kingdom-of-kaarta|Kingdom of Kaarta]] in 1854, the [[s:bamana-empire|Bamana Empire]] at Segou in 1861 and the [[s:massina-empire|Massina Empire]] in 1862.
toucouleur-empire.r: The empire was held together by Umar's [[e:toucouleur|Toucouleur]] followers from the [[e:senegal|Senegal]] valley, the authority of the Tijaniyya order and garrisons of [[e:musket|musketeers]]. It had little central administration: provinces were run by Umar's sons, nephews and commanders from fortified towns such as Segou, Nioro and Bandiagara. Umar was killed in 1864 during a Fulbe uprising in Massina, and his son Ahmadu Tall ruled from Segou amid rebellion and rivalry with his brothers.
toucouleur-empire.e: From 1890 the French under Louis Archinard took Segou, Nioro and finally Bandiagara in 1893. Ahmadu fled east and died in the [[s:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto Caliphate]], and the lands became part of [[s:french-sudan|French Sudan]].

tsongkha.t: A Tibetan kingdom in Amdo, centred on modern Xining, that allied with the Song against the Tanguts and controlled a southern branch of the Silk Road.
tsongkha.o: After the [[s:tibetan-empire|Tibetan Empire]] fragmented, Tibetan tribes in the Huangshui valley of Amdo brought in Gusiluo, a youth claiming descent from the old royal line, around 1008. After years as a figurehead of local strongmen he established his own court at Qingtang (modern Xining) around 1032.
tsongkha.r: Gusiluo was a Buddhist ruler presiding over a loose federation of Tibetan clans. He allied with the [[s:song-dynasty|Song Dynasty]], which gave him titles and [[e:subsidy|subsidies]], and defeated Tangut attacks from [[s:western-xia|Western Xia]] in the 1030s. When Tangut wars disrupted the [[e:gansu-corridor|Hexi Corridor]], caravans used the Qinghai route through his territory, and Qingtang grew rich on trade in horses and other goods.
tsongkha.e: After Gusiluo's death in 1065 the kingdom was divided among his descendants and weakened by feuds. The [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] annexed the region in campaigns of 1099 and 1104, though Song control was soon lost to the [[s:jin-dynasty-1115-1234|Jin dynasty]] (1115-1234) and [[s:western-xia|Western Xia]].

territory-of-papua-and-new-guinea.t: The joint Australian administration of Papua and the trust territory of New Guinea, which led to Papua New Guinea's independence in 1975.
territory-of-papua-and-new-guinea.o: After the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]] [[s:commonwealth-of-australia|Australia]] combined the [[s:territory-of-papua|Territory of Papua]] and the [[s:territory-of-new-guinea|Territory of New Guinea]] under the Papua and New [[e:guinea|Guinea]] Act of 1949, with a single administrator at Port Moresby. Legally, Papua remained an Australian territory and New Guinea a [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] trust territory.
territory-of-papua-and-new-guinea.r: Paul Hasluck, minister for territories from 1951 to 1963, pursued gradual uniform development through schools, health and patrol posts reaching the Highlands. A House of Assembly with an elected majority met from 1964. [[e:coffee-economy|Coffee]], copra and the Panguna [[e:copper|copper]] mine on Bougainville, opened in 1972, drove the economy. The Pangu Party under Michael Somare, founded in 1967, pressed for self-government, achieved in 1973.
territory-of-papua-and-new-guinea.e: [[s:territory-of-papua|Papua]] New [[e:guinea|Guinea]] became independent on 16 September 1975, with Somare as prime minister. The new state kept English, Tok Pisin and Hiri Motu as national languages and remained in the Commonwealth. Bougainville's grievances over the Panguna mine later fed secessionist war from 1988.
