tlaxcala.t: A confederation of four Nahua altepetl east of the Valley of Mexico that defied the Aztec Empire and became the decisive ally of Cortés.
tlaxcala.o: Tlaxcala (Tlaxcallan) was founded, according to tradition, in 1348 by Teochichimec groups who settled the hills of the Puebla-Tlaxcala valley after displacing earlier peoples. It grew into four allied altepetl: Tepeticpac, Ocotelolco, Quiahuixtlan and Tizatlan.
tlaxcala.r: Each of the four parts had its own ruler, and they decided matters of common interest in council, leading Spanish observers to compare Tlaxcala to a republic. Surrounded by the [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]], it fought ritual 'flower wars' and endured an economic [[e:naval-blockade|blockade]] that denied it salt and [[e:cotton|cotton]]. Recent archaeology suggests an unusually collective form of government.
tlaxcala.e: After fighting [[e:hernan-cortes|Cortés]] in 1519, Tlaxcala's leaders, among them Xicotencatl the Elder and Maxixcatzin, allied with him and supplied thousands of warriors for the conquest of [[e:tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]]. The Spanish Crown rewarded it with privileges, and Tlaxcala is now a Mexican state.

theme-of-longobardia.t: Byzantine province of southern Italy, governed from Bari, created after the empire recovered Apulia in the late 9th century.
theme-of-longobardia.o: After Louis II took [[s:principality-of-bari|Bari]] from the [[e:arabs|Arabs]] in 871, the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]] occupied it in 876 and, through the campaigns of Nikephoros Phokas the Elder in 885–886, recovered much of Apulia and Calabria. Around 891 these lands were organised as the Theme of Longobardia, named after its largely [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] population.
theme-of-longobardia.r: A [[e:strategos|strategos]] governed from [[s:principality-of-bari|Bari]], at times claiming overlordship over the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] principalities of Benevento, [[s:principality-of-capua|Capua]] and [[s:principality-of-salerno|Salerno]]. The population was mostly Latin-speaking and lived under Lombard law, while Greek officials, settlers and monasteries brought Byzantine influence. Tax registers, charters and the building of fortified towns show an active administration.
theme-of-longobardia.e: Around 965–970 Longobardia was combined with Calabria and Lucania under a new, higher-ranking governor, the catepan, creating the [[s:catepanate-of-italy|Catepanate of Italy]], which continued until the Norman conquest.

the-protectorate.t: The phase of the English republic in which Oliver Cromwell, and briefly his son Richard, ruled as Lord Protector of England, Scotland and Ireland.
the-protectorate.o: In December 1653, after the failure of Barebone's Parliament, army officers drew up the Instrument of Government, [[e:britain|Britain's]] [[e:1931-constitution-of-ethiopia|first written constitution]], which made Oliver Cromwell Lord Protector of the [[s:commonwealth-of-england|Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland]], with a Council of State and Parliament.
the-protectorate.r: Cromwell governed with mixed success: he quarrelled with his Parliaments, divided the country under the Major-Generals in 1655 to 1657 and refused the crown in 1657, accepting instead the Humble Petition and Advice. Abroad, the [[e:protectorate|Protectorate]] made peace with the [[e:dutch|Dutch]], fought [[e:spain|Spain]] and seized [[s:jamaica|Jamaica]] in 1655. [[e:jews|Jews]] were informally allowed to resettle in [[e:england|England]] from 1656.
the-protectorate.e: Oliver died in September 1658 and was succeeded by his son Richard, who lacked army support and resigned in May 1659. The [[s:commonwealth-of-england|Commonwealth of England]] was restored briefly before the Restoration of 1660.

tegea.t: Leading city of south-eastern Arcadia, long Sparta's rival and ally, famed for the temple of Athena Alea rebuilt by the sculptor Scopas.
tegea.o: Tegea formed from the union of nine villages in the high plain of south-eastern Arcadia, bordering Laconia. Its sanctuary of Athena Alea was a regional cult centre by the 8th century BCE. In the 6th century BCE Tegea defeated a Spartan invasion in the 'Battle of the Fetters', in which captured Spartans had to work Tegean fields in their own chains.
tegea.r: [[s:sparta|Sparta]] later prevailed, reportedly after recovering the bones of Orestes from Tegea, and Tegea became a leading member of the [[s:peloponnesian-league|Peloponnesian League]], fighting at [[s:plataea|Plataea]] in 479 BCE. Its temple of Athena Alea, burned in 395 BCE, was rebuilt by [[e:scopas|Scopas]] and was one of the finest in the Peloponnese.
tegea.e: After Leuctra, Tegea joined [[s:mantinea|Mantinea]] in founding the [[s:arcadian-league|Arcadian League]] in 370 BCE. In the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]] it passed among the [[s:aetolian-league|Aetolian League]], [[s:sparta|Sparta]] under Cleomenes III and the [[s:achaean-league|Achaean League]], coming under [[e:rome|Rome]] in 146 BCE.
tegea.re: Greek religion; cult of Athena Alea

taifa-of-jaen.t: A taifa in the upper Guadalquivir held by the warlord Ibn Hamushk, father-in-law and ally of the Wolf King, Ibn Mardanish.
taifa-of-jaen.o: In 1145, during the collapse of Almoravid rule, Jaén and its region came under local rebels. The most durable was Ibrahim ibn Hamushk, a commander who held Jaén and the castles of the Sierra de Segura and allied himself with Muhammad ibn Mardanish.
taifa-of-jaen.r: Jaén was a land of olive groves and frontier fortresses facing [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]] and the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]]. Ibn Hamushk was a military strongman who at times took [[e:granada|Granada]] and fought both Christian and Almohad forces, while relying on the wealth and [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] of the [[s:second-taifa-of-murcia|Second Taifa of Murcia]].
taifa-of-jaen.e: Around 1159 Jaén passed to the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]]. Ibn Hamushk later broke with Ibn Mardanish and joined the Almohads himself. [[e:ferdinand-iii-of-castile|Ferdinand III]] of the [[s:crown-of-castile|Crown of Castile]] took Jaén in 1246.

thailand.t: The only Southeast Asian state never colonised, a constitutional monarchy since 1932 whose politics have swung between elected governments and military rule.
thailand.o: The revolution of 24 June 1932 by the Khana Ratsadon, led by Pridi Banomyong and Plaek Phibunsongkhram, ended absolute monarchy in the [[s:rattanakosin-kingdom|Rattanakosin Kingdom]] and introduced a constitution. In 1939 Prime Minister Phibun changed the country's name from Siam to Thailand.
thailand.r: Thailand is a [[e:constitutional-monarchy|constitutional monarchy]] with Bangkok as its capital and [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] as the main faith. Phibun allied with [[e:japan|Japan]] in the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]]. King Bhumibol Adulyadej, who reigned from 1946 to 2016, became a powerful unifying figure. Military coups, including in 1947, 1957, 1976, 1991, 2006 and 2014, have repeatedly interrupted civilian rule. A Cold War ally of the [[s:united-states|United States]], it grew into a leading exporter of [[e:rice|rice]], cars and electronics and a major tourist destination.
thailand.e: Thailand continues today under King Vajiralongkorn. It was a founding member of ASEAN in 1967. Recent decades have been marked by political divisions, an insurgency in the Malay-Muslim south, and protests over the role of the military and monarchy.

tanzania.t: The union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar, shaped by Julius Nyerere's Ujamaa socialism and known for its stability and its national use of Swahili.
tanzania.o: On 26 April 1964 [[s:tanganyika|Tanganyika]] and the [[s:peoples-republic-of-zanzibar|People's Republic of Zanzibar]] united as the United Republic of Tanganyika and [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]], renamed Tanzania in October 1964. Julius Nyerere became president and Abeid Karume first vice-president, while Zanzibar kept its own autonomous government.
tanzania.r: Nyerere's Arusha Declaration of 1967 launched Ujamaa, African socialism with nationalised banks and industries and, in the 1970s, the often forced resettlement of rural people into villages, which hurt farm output. Tanzania backed liberation movements across southern [[e:africa|Africa]] and in 1979 overthrew Idi Amin in [[s:uganda|Uganda]]. [[e:swahili|Swahili]] became a strong unifying language.
tanzania.e: Under Ali Hassan Mwinyi the economy was liberalised from 1985, and multi-party politics returned in 1992, though the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi has held power throughout. Dodoma was designated capital in 1973. Samia Suluhu Hassan became the first woman president in 2021.

tinh-hai-circuit.t: The late Tang military circuit in northern Vietnam whose local governors, the Khuc family, laid the groundwork for Vietnamese independence.
tinh-hai-circuit.o: After the [[s:later-tang|Tang]] general [[e:gao|Gao]] Pian expelled [[s:nanzhao|Nanzhao]] from the [[s:protectorate-general-to-pacify-the-south|Protectorate General to Pacify the South]] in 866, the region was reorganised as Jinghai, in Vietnamese Tinh Hai, a military circuit governed by a [[e:jiedushi|jiedushi]]. Its seat was the citadel of Dai La, on the site of [[e:hanoi|Hanoi]].
tinh-hai-circuit.r: As the [[e:tang-dynasty|Tang dynasty]] disintegrated, local leaders took over. In 905 Khuc Thua Du, a powerful local landowner, seized the governorship, and his son Khuc Hao reformed taxes and administration. The circuit was nominally loyal to Chinese courts while acting autonomously. [[s:southern-han|Southern Han]], the new regime in [[e:guangzhou|Guangzhou]], tried to reassert control in 930.
tinh-hai-circuit.e: Duong Dinh Nghe expelled the [[s:southern-han|Southern Han]] in 931 but was murdered by Kieu Cong Tien in 937. Kieu called in the Southern Han, and in 938 Ngo Quyen defeated their fleet at the Bach Dang river, ending a millennium of Chinese rule and founding the [[s:ngo-dynasty|Ngo dynasty]].

triboci.t: Germanic people who crossed the Rhine with Ariovistus and settled in northern Alsace around Brumath.
triboci.o: The Triboci appear in Caesar's account of the battle against Ariovistus in 58 BCE as one of the peoples in his army. They had settled on the left bank of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]], in land previously held by the [[s:mediomatrici|Mediomatrici]].
triboci.r: Nothing is known of their institutions. They seem to have adopted Gallic ways quickly after settling west of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]].
triboci.e: After Caesar's victory over Ariovistus they remained in Alsace. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] they formed a civitas with its chief town at Brocomagus (Brumath), north of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Strasbourg]].

tamna.t: The island kingdom of Jeju, which kept its own rulers for six centuries as a tributary of Korean kingdoms before Goryeo made it a county in 1105.
tamna.o: Jeju legend tells of three founders, ancestors of the Go, Yang and Bu clans, who emerged from holes in the ground at Samseonghyeol and married princesses who arrived by sea. Tamna first appears in the Samguk sagi in 476, when it sent tribute to [[s:baekje|Baekje]].
tamna.r: The island was ruled by hereditary lords with the titles seongju and wangja, drawn from the Go clan. Tamna lived from fishing, diving and farming on volcanic soil and traded with [[e:korea|Korea]], [[e:china|China]] and [[e:japan|Japan]], sending envoys to the [[s:later-tang|Tang]] court and to Japan in the 7th century. It paid tribute to [[s:baekje|Baekje]], then to [[s:silla|Silla]] after 662, and to [[s:goryeo|Goryeo]] from 938.
tamna.e: [[s:goryeo|Goryeo]] turned Tamna into a county in 1105, ending its formal autonomy, though local lords kept their titles until the early [[s:joseon|Joseon]] period. The island was renamed Jeju in the early 13th century.

tomara-dynasty-of-delhi.t: The Rajput dynasty traditionally credited with founding Delhi as Dhillika and building its first citadel, Lal Kot.
tomara-dynasty-of-delhi.o: Bardic tradition says Anangapala I founded Dhillika, the first city of [[e:delhi|Delhi]], in 736. Historically, the Tomaras appear in the 9th and 10th centuries as chiefs in the Haryana region, probably feudatories of the [[s:gurjara-pratihara|Gurjara-Pratihara]]. Their rule at Delhi is attested mainly by later inscriptions and literary sources.
tomara-dynasty-of-delhi.r: Anangapala II is credited with building the fortified citadel of Lal Kot in the 11th century, the oldest identifiable city of [[e:delhi|Delhi]], and an inscription on the Iron Pillar names him. Surajkund, a stepped reservoir near Delhi, is traditionally attributed to a Tomara king. They ruled a modest kingdom and were repeatedly attacked by the [[s:ghaznavid-empire|Ghaznavids]].
tomara-dynasty-of-delhi.e: In the mid-12th century the Tomaras were defeated by Vigraharaja IV of the [[s:chahamanas-of-shakambhari|Chahamanas of Shakambhari]], who took [[e:delhi|Delhi]]; Tomara chiefs continued there as Chahamana [[e:vassal|vassals]] until the Ghurid conquest of 1192.

trust-territory-of-somaliland.t: The UN trust territory administered by Italy for ten years to prepare southern Somalia for independence in 1960.
trust-territory-of-somaliland.o: After British military administration from 1941, the UN decided in 1949 that [[e:italy|Italy]] would return to its former colony of [[s:italian-somaliland|Italian Somaliland]] as administering power, on condition that the territory become independent after ten years. The Italian Trusteeship Administration, AFIS, took over in April 1950, with [[s:sultanate-of-mogadishu|Mogadishu]] as capital.
trust-territory-of-somaliland.r: [[e:italy|Italy]] was supervised by a UN advisory council and built up schools, a civil service and elected councils. The [[e:somalis|Somali]] Youth League, the leading nationalist party, won the elections of 1956 and 1959, and Somalis took over ministries under Prime Minister Abdullahi Issa. Bananas remained the main export, and Somali was not yet a written official language.
trust-territory-of-somaliland.e: On 1 July 1960 the territory became independent and united with the [[s:state-of-somaliland|State of Somaliland]] to form the [[s:somali-republic|Somali Republic]], with Aden Abdullah Osman as president.

tehri-garhwal-state.t: The Himalayan kingdom of the Garhwal dynasty, restored by the British in 1815 after Gorkha occupation and ruled from Tehri until 1949.
tehri-garhwal-state.o: The Panwar kings of Garhwal had ruled the upper [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges]] hills from Srinagar since medieval times. The Gorkhas conquered Garhwal in 1804. After the Anglo-Nepalese War, the British in 1815 restored Sudarshan Shah to the western part of his kingdom, keeping the east as British Garhwal; he founded a new capital at Tehri.
tehri-garhwal-state.r: Tehri Garhwal was a mountain state of terraced farms, forests and pilgrimage routes to Gangotri and Yamunotri. Its rulers profited from [[e:timber|timber]] and controlled access to forest lands, provoking peasant protests such as the one crushed at Tilari in 1930. Narendra Shah founded the new capital of Narendranagar.
tehri-garhwal-state.e: After popular agitation ended the monarchy's authority, Manabendra Shah acceded to [[e:india|India]], and Tehri Garhwal was merged into Uttar Pradesh in 1949. It is now in Uttarakhand; old Tehri town was submerged by the Tehri Dam.

terek-soviet-republic.t: A Soviet republic of 1918 in the Terek region, where Bolsheviks tried to govern Cossacks and mountain peoples amid civil war.
terek-soviet-republic.o: In March 1918 a congress of the peoples of the Terek region at Pyatigorsk proclaimed the Terek Soviet Republic as part of the [[s:russian-sfsr|Russian SFSR]]. It covered the lands of the [[s:terek-cossack-host|Terek Cossack Host]] and of the Chechens, Ingush, Ossetians and Kabardians, with its government at Pyatigorsk and Vladikavkaz.
terek-soviet-republic.r: The republic was led by a people's council and council of commissars under Samuil Buachidze until his murder in June 1918. It tried to balance the claims of [[e:cossacks|Cossacks]] and mountain peoples over land, while fighting the [[s:mountainous-republic-of-the-northern-caucasus|Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus]] and anti-Bolshevik Cossacks. A Cossack uprising broke out in June 1918.
terek-soviet-republic.e: In July 1918 it was merged into the [[s:north-caucasian-soviet-republic|North Caucasian Soviet Republic]], though its government survived in Vladikavkaz until the White advance of early 1919. Soviet power returned in 1920, and the region was later divided into autonomous units for its peoples.

tarumanagara.t: The first known kingdom of Java, whose King Purnawarman left Sanskrit inscriptions around Bogor and Jakarta in the 5th century.
tarumanagara.o: The kingdom is known chiefly from seven stone inscriptions in western [[e:java|Java]], written in [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] with Pallava script and dated on palaeographic grounds to the 5th century. The register's founding date of 358 comes from the late Wangsakerta [[e:manuscript|manuscripts]], whose reliability historians doubt. Chinese records of embassies from To-lo-mo between 528 and 669 probably refer to it.
tarumanagara.r: Purnawarman compared himself to Vishnu and left carved footprints on the Ciaruteun stone. The Tugu inscription records a canal more than 11 kilometres long dug in 21 days, completed with a gift of 1,000 [[e:cattle|cattle]] to [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]], evidence of organised labour and [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] ritual. [[e:rice|Rice]] farming and coastal trade supported the state.
tarumanagara.e: Sundanese tradition holds that the kingdom split around 669 into the [[s:sunda-kingdom|Sunda Kingdom]] and the [[s:galuh-kingdom|Galuh Kingdom]], separated by the Citarum River. Its name lives on in the Tarum River, and its inscriptions are among the oldest written records of [[s:indonesia|Indonesia]].

tumed-altan-khan.t: The realm of Altan Khan in Inner Mongolia, which made peace with Ming China, founded Hohhot and gave the Dalai Lama his title.
tumed-altan-khan.o: Altan Khan, a grandson of Dayan Khan of the [[s:northern-yuan|Northern Yuan]], became leader of the Tümed [[e:tumen|tumen]] in the 1530s and turned it into the strongest power among the eastern [[e:mongols|Mongols]]. His raids reached the Ming capital, which he besieged in 1550, in an effort to force [[e:china|China]] to open border trade.
tumed-altan-khan.r: After a peace in 1571 the [[s:ming-empire|Ming Empire]] granted Altan Khan the title Shunyi Wang and opened horse markets on the frontier. He welcomed Chinese farmers and craftsmen, many of them refugees, and built the walled town of Guihua (Hohhot). In 1578 he met the Gelug lama Sonam Gyatso at Kokonor, gave him the title [[e:dalai-lama|Dalai Lama]] and adopted [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]], launching the conversion of the [[e:mongols|Mongols]].
tumed-altan-khan.e: After Altan Khan's death in 1582 his descendants, guided at first by his widow Jönggen Khatun, kept the peace with the Ming but lost influence. In 1632 Ligdan Khan of the Chahar seized Guihua, and the Tümed soon submitted to the [[s:later-jin-1616-1636|Later Jin]] (1616-1636).

timocani.t: Slavic tribe of the Timok valley that broke from Bulgaria in 818 and sought the protection of the Frankish emperor.
timocani.o: The Timočani lived along the Timok river in modern eastern [[s:serbia|Serbia]] and north-western [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]], among the [[e:slavs|Slavs]] who settled the area in the 7th century. They are known almost entirely from the Royal Frankish Annals.
timocani.r: Little is known of their society. In 818 their envoys came to [[e:louis-the-pious|Louis the Pious]], having left the alliance of the Bulgarians, and they then joined the rising of Ljudevit of the [[s:duchy-of-pannonian-croatia|Duchy of Pannonian Croatia]] against the [[s:franks|Franks]].
timocani.e: After 819 they disappear from the sources. The [[s:first-bulgarian-empire|First Bulgarian Empire]] under Omurtag reasserted control over the middle [[e:danube|Danube]] in the 820s, and the Timok valley remained Bulgarian.

tanukhids.t: An Arab tribal confederation that served Rome as allied frontier troops in Syria, remembered for Queen Mavia's revolt against the emperor Valens.
tanukhids.o: Arabic tradition says the Tanukh were a coalition of tribes that migrated from eastern [[e:arabia|Arabia]] into [[e:iraq|Iraq]], where some settled around al-Hira, while others moved into [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] in the later 3rd century. There they became foederati, allies who guarded the desert frontier for [[e:rome|Rome]] in return for [[e:subsidy|subsidies]].
tanukhids.r: The Tanukhids were pastoral and semi-settled [[e:arabs|Arabs]] who adopted [[e:christianity|Christianity]] during the 4th century. Their best-known leader is Mavia, who around 378 led a revolt that ravaged [[e:palestine|Palestine]] and Phoenicia and ended only when [[e:valens|Valens]] agreed to her demand for an orthodox Arab hermit, Moses, as [[e:bishop|bishop]] of her people. Her troops then helped defend [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] against the Goths after the battle of Adrianople. Little else about their organisation is recorded.
tanukhids.e: In the 5th century the [[s:salihids|Salihids]] replaced them as [[e:rome|Rome's]] leading Arab allies. Tanukh clans remained in northern [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] around Qinnasrin and [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]], accepted [[e:islam|Islam]] after the Arab conquest, and later Tanukhid families played a part in the history of Mount [[s:lebanese-republic|Lebanon]].

taiwan-under-japanese-rule.t: Japan's first colony, held for fifty years, during which Taiwan was transformed by railways, sugar and schooling under a strict colonial government.
taiwan-under-japanese-rule.o: The [[s:qing-empire|Qing Empire]] ceded [[s:republic-of-china|Taiwan]] and the Penghu islands to [[e:japan|Japan]] by the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895. Japanese troops overcame the resistance of the [[s:republic-of-formosa|Republic of Formosa]] that year, but armed opposition by [[e:han-chinese|Han Chinese]] and indigenous groups continued for years.
taiwan-under-japanese-rule.r: A governor-general with wide powers ruled from Taihoku (Taipei). Under Governor-General Kodama Gentarō and his civil administrator Gotō Shinpei from 1898, the colony carried out land surveys and [[e:census|censuses]], built railways and ports, and developed [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], [[e:rice|rice]] and [[e:camphor|camphor]] for the [[s:empire-of-japan|Empire of Japan]], while policing heavily. Resistance continued, notably the Tapani incident of 1915 and the Seediq uprising at Musha in 1930. From 1937 assimilation policies pushed Japanese names, language and Shinto.
taiwan-under-japanese-rule.e: After [[e:japan|Japan's]] defeat in 1945, the [[s:republic-of-china|Republic of China]] took over [[e:taiwan|Taiwan]] in October 1945. The colonial legacy of infrastructure, education and public health, and the painful memories of repression and wartime mobilisation, have both shaped modern Taiwan.
taiwan-under-japanese-rule.re: Chinese folk religion, Buddhism, State Shinto

teke.t: A Turkish beylik on the Mediterranean coast around Antalya, a branch of the Hamidids that briefly lost its capital to the King of Cyprus.
teke.o: In the early 14th century a branch of the [[s:hamidids|Hamidids]] took control of Antalya and the surrounding coastland, known from its [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] inhabitants as Teke. Around 1321 it became a separate [[e:beylik|beylik]].
teke.r: The [[e:beylik|beylik]] lived from Antalya's port, which traded with [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]], [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and the Italian republics. [[e:ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] visited in the 1330s and met its ruler Khidr Bey. In 1361 [[e:peter-the-great|Peter I]] of Cyprus captured Antalya, holding it until 1373, when the beylik regained it. The Teke rulers built mosques and a [[e:madrasa|madrasa]] in Antalya.
teke.e: [[e:bayezid-i|Bayezid I]] annexed Teke around 1390, and [[e:timur|Timur]] restored it in 1402. Osman Bey, the last ruler, was killed besieging Antalya in 1423, and the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] annexed the [[e:beylik|beylik]].

taifa-of-calatayud.t: A short-lived Hudid principality at Calatayud, created when the founder of the Hudid dynasty divided his lands among his sons.
taifa-of-calatayud.o: When Sulayman ibn Hud al-Mustain of the [[s:taifa-of-zaragoza|Taifa of Zaragoza]] died in 1046, his realm was split among his sons. Muhammad received Calatayud, an old town on the Jalón controlling the road from [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]] to [[e:toledo|Toledo]].
taifa-of-calatayud.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, the principality was a fortified district rather than a full kingdom, and its ruler was quickly drawn into conflict with his ambitious brother Ahmad al-Muqtadir.
taifa-of-calatayud.e: By around 1055 al-Muqtadir had removed his brothers and reunited Calatayud with the [[s:taifa-of-zaragoza|Taifa of Zaragoza]]. [[e:alfonso-i-of-aragon|Alfonso I of Aragon]] took the town in 1120.

tuvan-peoples-republic.t: A nominally independent Soviet satellite in southern Siberia, recognised only by the USSR and Mongolia, which was quietly annexed in 1944.
tuvan-peoples-republic.o: After years of civil war on the upper Yenisei, Tuvan leaders with Soviet support proclaimed the People's Republic of Tannu Tuva in August 1921, replacing the Russian [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] of [[s:uryankhay-krai|Uryankhay Krai]]. Its capital, renamed Kyzyl, lay near the geographical centre of [[e:asia|Asia]].
tuvan-peoples-republic.r: Under Prime Minister Buyan-Badyrgy in the 1920s the state followed a moderate, Buddhist-friendly course. [[e:moscow|Moscow]] had him removed and later executed, and from 1932 Salchak Toka, leader of the Tuvan People's Revolutionary Party, ran a Stalinist regime: herds were collectivised, monasteries closed and lamas persecuted. A [[e:latin|Latin]] alphabet for Tuvan was introduced in 1930.
tuvan-peoples-republic.e: During the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]] Tuva gave horses, gold and volunteers to the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]]. In October 1944 it was admitted to the USSR as an autonomous oblast of the [[s:russian-sfsr|Russian SFSR]]; Salchak Toka remained its party leader until 1973.

taifa-of-seville.t: The most powerful taifa of al-Andalus, ruled by the Abbadids, whose poet-king al-Mutamid invited the Almoravids and lost his throne to them.
taifa-of-seville.o: In 1023 the leading families of [[e:seville|Seville]] expelled the Hammudid garrison and entrusted the city to the qadi Abu al-Qasim Muhammad ibn Abbad, of an old Arab family. He ruled in the name of a shadowy pretender, supposedly the vanished [[e:caliphate|caliph]] Hisham II, which gave the Abbadids a claim to wider authority.
taifa-of-seville.r: Al-Mutadid (1042-1069) expanded ruthlessly, annexing the [[e:berbers|Berber]] and Arab [[e:taifa|taifas]] of the south-west, from the Algarve to Ronda. His son al-Mutamid (1069-1091), himself a celebrated poet, added [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]] in 1070 and [[e:murcia|Murcia]] in 1078, with the poet Ibn Ammar as [[e:vizier|vizier]]. [[e:seville|Seville's]] [[e:olive-oil|olive oil]], textiles and river port made it the wealthiest city in the west, though it paid tribute to [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]].
taifa-of-seville.e: After [[e:toledo|Toledo]] fell in 1085, al-Mutamid called in the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]], who won at [[e:battle-of-sagrajas|Sagrajas]] in 1086 but deposed him in 1091. He died in exile at Aghmat in [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]], and his poems of loss became classics of Arabic literature.

terek-cossack-host.t: The self-governing Cossack community of the Terek river, for over three centuries Russia's armed frontier society in the North Caucasus.
terek-cossack-host.o: Free [[e:cossacks|Cossacks]] from the Don and [[e:volga|Volga]] settled on the lower Terek in the 16th century, and the Greben Cossacks lived in the foothills. The host traditionally dates its founding to 1577, when Russian Cossacks were recorded on the Terek after Muscovy's push down the Volga to Astrakhan. They served the [[s:tsardom-of-russia|Tsardom of Russia]] in return for pay and freedoms.
terek-cossack-host.r: [[e:cossacks|Cossack]] villages, or stanitsas, elected atamans and held assemblies, combining farming, fishing, vineyards and [[e:horse-breeding|horse breeding]] with military service. Many were Old Believers. Under the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] the host manned the fortified Caucasian Line from Kizlyar and Mozdok, was steadily placed under state control, and was formally reorganised in 1860 with its centre at Vladikavkaz.
terek-cossack-host.e: After 1917 the Terek [[e:cossacks|Cossacks]] briefly joined the [[s:mountainous-republic-of-the-northern-caucasus|Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus]], then fought the Bolsheviks. In 1920 the [[s:russian-sfsr|Russian SFSR]] crushed them, abolished the host and deported many stanitsas, giving their lands to Chechens and Ingush.

thonburi-kingdom.t: The kingdom of Taksin, who reunited Siam within a few years of Ayutthaya's destruction and ruled from Thonburi on the Chao Phraya.
thonburi-kingdom.o: Taksin, a provincial governor of part-Chinese descent, broke out of besieged [[s:ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya]] in 1767, gathered forces in the south-east at Chanthaburi and drove the Burmese garrison from the [[e:ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya]] area later that year. He chose Thonburi, a fortified town downriver, as his capital and was crowned king.
thonburi-kingdom.r: Between 1768 and 1770 Taksin defeated the rival regimes of Phimai, Phitsanulok, Sawangkhaburi and Nakhon Si Thammarat. His generals, the brothers Chao Phraya Chakri and Surasi, expelled the Burmese from [[s:lan-na|Lan Na]] and conquered the [[s:kingdom-of-vientiane|Kingdom of Vientiane]] in 1779, bringing back the Emerald Buddha. Taksin encouraged Chinese trade and settlement to rebuild the economy.
thonburi-kingdom.e: In his later years Taksin was said to have become religiously obsessive and erratic. A revolt in 1782 deposed him, and Chao Phraya Chakri returned from [[s:kingdom-of-cambodia-1953-1970|Cambodia]], had Taksin executed and became Rama I, founding the [[s:rattanakosin-kingdom|Rattanakosin Kingdom]] and moving the capital across the river to Bangkok.

territory-of-nauru.t: A tiny phosphate island administered by Australia for the British Empire, whose mining stripped most of its land before independence in 1968.
territory-of-nauru.o: [[e:germany|Germany]] had attached Nauru to its [[s:marshall-islands-protectorate|Marshall Islands Protectorate]] in 1888, and rich phosphate deposits were found in 1900. Australian forces took the island in 1914, and in 1920 the [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] granted a mandate to the [[s:british-empire|British Empire]], which [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], [[s:commonwealth-of-australia|Australia]] and [[s:new-zealand|New Zealand]] shared, with [[e:australia|Australia]] administering it.
territory-of-nauru.r: The British [[e:phosphate|Phosphate]] Commissioners mined the island to supply cheap fertiliser to Australian and [[s:new-zealand|New Zealand]] farms, paying Nauruans small royalties. An administrator ruled with a council of chiefs. [[e:japan|Japan]] occupied Nauru from 1942 to 1945 and deported about 1,200 Nauruans to Chuuk, where many died. After 1947 it was a [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] trust territory, and proposals to resettle the population on Curtis Island in [[s:colony-of-queensland|Queensland]] were rejected.
territory-of-nauru.e: Led by Head Chief Hammer DeRoburt, Nauru became independent on 31 January 1968, and soon bought the phosphate industry. A case at the International Court of Justice over mining damage was settled by [[s:commonwealth-of-australia|Australia]] in 1993.

taifa-of-majorca.t: The Balearic Islands as an independent taifa, a base for corsairs whose raids provoked the Pisan-Catalan crusade of 1113-1115.
taifa-of-majorca.o: The Balearics had been ruled from the [[s:taifa-of-denia|Taifa of Dénia]]. When al-Muqtadir of the [[s:taifa-of-zaragoza|Taifa of Zaragoza]] annexed Dénia in 1076, the island governor Abd Allah al-Murtada declared himself independent in Madina Mayurqa, the later Palma.
taifa-of-majorca.r: The islands lived from farming, fishing and [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] trade, and from corsair raids on Christian shipping and the coasts of [[s:principality-of-catalonia|Catalonia]], [[s:county-of-provence|Provence]] and [[e:italy|Italy]], which brought in captives and booty. Al-Murtada was succeeded by Mubashshir Nasir al-Dawla, a freedman who ruled until 1114.
taifa-of-majorca.e: In 1113-1115 a fleet of Pisans and Catalans under Ramon Berenguer III of Barcelona sacked [[s:ebusus|Ibiza]] and Madina Mayurqa, but withdrew. The [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] then occupied the islands, which later formed the base of [[s:banu-ghaniya-majorca|Banu Ghaniya Majorca]].

theocracy-of-amun-at-thebes.t: Upper Egypt ruled by the High Priests of Amun at Thebes, who governed through the god's oracle at the end of the New Kingdom.
theocracy-of-amun-at-thebes.o: As the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]] disintegrated under [[e:ramesses-xi|Ramesses XI]], the general and [[e:high-priest-of-amun|High Priest of Amun]] Herihor took control of [[s:thebes|Thebes]] around 1080 BCE and even wrote his name in a royal cartouche. The country was divided: the [[s:twenty-first-dynasty-of-egypt|Twenty-first Dynasty of Egypt]] ruled the north from [[e:tanis|Tanis]] while the high priests held the south.
theocracy-of-amun-at-thebes.r: The high priests were also army commanders, and they ruled from [[s:thebes|Thebes]] in the name of [[e:amun|Amun]], whose oracle was consulted on appointments, property and justice. They nominally recognised the Tanite kings, and the two houses intermarried. Pinedjem I took royal titles. Faced with tomb robbery, the priests moved the royal mummies to caches such as Deir el-Bahari tomb DB320, where many were found in 1881.
theocracy-of-amun-at-thebes.e: Around 943 BCE Sheshonq I of the [[s:twenty-second-dynasty-of-egypt|Twenty-second Dynasty of Egypt]] installed his own son Iuput as High Priest, ending the independent theocracy. The office kept great prestige, and power at [[s:thebes|Thebes]] later passed to the God's Wife of [[e:amun|Amun]].

taifa-of-lisbon.t: A brief taifa at Lisbon on the Tagus estuary, held by the heirs of the freedman Sabur before its absorption by Badajoz.
taifa-of-lisbon.o: [[e:lisbon|Lisbon]] had been part of the territory controlled by the freedman Sabur al-Saqlabi from [[e:badajoz|Badajoz]]. When he died in 1022 and his [[e:vizier|vizier]] seized Badajoz, Sabur's sons are said to have kept Lisbon as a separate principality.
taifa-of-lisbon.r: Known only from a few lines in Arabic chronicles, the [[e:taifa|taifa]] consisted of [[e:lisbon|Lisbon]] and its estuary, an Atlantic port trading in fish, salt and agricultural produce. Its rulers had no lasting dynasty or court to speak of.
taifa-of-lisbon.e: By 1034 the Aftasids of the [[s:taifa-of-badajoz|Taifa of Badajoz]] had absorbed [[e:lisbon|Lisbon]]. It stayed under [[e:badajoz|Badajoz]] until 1093, was briefly ceded to [[e:alfonso-vi-of-castile|Alfonso VI of Castile]], then passed to the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]], and [[e:afonso-i-of-kongo|Afonso I]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-portugal|Kingdom of Portugal]] took it in 1147 with the help of crusaders.

taifa-of-ceuta.t: A taifa across the Strait in Ceuta and Tangier, founded by a former Hammudid slave commander and the last obstacle to Almoravid control of the Strait.
taifa-of-ceuta.o: [[e:ceuta|Ceuta]] had been a Hammudid possession. Around 1061 Suqut al-Barghawati, a commander of slave origin who had served the Hammudids, made himself independent there and in Tangier, ruling the African shore of the [[e:strait-of-gibraltar|Strait of Gibraltar]].
taifa-of-ceuta.r: Suqut controlled the vital ports linking [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]] to [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]] and maintained ties with the [[e:taifa|taifas]], including the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]]. His state was essentially a military regime defending the coast against the [[s:almoravid-empire|Almoravid Empire]], which was expanding across [[e:morocco|Morocco]].
taifa-of-ceuta.e: The [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] took Tangier in 1077, killing the aged Suqut in battle, and captured [[e:ceuta|Ceuta]] from his son around 1083-1084. Control of Ceuta allowed them to cross into [[e:iberia|Iberia]] in 1086.

tusculum.t: Latin hill town in the Alban Hills, once a leader of the Latins against Rome, which in 381 BCE became the first community given Roman citizenship.
tusculum.o: Tusculum stood on a high ridge of the Alban Hills above modern Frascati, overlooking the routes south-east from [[e:rome|Rome]]. Legend made Telegonus, son of Odysseus and Circe, its founder. It was an important [[e:latin|Latin]] town by the 6th century BCE, with links to Rome's last kings.
tusculum.r: Its leading family, the Mamilii, intermarried with the Tarquins; Octavius Mamilius, son-in-law of Tarquinius Superbus, is said to have led the [[e:latins|Latins]] against [[e:rome|Rome]] at Lake Regillus around 496 BCE. Afterwards Tusculum became one of Rome's most loyal allies in the wars against the [[s:aequi|Aequi]] and [[s:volsci|Volsci]], and it hosted shrines of Castor and Pollux, gods also linked to Regillus.
tusculum.e: In 381 BCE, after a brief suspicion of disloyalty, [[e:rome|Rome]] granted Tusculum full citizenship while letting it keep its own magistrates, making it the first municipium. It produced leading Roman families, among them that of [[e:cato-the-elder|Cato the Elder]], and Cicero's villa there gave its name to his Tusculan Disputations.

taceddinids.t: A small Turkmen beylik around Niksar in the hinterland of the Black Sea, closely tied by marriage to the Empire of Trebizond.
taceddinids.o: As Eretnid authority weakened in the mid 14th century, local [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] chiefs took control of the Pontic hinterland between Niksar and the coast. One of them, Taceddin Bey, founded a [[e:beylik|beylik]] around Niksar.
taceddinids.r: The [[e:beylik|beylik]] held the inland valleys and parts of the coast near Unye and ruled [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] tribes, including the Chepni. Its relations with the [[s:empire-of-trebizond|Empire of Trebizond]] mixed raiding and alliance: Taceddin married a daughter of Alexios III. Taceddin died fighting Trebizond in 1362. The beylik was later drawn into the struggles between Kadi Burhan al-Din and the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]].
taceddinids.e: The [[e:beylik|beylik]] came under Ottoman control in the early 15th century and was absorbed around 1428.

tajik-assr.t: The first Tajik national republic, created in 1924 as an autonomous part of Soviet Uzbekistan.
tajik-assr.o: In the national delimitation of 1924 the mainly Tajik-speaking mountain districts of eastern [[e:bukhara|Bukhara]] and the Pamirs were organised as the Tajik ASSR within the [[s:uzbek-ssr|Uzbek SSR]]. The village of Dushanbe was chosen as capital and grew rapidly.
tajik-assr.r: The republic was a poor, mountainous territory still fighting the last Basmachi bands. Soviet authorities built roads, schools and irrigation for [[e:cotton|cotton]], and promoted the Tajik language, which was written in a [[e:latin|Latin]] alphabet from 1928. Tajik intellectuals argued that [[e:samarkand|Samarkand]] and [[e:bukhara|Bukhara]], both Tajik-speaking cities, had been wrongly given to [[s:uzbekistan|Uzbekistan]].
tajik-assr.e: In 1929 the republic was separated from [[s:uzbekistan|Uzbekistan]] and raised to a union republic, the [[s:tajik-ssr|Tajik SSR]], with the Khujand region added. Dushanbe was renamed Stalinabad. Disputes over the borders drawn in 1924 continued to colour relations between Tajiks and [[e:uzbeks|Uzbeks]].

tanagra.t: Boeotian city famed for its painted terracotta figurines and the poet Corinna, and site of the battle where Sparta defeated Athens in 457 BCE.
tanagra.o: Tanagra lay in eastern Boeotia on a hill above the Asopus valley, near the border with Attica. Settled since the [[e:bronze-age|Bronze Age]], it was a city by the Archaic period and a member of the [[s:boeotian-league|Boeotian League]], often second only to [[s:thebes|Thebes]].
tanagra.r: Tanagra was the home of the lyric poet Corinna, said to have competed with Pindar. In 457 BCE [[s:sparta|Sparta]] and its allies defeated [[s:athens|Athens]] at the Battle of Tanagra, though [[e:athens|Athens]] won at nearby Oenophyta soon afterwards and controlled Boeotia for a decade. In the 4th century BCE Tanagra's workshops produced elegant terracotta figurines of women, now called Tanagras.
tanagra.e: Tanagra survived Theban dominance and the Macedonian period as a prosperous town and came under Roman control in 146 BCE. Its cemeteries, looted in the 1870s, filled museums with its figurines.

tigiria-state.t: One of the smallest princely states of Odisha, a tiny chiefship on the Mahanadi west of Cuttack.
tigiria-state.o: Tradition places the founding in the 13th century, but little is reliably known about its origins.
tigiria-state.r: Tigiria covered only a few dozen square miles of farmland on the south bank of the Mahanadi. It was one of the Orissa Tributary Mahals under British supervision after 1803. Its history is poorly recorded.
tigiria-state.e: Tigiria merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948 and is now in Cuttack district.

third-portuguese-republic.t: Portugal's democratic republic, born in the Carnation Revolution of 1974, which ended the empire and took the country into Europe.
third-portuguese-republic.o: On 25 April 1974 the Armed Forces Movement, junior officers weary of the colonial wars, overthrew the [[s:estado-novo-portugal|Estado Novo (Portugal)]] in the almost bloodless [[e:carnation-revolution|Carnation Revolution]]. A turbulent revolutionary period followed, with nationalisations and land seizures, until a moderate coup on 25 November 1975.
third-portuguese-republic.r: The Constitution of 1976 established a semi-presidential democracy. Portugal granted independence to [[e:guinea-bissau|Guinea-Bissau]], [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Mozambique]], [[s:portuguese-angola|Angola]], [[e:cape-verde|Cape Verde]] and [[e:sao-tome|São Tomé]] in 1974-1975, receiving hundreds of thousands of returnees. Mário Soares's Socialists and the Social Democrats alternated in power. Portugal joined the European Economic Community in 1986 and adopted the euro in 1999, and handed [[e:macau|Macau]] to [[e:china|China]] the same year.
third-portuguese-republic.e: Portugal remains a parliamentary democracy and member of the [[e:european-union|European Union]] and NATO. After the 2011 debt crisis and bailout, it recovered with growing tourism and investment.

tajikistan.t: The only Persian-speaking state of former Soviet Central Asia, which recovered from a devastating civil war under the long rule of Emomali Rahmon.
tajikistan.o: The [[s:tajik-ssr|Tajik SSR]] declared independence on 9 September 1991. Tension between the old communist elite, largely from Khujand and Kulob, and an opposition of democrats, Islamists and Pamiris from Gharm and Gorno-Badakhshan erupted into civil war in 1992.
tajikistan.r: The civil war of 1992 to 1997 killed tens of thousands and displaced hundreds of thousands. Emomali Rahmon, from Kulob, became head of state in 1992 and president in 1994. A UN-brokered peace agreement in 1997 brought the United Tajik Opposition into government, but Rahmon later sidelined it and banned the Islamic [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] Party in 2015. The economy depends on aluminium, [[e:cotton|cotton]], hydropower such as the Rogun dam, and remittances from migrants in [[e:russia|Russia]].
tajikistan.e: Tajikistan remains a presidential republic dominated by Rahmon and his family, with close security ties to [[e:russia|Russia]] and growing Chinese investment, and periodic border clashes with [[s:kyrgyzstan|Kyrgyzstan]] over disputed enclaves.

tuttul.t: Tuttul, a city on the Euphrates near modern Raqqa, sacred to the god Dagan, where Sargon of Akkad prayed before conquering the upper Euphrates.
tuttul.o: Tuttul stood at Tell Bi'a where the Balikh river meets the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]], an ideal place for river and caravan traffic. It was a substantial city by the mid-3rd millennium BCE and became famous as the cult centre of Dagan, the chief god of the middle Euphrates.
tuttul.r: [[e:sargon-of-akkad|Sargon]] of the [[s:akkadian-empire|Akkadian Empire]] recorded that he bowed to Dagan at Tuttul, who granted him [[s:mari|Mari]], [[s:ebla|Ebla]] and the cedar forests. In the 18th century BCE Tuttul was a seat of Amorite tribal kings who fought Yahdun-Lim of [[e:mari|Mari]], and later fell under Shamshi-Adad and [[e:zimri-lim|Zimri-Lim]]. German excavations from 1980 uncovered palaces and tombs.
tuttul.e: After [[e:hammurabi|Hammurabi]] of the [[s:babylonian-empire|Babylonian Empire]] destroyed [[s:mari|Mari]], Tuttul declined and lost its independence around 1760 BCE. It remained a minor settlement, and its sanctuary of Dagan faded from the record.

taifa-of-granada.t: The Zirid kingdom of Granada, founded by Sanhaja Berbers, which made Granada a major city and left a rare royal memoir by its last king.
taifa-of-granada.o: Around 1013 the Sanhaja [[e:berbers|Berber]] leader Zawi ibn Ziri, a veteran of the caliphal wars, took over the district of Elvira and moved its centre to the more defensible hill of [[e:granada|Granada]]. His nephew Habbus established the dynasty when Zawi returned to [[e:ifriqiya|Ifriqiya]].
taifa-of-granada.r: Badis (1038-1073) built much of the Alcazaba and ruled with the Jewish [[e:vizier|vizier]] Samuel ibn Naghrela, a poet and general, and then his son Joseph. Resentment against Joseph led to the [[e:granada|Granada]] massacre of 1066. The kingdom fought Almería and [[e:seville|Seville]] and paid heavy tribute to [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]].
taifa-of-granada.e: The [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] deposed the last king, Abd Allah ibn Buluggin, in 1090 and exiled him to Aghmat, where he wrote his memoirs, a unique first-hand account of [[e:taifa|taifa]] politics. [[e:granada|Granada]] later became the capital of the [[s:emirate-of-granada|Emirate of Granada]].

turduli.t: A people of the south-west, close kin of the Turdetani, with a northern branch, the Turduli Veteres, living near the Douro in Portugal.
turduli.o: The Turduli lived in the middle Guadiana and Guadalquivir regions next to the [[s:turdetani|Turdetani]], from whom Strabo said they could hardly be distinguished. A separate group, the Turduli Veteres or Old Turduli, settled south of the lower Douro in northern Portugal, probably after migrating from the south.
turduli.r: Little is recorded of their government. Their economy relied on farming, herding and the mineral wealth of the Sierra Morena. Pliny lists their towns in both [[s:hispania-baetica|Baetica]] and [[s:lusitania|Lusitania]], which shows how widespread the group was.
turduli.e: They were absorbed into Roman [[s:hispania-ulterior|Hispania Ulterior]] during the 2nd century BCE, following the conquest of the south after 206 BCE and the Lusitanian wars. Under Augustus their lands were divided between [[s:hispania-baetica|Baetica]] and [[s:lusitania|Lusitania]].

thanjavur-nayak-kingdom.t: A Nayaka kingdom of the Kaveri delta whose rulers made Thanjavur a centre of Carnatic music, painting and Telugu literature.
thanjavur-nayak-kingdom.o: Sevappa Nayak, a [[s:vijayanagara-empire|Vijayanagara]] noble married into the royal family, was appointed to govern the Thanjavur region around 1532. His dynasty ruled the [[e:rice|rice]]-rich Kaveri delta as [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[e:vijayanagara-empire|Vijayanagara Empire]] and, after its decline, as independent kings.
thanjavur-nayak-kingdom.r: Raghunatha Nayak, the most celebrated ruler, was a poet, musician and patron who supported [[s:vijayanagara-empire|Vijayanagara]] in its last wars. The court produced Telugu yakshagana dramas and musical treatises, laying foundations of Carnatic music. The Nayaks permitted the [[s:danish-india|Danish East India]] Company to settle at Tranquebar in 1620. Temples at Kumbakonam and Thanjavur were enlarged.
thanjavur-nayak-kingdom.e: Conflict with the [[s:madurai-nayak-dynasty|Madurai Nayak dynasty]] led to the death of Vijayaraghava Nayak in 1673. The [[s:bijapur-sultanate|Bijapur Sultanate]] then sent the [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] general Ekoji, who seized Thanjavur in 1675 and founded the Maratha line of Thanjavur.

taranchi-sultanate.t: A short-lived Muslim sultanate in the Ili valley that rose during the Dungan revolt and was occupied by Russia in 1871.
taranchi-sultanate.o: In 1864 a rebellion of Hui (Dungan) and Turkic Muslims against Qing rule spread across [[e:xinjiang|Xinjiang]]. In the Ili valley, the Taranchis, [[e:uyghurs|Uyghur]] farmers descended from settlers brought by the [[e:dzungars|Dzungars]], joined the Dungans, captured the Qing garrisons of Ili, including Huiyuan, and established a sultanate at Ghulja.
taranchi-sultanate.r: The Taranchi leader Abil Oghlu became sultan in 1866 after the Taranchis turned on the Dungans. The sultanate ruled a farming population in the Ili valley, under Islamic law, and dealt with Russian merchants and neighbouring [[s:yettishar|Yettishar]].
taranchi-sultanate.e: Fearing that Yaqub Beg of [[s:yettishar|Yettishar]] would take Ili and alarmed by instability on its frontier, [[e:russia|Russia]] occupied the Ili valley in 1871, ending the sultanate. Russia returned most of the region to the Qing under the Treaty of [[e:saint-petersburg|Saint Petersburg]] of 1881.

transvaal-colony.t: The British colony made from the conquered Transvaal republic, rebuilt around the gold mines of the Witwatersrand.
transvaal-colony.o: British forces occupied Pretoria in June 1900 and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] proclaimed the annexation of the [[s:south-african-republic|South African Republic]] in September 1900. The Treaty of Vereeniging in May 1902 ended [[e:boers|Boer]] resistance and confirmed the Transvaal Colony.
transvaal-colony.r: High Commissioner Lord Milner's administration rebuilt railways and farms and restarted the gold mines, recruiting young British administrators known as Milner's Kindergarten. To solve a labour shortage, more than 60,000 Chinese indentured labourers were brought to the mines between 1904 and 1907, a scandal in [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]]. Self-government came in 1907, and the Het Volk party of Louis Botha and Jan Smuts won the election.
transvaal-colony.e: Botha and Smuts led the negotiations for union, and in 1910 the [[s:south-african-republic|Transvaal]] joined the [[s:union-of-south-africa|Union of South Africa]] as the Transvaal Province, with Pretoria as the administrative capital of the new state.

taqali.t: A Muslim kingdom in the Nuba Mountains of Kordofan whose kings, the meks, kept their throne for over four centuries until 1969.
taqali.o: Taqali arose in the hills of the north-eastern Nuba Mountains in the early 16th century. Its traditions tell of a Muslim holy man from the [[e:nile|Nile]] who married into a local ruling family, founding a dynasty that drew on both Islamic and Nuba roots, with its seat at Tasi.
taqali.r: The meks ruled a mixed population of Nuba hill farmers and Arab settlers, protected by rugged terrain. Taqali paid tribute at times to the [[s:funj-sultanate|Funj Sultanate]] and fought off raids from the [[s:musabbaat-sultanate|Musabba'at sultanate]] and the [[s:darfur-sultanate|Darfur Sultanate]]. It traded slaves, gold and [[e:cattle|cattle]] with the [[e:nile|Nile]] valley and served as a centre of [[e:islam|Islam]] in the Nuba Mountains.
taqali.e: Taqali survived [[s:turco-egyptian-sudan|Turco-Egyptian Sudan]] as a tributary; Mek Adam Umm Dabbalo supported the [[s:mahdist-state|Mahdist State]]. Under [[s:anglo-egyptian-sudan|Anglo-Egyptian Sudan]] the meks served as native administrators. [[e:sudan|Sudan's]] government abolished the native administration system in 1969, ending the kingdom's official role.

tlacopan.t: The Tepanec city on the western shore of Lake Texcoco that became the third and junior member of the Aztec Triple Alliance.
tlacopan.o: Tlacopan (modern Tacuba) was a [[e:tepanecs|Tepanec]] town subject to [[s:tepanec-empire|Azcapotzalco]]. In the Tepanec war of 1428, its ruler Totoquihuaztli supported [[e:tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] and [[s:texcoco|Texcoco]] against [[e:maxtla|Maxtla]] of [[e:azcapotzalco|Azcapotzalco]], and Tlacopan was then made a partner in the new [[e:aztec-empire|Triple Alliance]].
tlacopan.r: As the third member of the alliance, Tlacopan received one fifth of the tribute from joint conquests, against two fifths each for [[e:tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] and [[s:texcoco|Texcoco]]. It led the [[e:tepanecs|Tepanec]] towns of the western valley and controlled lands in the Toluca valley. Its ruler held the title of [[s:tepanec-empire|Tepaneca]] tecuhtli.
tlacopan.e: Tlacopan's ruler Tetlepanquetzal fought the Spanish with Cuauhtemoc and was executed by [[e:hernan-cortes|Cortés]] in 1525 during the expedition to [[s:republic-of-honduras|Honduras]]. The Spanish had fled [[e:tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] along the Tlacopan causeway on the Noche Triste of 1520, and Tlacopan, called Tacuba, is now a district of [[e:mexico-city|Mexico City]].

tencteri.t: A Germanic people of the lower Rhine famous for their cavalry, nearly destroyed by Caesar in 55 BCE yet still present in Roman sources centuries later.
tencteri.o: The Tencteri and their neighbours the Usipetes were driven from their homes by the [[s:suebi|Suebi]] and crossed the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] into Gaul in 55 BCE. [[e:julius-caesar|Julius Caesar]] attacked them during negotiations near the Meuse and Rhine and massacred large numbers, an act condemned at the time in the [[s:commune-of-rome|Roman Senate]]. The survivors fled to the [[s:sugambri|Sugambri]].
tencteri.r: [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] singles out the Tencteri for their horsemanship, writing that the horses and herds passed to the bravest son rather than simply to the eldest. They lived on the right bank of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] opposite [[s:free-imperial-city-of-cologne|Cologne]] and dealt with the Roman city of the Ubii. In 16 BCE they joined the [[s:sugambri|Sugambri]] in defeating Marcus Lollius.
tencteri.e: The Tencteri appear in the Batavian revolt of 69 and are last mentioned in the late Roman period. By the later 3rd century their territory lay within the area of the [[s:franks|Frankish confederation]], into which they were most likely absorbed.

tottori-domain.t: The domain of Inaba and Hoki on the Sea of Japan coast, ruled for most of the Edo period by a senior branch of the Ikeda family.
tottori-domain.o: Tottori castle had been the scene of [[e:toyotomi-hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi's]] notorious starvation siege of 1581. After [[e:battle-of-sekigahara|Sekigahara]], Ikeda Nagayoshi held Tottori with a small fief. In 1617 the [[e:shogun|shogunate]] gave Ikeda Mitsumasa the provinces of Inaba and Hoki, with 325,000 koku.
tottori-domain.r: In 1632 Mitsumasa exchanged domains with his cousin Ikeda Mitsunaka of Okayama, and Mitsunaka's line ruled Tottori until 1871. The domain governed Hoki through a senior retainer family stationed at Yonago castle. Its economy rested on [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:cotton|cotton]] and iron sand smelting in the Chugoku mountains, and it guarded the Sea of [[e:japan|Japan]] coast.
tottori-domain.e: The last lord, Ikeda Yoshinori, a brother of the last [[e:shogun|shogun]] [[e:tokugawa-yoshinobu|Tokugawa Yoshinobu]], nevertheless sided with the imperial forces in 1868. After abolition in 1871 the domain became Tottori Prefecture.

tharoch-state.t: A small Rajput hill state in the upper Pabbar region east of Shimla, one of the minor Simla Hill States.
tharoch-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500, but little is reliably known of its origins.
tharoch-state.r: Tharoch was a small mountain state related to its neighbour [[s:jubbal-state|Jubbal State]]. It was occupied by Gurkhas of the [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Kingdom of Nepal]] in the early 19th century and restored as a Simla Hill State under British protection after 1815. Its history is poorly recorded.
tharoch-state.e: Tharoch merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now part of Shimla district.

tyre.t: Tyre, the island city that led Phoenician trade across the Mediterranean, founded Carthage and resisted Alexander in a seven-month siege.
tyre.o: Tyre was built on an offshore island with a mainland suburb, giving it a nearly impregnable harbour. It was a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]] in the [[e:akhetaten|Amarna]] age under King Abimilki, and after the [[e:late-bronze-age-collapse|Late Bronze Age collapse]] it emerged in the 10th century BCE as the strongest Phoenician city.
tyre.r: Its kings, such as Hiram I, ally of [[e:solomon|Solomon]] of the [[s:united-kingdom-of-israel|United Kingdom of Israel]], ruled a merchant state with the temple of Melqart at its heart. Tyre produced [[e:tyrian-purple|murex]] purple dye and glass, and its sailors founded colonies across the western [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]], including [[e:carthage|Carthage]], traditionally in 814 BCE.
tyre.e: Tyre paid tribute to the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] and survived a 13-year siege by [[e:nebuchadnezzar-ii|Nebuchadnezzar II]] of the [[s:chaldean-empire|Chaldean Empire]]. Under the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]] it kept its kings. In 332 BCE Alexander of the [[s:macedonian-empire|Macedonian Empire]] built a causeway, stormed the island and sold its people into [[e:slavery|slavery]].

territory-of-hawaii.t: Hawaii's six decades as an American territory, dominated by sugar companies and transformed by Pearl Harbor, before it became the 50th state.
territory-of-hawaii.o: After the [[s:united-states|United States]] annexed the [[s:republic-of-hawaii|Republic of Hawaii]] in 1898, the Organic Act of 1900 organised the islands as a territory, granting US citizenship to its citizens and an elected legislature, with a governor appointed by the president. Sanford B. Dole, president of the republic, became the first territorial governor.
territory-of-hawaii.r: Five corporations, the Big Five, controlled [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], shipping and banking, while James Dole made the islands the world's leading pineapple producer. Japanese immigrants and their children became the largest ethnic group. The Japanese attack on [[e:attack-on-pearl-harbor|Pearl Harbor]] on 7 December 1941 brought martial law until 1944. Nisei soldiers of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team won fame in [[e:europe|Europe]], and in 1954 Democrats backed by labour unions ended Republican dominance.
territory-of-hawaii.e: Statehood was long delayed by racial prejudice and Southern opposition. Congress passed the Admission Act in 1959, voters approved it overwhelmingly, and Hawaii became the 50th state on 21 August 1959.

thaton-kingdom.t: A Mon kingdom of Lower Myanmar, remembered as a centre of Theravada Buddhism whose conquest by Pagan in 1057 brought Mon learning to the Burmans.
thaton-kingdom.o: Thaton, near the Gulf of [[s:hanthawaddy-kingdom|Martaban]], appears in Mon and Burmese tradition as the capital of [[s:suphannaphum|Suvarnabhumi]], the 'golden land' of Buddhist legend. Inscriptions and archaeology suggest a Mon Buddhist town of the later first millennium, though the scale of its kingdom and its early history are uncertain.
thaton-kingdom.r: Thaton was a port and religious centre in the Mon-speaking region of [[s:hanthawaddy-kingdom|Ramannadesa]]. It was famed for its monks and Pali scriptures, and Burmese chronicles credit the monk Shin Arahan, said to have come from Thaton, with converting Anawrahta of Pagan to [[e:theravada-buddhism|Theravada Buddhism]]. Its last king, Manuha, is the best known ruler.
thaton-kingdom.e: According to the chronicles, Anawrahta of the [[s:pagan-kingdom|Pagan Kingdom]] attacked Thaton in 1057 after Manuha refused to give up Buddhist scriptures, and carried off the king, monks and craftsmen. Manuha's captivity is recalled by the Manuha temple at Bagan. Mon culture revived later under the [[s:hanthawaddy-kingdom|Hanthawaddy Kingdom]].

thamud.t: An ancient Arab people of the Hejaz, known from Assyrian annals to the Quran, whose name lives on in thousands of rock inscriptions.
thamud.o: The Thamud are first named among Arab groups defeated by [[e:sargon-ii|Sargon II]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] in 715 BCE. They lived in north-western [[e:arabia|Arabia]], between the [[s:kingdom-of-hejaz|Hejaz]] and the Nafud, and later Greek and Roman writers such as Diodorus, Pliny and Ptolemy also place them there.
thamud.r: They seem to have been a confederation of herding and oasis tribes rather than a centralised kingdom. Their name was given by modern scholars to a large body of Ancient North Arabian graffiti, though not all were written by Thamud. At Ruwafa, Thamudic tribesmen built a temple in the 160s CE honouring the Roman emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus.
thamud.e: Around 400 CE Roman lists record a cavalry unit of Thamudeni in [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and [[e:palestine|Palestine]], after which they disappear. The [[e:quran|Quran]] tells of the Thamud as a people destroyed for rejecting the prophet [[s:salihids|Salih]], and links them to the rock tombs of Hegra, which were in fact Nabataean.

tippu-tips-state.t: The commercial empire of the Zanzibari trader Tippu Tip on the upper Congo, built on ivory and slaves and broken by the Congo Free State.
tippu-tips-state.o: Hamed bin Muhammad al-Murjebi, called Tippu Tip, was a Swahili-Arab trader from [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]] who led caravans deep into the interior from the 1860s. Around 1870 he established himself in [[e:manyema|Manyema]] on the upper Lualaba, making Kasongo the centre of a domain of trading posts, allied chiefs and armed followers.
tippu-tips-state.r: The state was a commercial network rather than a kingdom: armed bands collected [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and captives, plantations of [[e:rice|rice]] and other crops fed the settlements, and goods moved east to [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]]. Tippu Tip helped Henry Morton Stanley down the Lualaba in 1876, and in 1887 the [[s:congo-free-state|Congo Free State]] appointed him governor of the Stanley Falls district.
tippu-tips-state.e: Tippu Tip retired to [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]] in 1890. War broke out between the Free State and the Swahili-Arab traders in 1892, Kasongo fell in 1893, and by 1894 the state had been destroyed, its lands absorbed into the [[s:congo-free-state|Congo Free State]].

travancore.t: The kingdom of the southern tip of India, built by Marthanda Varma and known for its temple-state ideology, high literacy and social reform.
travancore.o: Marthanda Varma, ruler of the small chiefdom of [[s:kingdom-of-venad|Venad]] from 1729, crushed rival nobles, annexed neighbouring principalities and defeated the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] at Colachel in 1741. In 1750 he dedicated the enlarged kingdom to the deity Padmanabha, ruling thereafter as the god's servant from Thiruvananthapuram.
travancore.r: Travancore allied with the British against Tipu [[e:sultan|Sultan]] and became a subsidiary ally in 1795 and 1805; the [[e:diwan|diwan]] Velu Thampi's revolt of 1809 was suppressed. Rulers such as Swathi Thirunal patronised music and learning, and the state invested early in schools, so that literacy rose far above the Indian average. The Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936 opened state temples to all [[e:hinduism|Hindus]]. Its economy rested on [[e:pepper|pepper]], coconut and [[e:rubber|rubber]].
travancore.e: In 1947 the [[e:diwan|diwan]] C. P. Ramaswami Iyer proposed independence, but after protests and an attack on him the Maharaja acceded to [[e:india|India]]. On 1 July 1949 Travancore merged with Cochin to form [[s:travancore-cochin|Travancore-Cochin]], the core of Kerala from 1956.
travancore.re: Hinduism; large Christian and Muslim minorities

tyumen-khanate.t: A Shibanid khanate of western Siberia that briefly ruled the Golden Horde's eastern steppes and was the forerunner of the Khanate of Sibir.
tyumen-khanate.o: The Tyumen Khanate grew from the old [[s:ulus-of-shiban|Ulus of Shiban]] around Chimgi-Tura on the Tura River in the early 15th century, as [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]] authority faded. Shibanid princes ruled there, and the khan Abu'l-Khayr was proclaimed in this region in 1428 before moving south.
tyumen-khanate.r: The khanate ruled [[e:tatars|Tatar]] nomads and the forest peoples of western [[e:siberia|Siberia]], collecting tribute in [[e:fur-trade|furs]] that were traded south and west. Its most notable ruler, Ibak Khan, took part in the destruction of the [[s:great-horde|Great Horde]], killing its khan Ahmad in 1481 after the [[e:great-stand-on-the-ugra-river|Great Stand on the Ugra River]], and claimed leadership among the Jochids.
tyumen-khanate.e: Around 1495 the local Taibugid clan seized power, killing Ibak and moving the capital to Qashliq on the Irtysh, founding the [[s:khanate-of-sibir|Khanate of Sibir]]. Chimgi-Tura was later rebuilt by the Russians as Tyumen in 1586.

tetrarchy-of-philip.t: The north-eastern share of Herod the Great's kingdom, ruled for almost four decades by his son Philip from the new city of Caesarea Philippi.
tetrarchy-of-philip.o: When Herod the Great died in 4 BCE, Augustus confirmed his will with changes and divided the kingdom among three sons. Philip received the lands north and east of the [[e:sea-of-galilee|Sea of Galilee]]: Gaulanitis, Batanaea, Trachonitis, Auranitis and part of [[s:ituraea|Ituraea]], a frontier zone the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] had entrusted to Herod to suppress brigandage.
tetrarchy-of-philip.r: Philip governed as a Roman client with the title tetrarch. His subjects were largely Syrian, Arab and Greek-speaking pagans with Jewish communities, and he was the first Jewish ruler to put the emperor's portrait on his coins. He refounded Paneas at the springs of the [[s:hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan|Jordan]] as [[s:lordship-of-caesarea|Caesarea]] Philippi and raised Bethsaida to a city named Julias. Josephus describes him as a mild, accessible ruler who travelled his territory to judge cases.
tetrarchy-of-philip.e: Philip died in 34 CE without children, and Tiberius attached the tetrarchy to the province of [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]]. In 37 Caligula granted it to Herod Agrippa I, making it the core of the [[s:kingdom-of-herod-agrippa|Kingdom of Herod Agrippa]]. [[s:lordship-of-caesarea|Caesarea]] Philippi remains known from the Gospels as the place of Peter's confession.

tharad-state.t: A small Vaghela Rajput state in the Banas Kantha country of northern Gujarat.
tharad-state.o: Tharad was held by a Vaghela [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] family in the dry country north of the Banas river. The register dates it to around 1700, and the town had an older history as a medieval centre.
tharad-state.r: The ruler governed a territory of [[e:millet|millet]] fields and grazing land, under the [[s:palanpur-state|Palanpur]] and later the Banas Kantha Agency in the British period. Little else is recorded in standard references.
tharad-state.e: Tharad merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in Banaskantha district.

taifa-of-murcia.t: A south-eastern taifa that shifted between local rulers and powerful neighbours before falling to the Almoravids, with Murcia's huerta as its core.
taifa-of-murcia.o: [[e:murcia|Murcia]], heir to the old Visigothic-era region of [[s:tudmir|Tudmir]], broke from [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]] around 1011. For its first decades it was usually governed for the Amirid rulers of Almería and [[e:valencia|Valencia]], until the local family of the [[s:tahirid-sultanate|Banu Tahir]] took effective control under Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Tahir.
taifa-of-murcia.r: The Segura valley's irrigation supported grain, fruit and textile production. The [[s:tahirid-sultanate|Banu Tahir]] ruled as patricians, nominally under [[e:valencia|Valencia]]. In 1078 al-Mutamid of the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]] sent his [[e:vizier|vizier]], the poet Ibn Ammar, to seize the city; Ibn Ammar and then his officer Ibn Rashiq ruled it in defiance of [[e:seville|Seville]].
taifa-of-murcia.e: Ibn Rashiq's double dealing with [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]], which held the nearby fortress of Aledo, made him unpopular. The [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] took [[e:murcia|Murcia]] in 1091. It re-emerged as the [[s:second-taifa-of-murcia|Second Taifa of Murcia]] in 1147.

taebong.t: The kingdom of the one-eyed monk-king Gung Ye in central Korea, from whose collapse Wang Geon founded Goryeo.
taebong.o: Gung Ye, said to be an outcast [[s:silla|Silla]] prince who lost an eye as an infant, became a monk and then a rebel commander in the 890s. Gathering support in the central and northern regions, including from the Wang family of Songak, he proclaimed a kingdom in 901 called Later [[s:goguryeo|Goguryeo]], appealing to the memory of Goguryeo.
taebong.r: The state changed name to Majin in 904 and to Taebong in 911, and moved its capital from Songak to Cheorwon in 905. Gung Ye set up a central bureaucracy with new ministries and expanded southward, using the general Wang Geon to win battles against [[s:later-baekje|Later Baekje]]. He increasingly proclaimed himself the Maitreya Buddha and ruled with suspicion and violence.
taebong.e: In 918 leading generals overthrew Gung Ye, who was killed while fleeing, and placed Wang Geon on the throne. Wang Geon renamed the state [[s:goryeo|Goryeo]] and moved the capital back to Songak.

tripolitania-vilayet.t: Libya under direct Ottoman rule from 1835, the last Ottoman province in Africa until the Italian invasion of 1911.
tripolitania-vilayet.o: In 1835 the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]], fearing French intervention after the conquest of [[e:algiers|Algiers]], ended the rule of [[s:karamanli-tripoli|Karamanli Tripoli]] and restored direct administration. Ottoman forces spent the following decades subduing tribal revolts, notably that of Ghuma al-Mahmudi in the Jabal Nafusa, which lasted until 1858.
tripolitania-vilayet.r: The province, organised as a vilayet under the [[e:tanzimat|Tanzimat]] reforms, included [[s:tripolitania|Tripolitania]] and the [[s:sultanate-of-fezzan|Fezzan]], while [[e:cyrenaica|Cyrenaica]] was later administered separately. Governors introduced new courts, schools and conscription, but authority in the interior was limited, and the [[s:senussi-order|Senussi Order]] dominated Cyrenaica's hinterland. The trans-Saharan [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] persisted until late in the century.
tripolitania-vilayet.e: [[e:italy|Italy]] invaded in 1911, and after war with the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] the Treaty of Ouchy in 1912 transferred the province to [[s:italian-libya|Italian Libya]]. Local resistance, supported by Ottoman officers, continued for years.

thakuri-dynasty.t: The medieval rulers of the Kathmandu Valley between the Licchavis and the Mallas, an age of trade with Tibet and Buddhist manuscript copying.
thakuri-dynasty.o: After the [[s:licchavi-kingdom-of-nepal|Licchavi Kingdom of Nepal]] faded in the 8th century, the history of the valley is obscure. The Thakuri period is conventionally dated from 879, the start of the [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Nepal]] Sambat era, though the founder is uncertain; later chronicles name Raghavadeva and credit Gunakamadeva with founding Kantipur, the city that became Kathmandu.
thakuri-dynasty.r: Royal power was often divided, with rival kings ruling different towns of the valley at the same time. The valley prospered as the main route between [[e:india|India]] and [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]], and its monasteries produced many illustrated Buddhist [[e:manuscript|manuscripts]], which became important sources as [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] declined in India. Shaiva [[e:hinduism|Hinduism]], centred on Pashupatinath, and Newar Buddhism flourished side by side, and Newari began to be written.
thakuri-dynasty.e: Thakuri rule ended around 1200 with the accession of Arimalla, founder of the Malla dynasty, which ruled the valley until the [[s:gorkha-kingdom|Gorkha]] conquest of 1768 to 1769.

territory-of-new-guinea.t: The former German New Guinea, governed by Australia under a League of Nations mandate, where the 1930s brought gold rushes and first contact with the Highlands.
territory-of-new-guinea.o: An Australian force captured [[s:german-new-guinea|German New Guinea]] in 1914 and held it under military rule. In 1920 the [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] granted [[s:commonwealth-of-australia|Australia]] a mandate over the territory, covering northeastern New [[e:guinea|Guinea]], the [[e:otto-von-bismarck|Bismarck]] Archipelago and Bougainville, and civil government began in 1921 with Rabaul as capital.
territory-of-new-guinea.r: German plantations were expropriated and sold to Australian ex-servicemen. Gold strikes at Edie Creek and Bulolo from 1926 led to dredges being flown in by aircraft, making New [[e:guinea|Guinea]] a pioneer of air freight. In 1933 the Leahy brothers and patrol officer Jim Taylor entered the densely populated Highlands, unknown to outsiders. Volcanic eruptions in 1937 led to plans to move the capital to Lae.
territory-of-new-guinea.e: [[e:japan|Japan]] seized Rabaul in January 1942 and made it its major base in the South Pacific. Civil administration was suspended until 1945, and in 1949 the territory, now a UN trust territory, was joined with [[s:territory-of-papua|Papua]] as the [[s:territory-of-papua-and-new-guinea|Territory of Papua and New Guinea]].
territory-of-new-guinea.la: English, Tok Pisin, Papuan and Austronesian languages

taifa-of-guadix.t: A short-lived highland taifa around Guadix and Baza, east of Granada, formed during the revolts against the Almoravids.
taifa-of-guadix.o: In 1145, as the Almoravid regime in [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]] disintegrated, local leaders took control of Guadix and Baza, two towns on the high plateau between [[e:granada|Granada]] and the coast at Almería region.
taifa-of-guadix.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, the state was centred on irrigated basins and cave settlements and controlled the route from [[e:granada|Granada]] to the east coast. Its leaders were caught between Ibn Mardanish of [[e:murcia|Murcia]], the Almoravid loyalists of Granada and the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]].
taifa-of-guadix.e: Around 1151 the district passed under [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] control. Guadix later belonged to the [[s:emirate-of-granada|Emirate of Granada]] until 1489.

taifa-of-carmona.t: A Berber taifa ruled by the Banu Birzal from the fortress town of Carmona, a rival of Seville in the lower Guadalquivir valley.
taifa-of-carmona.o: The Banu Birzal, [[e:zanata-berbers|Zanata Berbers]] brought to [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]] as soldiers by al-Mansur, took control of Carmona around 1013 during the civil war that destroyed the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]]. Their leader Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Birzali made the town the base of an independent principality.
taifa-of-carmona.r: Carmona, with strong Roman walls on a ridge above the fertile Vega, was one of the most defensible towns of the region. Its rulers at times also held Écija and Almodóvar and allied with the Hammudids of Málaga against [[e:seville|Seville]]. The state was a military lordship rather than a court of letters.
taifa-of-carmona.e: After long wars, al-Mutadid of the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]] took Carmona in 1067, and the Birzalid family was eclipsed. [[e:ferdinand-iii-of-castile|Ferdinand III of Castile]] captured the town in 1247.

tambralinga.t: A Buddhist trading kingdom on the Malay Peninsula centred on Nakhon Si Thammarat, whose king Chandrabhanu invaded Sri Lanka in the 13th century.
tambralinga.o: Tambralinga appears in Chinese sources as Danmaling and in [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] inscriptions from around the 8th century. Its centre lay at or near Nakhon Si Thammarat on the east coast of the peninsula. For long periods it was tied to the maritime network of [[e:srivijaya|Srivijaya]], before asserting itself as an independent power.
tambralinga.r: The kingdom drew its wealth from the trans-peninsular trade and exports such as aromatic woods and [[e:tin|tin]]. It sent missions to the [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] court in the 11th century. Its most famous ruler, Chandrabhanu Sridhamaraja, recorded in an inscription at Chaiya dated 1230, built up a navy and twice invaded [[s:sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], partly to obtain a sacred relic.
tambralinga.e: Chandrabhanu was defeated in [[s:sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]] by Pandyan forces in the 1260s, and Tambralinga weakened. By the late 13th century it had become the [[s:nakhon-si-thammarat-kingdom|Nakhon Si Thammarat Kingdom]], which accepted the overlordship of [[s:sukhothai-kingdom|Sukhothai]] and later [[s:ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya]], while retaining strong Sinhalese [[e:theravada-buddhism|Theravada]] links.

transcaucasian-democratic-federative-rep.t: A short-lived federation of Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, proclaimed in April 1918, which lasted barely a month before breaking into three states.
transcaucasian-democratic-federative-rep.o: Facing an Ottoman offensive and the loss of Kars, Ardahan and Batum under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, the Transcaucasian [[e:sejm|Sejm]] in Tiflis declared independence from [[e:russia|Russia]] on 22 April 1918, replacing the [[s:transcaucasian-commissariat|Transcaucasian Commissariat]] with a federal republic. Independence was declared reluctantly, mainly so that the region could negotiate with the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] as a sovereign state.
transcaucasian-democratic-federative-rep.r: The government was headed by the Georgian Menshevik Akaki Chkhenkeli, with Nikolay Chkheidze chairing the [[e:sejm|Sejm]]. It negotiated with the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] at [[s:empire-of-trebizond|Trebizond]] and Batum while Ottoman troops advanced. The three national groups had conflicting goals: Azerbaijani leaders sympathised with the Ottomans, [[e:armenians|Armenians]] feared them, and Georgians sought German protection.
transcaucasian-democratic-federative-rep.e: As the Ottoman army pushed into [[s:armenia|Armenia]], [[s:georgia|Georgia]] declared independence on 26 May 1918, and [[e:armenia|Armenia]] and [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]] followed two days later, dissolving the federation. The Soviets later revived the idea of union in the [[s:transcaucasian-sfsr|Transcaucasian SFSR]].

tatar-confederation.t: A powerful group of tribes in eastern Mongolia, enemies of Genghis Khan's family, whose name Europeans later applied to all the Mongol peoples.
tatar-confederation.o: [[e:tatars|Tatars]] appear in Old Turkic inscriptions of the 8th century as the Otuz Tatar and Toquz Tatar. By the 10th century tribes under this name occupied the grasslands of eastern [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]] around Lakes Hulun and Buir, a numerous and wealthy people organised in several clans under their own chiefs.
tatar-confederation.r: They lived by pastoral nomadism, herding horses, [[e:cattle|cattle]] and sheep, and traded and fought with their settled neighbours.
