The [[s:jin-dynasty-1115-1234|Jin dynasty]] (1115-1234) used them as allies against other steppe peoples; according to the Secret History of the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] they handed the Mongol leader Ambaghai to the Jin for execution and poisoned [[e:genghis-khan|Temüjin's]] father Yesügei. There was no lasting central government.
tatar-confederation.e: In 1196 the Jin, with [[e:genghis-khan|Temüjin]] and the Keraite ruler Toghrul, defeated the [[e:tatars|Tatar]] chief Megüjin Seultü. In 1202 Temüjin crushed the remaining Tatars and had most of their men killed, absorbing the survivors into the future [[s:mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]].

taifa-of-zaragoza.t: The powerful taifa of the Ebro valley whose Hudid kings built the Aljafería palace, employed El Cid and held off Christian advance until 1110.
taifa-of-zaragoza.o: [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]], capital of the Upper March, came under the Arab Tujibid governor Mundhir I around 1018. In 1039 the Tujibids were overthrown and Sulayman ibn Hud al-Mustain founded the Hudid dynasty, which went on to rule for some seventy years.
taifa-of-zaragoza.r: Ahmad I al-Muqtadir (1046-1081) annexed Tortosa and Dénia and built the Aljafería palace. His son Yusuf al-Mutaman wrote a major treatise on geometry. The kingdom paid tribute to [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]] and Barcelona and from 1081 employed El Cid against [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]]. Its farmland, trade and learning made it one of the richest [[e:taifa|taifas]].
taifa-of-zaragoza.e: Ahmad II al-Mustain was killed fighting [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]] at Valtierra in 1110, and the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] then took [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]]. His son held on at [[s:rueda-de-jalon-hudid|Rueda de Jalón (Hudid)]]. [[e:alfonso-i-of-aragon|Alfonso I of Aragon]] captured Zaragoza in 1118.

tapajo.t: A large chiefdom at the meeting of the Tapajós and Amazon rivers, known for its intricate pottery and dark earth soils.
tapajo.o: The Tapajó people dominated the lower Tapajós river around the site of modern Santarém in [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]] from about 1000. The Santarém culture associated with them developed from earlier Amazonian traditions, and its main settlement covered several square kilometres.
tapajo.r: Spanish and Portuguese explorers in the 16th and 17th centuries described a numerous people under powerful chiefs who could field many warriors armed with poisoned arrows. The Tapajó farmed on terra preta, fertile dark earth created by long settlement, and fished in the rivers. Their potters made elaborate caryatid vessels and vases decorated with modelled animals and figures, and they carved green stone pendants called muiraquitãs.
tapajo.e: Portuguese slaving expeditions from the 1620s and the founding of a [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] mission in 1661, which became Santarém, ended Tapajó independence. Epidemics and enslavement destroyed most of the population. The Santarém ceramic style is today among the best known Amazonian archaeological traditions.

tututepec.t: The powerful Mixtec kingdom of the Pacific coast of Oaxaca, founded under Lord Eight Deer, which resisted the Aztecs to the end.
tututepec.o: Tututepec, Yucu Dzaa in Mixtec, became a royal seat in the late 11th century, when Lord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw established himself there around 1083 and used it as a base for conquests. It grew into the largest state of the Mixteca Costa.
tututepec.r: Tututepec controlled a large coastal territory with many subject towns, drawing tribute in [[e:cotton|cotton]], [[e:cacao|cacao]], gold and shells. Its rulers fought the Zapotecs and the [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]], which never fully conquered it. Archaeological survey shows a city of perhaps 20,000 people with outlying settlements across the lower Río Verde valley.
tututepec.e: In 1522 Pedro de Alvarado conquered Tututepec and seized its gold. The kingdom became a Spanish [[e:encomienda|encomienda]], and its native lords survived as caciques in the colonial era.

taras.t: The only Spartan colony in Italy, which grew into the leading Greek city of southern Italy and fought Rome with the help of Pyrrhus.
taras.o: Tradition says that the Partheniai, sons of Spartan women born during the Messenian War, were sent out under Phalanthus and founded Taras in 706 BCE. The city occupied a peninsula between the Mar Piccolo lagoon and the open sea, giving it the best harbour on the Gulf of [[s:principality-of-taranto|Taranto]].
taras.r: Taras grew rich on fishing, purple dye, fine wool, horses and pottery; Apulian red-figure vases were made there. After a heavy defeat by the Iapygians around 473 BCE it became a democracy. In the 4th century BCE the philosopher Archytas, a friend of [[e:plato|Plato]], was repeatedly elected general. Taras led the [[s:italiote-league|Italiote League]] and hired Greek commanders, including Archidamus III of [[s:sparta|Sparta]] and Alexander of Epirus, against Italic peoples.
taras.e: Conflict with [[e:rome|Rome]] began in 282 BCE when Tarentines attacked a Roman squadron. Pyrrhus of Epirus came to their aid, but after his departure Taras surrendered in 272 BCE. It defected to [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]] in 212 BCE and was sacked when retaken in 209 BCE. Roman Tarentum survives as [[s:principality-of-taranto|Taranto]].

tenkasi-pandyas.t: A late branch of the Pandya dynasty that survived in the far south of Tamil Nadu, ruling from Tenkasi under Vijayanagara and Nayak overlords.
tenkasi-pandyas.o: After the [[s:later-pandyan-empire|Later Pandyan Empire]] lost [[e:madurai|Madurai]] to the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] and the [[s:madurai-sultanate|Madurai Sultanate]], [[e:pandya-dynasty|Pandya]] princes continued to hold small territories in the Tirunelveli region. In the 15th century one branch settled at Tenkasi, where Arikesari Parakrama Pandya began the great Kasi Viswanathar temple in the 1440s.
tenkasi-pandyas.r: The Tenkasi [[s:later-pandyan-empire|Pandyas]] ruled as subordinate chiefs, first of the [[s:vijayanagara-empire|Vijayanagara Empire]] and then of the [[s:madurai-nayak-dynasty|Madurai Nayak dynasty]], rather than as independent kings. Their importance lay in culture: several were poets in Tamil, notably Ativira Rama [[e:pandya-dynasty|Pandya]], author of the Naidatham, and they endowed temples in Tenkasi and Tirunelveli.
tenkasi-pandyas.e: The line faded into obscurity during the 17th century as the [[s:madurai-nayak-dynasty|Madurai Nayaks]] consolidated their rule over the south, and its last members are poorly documented. The Kasi Viswanathar temple at Tenkasi remains their chief monument.

tortuga.t: Rocky island off northern Hispaniola that became the most famous base of the Caribbean buccaneers before France turned it into the seed of Saint-Domingue.
tortuga.o: From around 1630 French and English hunters, the boucaniers who smoked wild [[e:cattle|cattle]] meat on Hispaniola, used Tortuga as a refuge. [[e:spain|Spain]] raided it several times, in 1635 and 1638 among others. In 1640 the Huguenot engineer Jean Le Vasseur took control on behalf of the French governor of [[s:colony-of-saint-christopher|Saint Kitts]] and built the Fort de la Roche above Basse-Terre harbour.
tortuga.r: Government was loose and personal: Le Vasseur ruled almost as an independent lord until his murder in 1653. The island's economy rested on trading hides and meat, and increasingly on buccaneering raids against Spanish shipping and towns, with the plunder sold in its harbour. Settlers were a mix of French Catholics and Protestants, English adventurers and indentured servants.
tortuga.e: After a final Spanish occupation in 1654 to 1655, French control returned. In 1665 the French West [[e:india|India]] Company appointed Bertrand d'Ogeron as governor, who encouraged settlers to plant on the Hispaniola mainland. Tortuga faded as the capital moved across the water to the new colony of [[s:saint-domingue|Saint-Domingue]].

titti.t: A small Celtiberian people of the Jalón valley, allies of the Belli in the war with Rome that began at Segeda in 153 BCE.
titti.o: The Titti were one of the Celtiberian peoples of the middle [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]] tributaries, probably around the Jalón valley in modern [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]] province. They are known almost only from Appian's account of the Celtiberian wars, which links them closely with the [[s:belli|Belli]].
titti.r: Nothing is known of their institutions beyond their dependence on the [[s:belli|Belli]]. When Segeda enlarged its walls, it forced the Titti to settle there, which [[e:rome|Rome]] treated as a breach of the treaty of Gracchus.
titti.e: They fought with the [[s:belli|Belli]] and [[s:arevaci|Arevaci]] in the wars of 153 to 133 BCE and are last mentioned in that conflict. After the fall of Numantia in 133 BCE their territory was absorbed into [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]].

twenty-sixth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The Saite Dynasty, which freed Egypt from Assyrian and Kushite control and gave it a last long era of native prosperity.
twenty-sixth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Psamtik I, son of the Saite ruler Necho I, began in 664 BCE as an Assyrian [[e:vassal|vassal]] after [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] drove out the [[s:kushite-empire|Kushite Empire]]. As Assyria weakened he threw off its overlordship, and in 656 BCE he took [[s:thebes|Thebes]] peacefully by having his daughter Nitocris adopted as the future God's Wife of [[e:amun|Amun]].
twenty-sixth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The Saite kings relied on Greek and Carian [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] and allowed Greek traders to settle at Naukratis. [[e:necho-ii|Necho II]] began a canal from the [[e:nile|Nile]] to the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]], sent a Phoenician fleet around [[e:africa|Africa]] and killed King Josiah of [[s:kingdom-of-judah|Judah]] at [[s:megiddo|Megiddo]], but lost to [[e:babylon|Babylon]] at [[s:kingdom-of-carchemish|Carchemish]] in 605 BCE. Art and texts deliberately revived [[s:old-kingdom-of-egypt|Old Kingdom]] models, and the Demotic script came into use. Amasis II courted Greek cities.
twenty-sixth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: In 525 BCE the Persian king [[e:cambyses-ii|Cambyses II]] defeated [[e:psamtik-iii|Psamtik III]] at Pelusium and took Memphis, turning the country into [[s:achaemenid-egypt|Achaemenid Egypt]]. Saite art and religion shaped Late Period [[e:egypt|Egypt]], and Greek knowledge of Egypt, through [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]], rests largely on this era.

troezen.t: Small city of the eastern Argolid, mythical birthplace of Theseus, which sheltered Athenian families during Xerxes's invasion of 480 BCE.
troezen.o: Troezen lay on the Argolid peninsula facing the Saronic Gulf, with Ionian traditions shared with [[s:athens|Athens]] and later Dorian settlement. Myth made it the birthplace of Theseus and the home of his grandfather Pittheus. In the Archaic period it was a small independent city with a harbour at Pogon.
troezen.r: Troezenians helped found [[s:halicarnassus|Halicarnassus]] and, with Achaeans, [[s:sybaris|Sybaris]] in [[e:italy|Italy]]. In 480 BCE Athenian women and children were evacuated to Troezen before Salamis, as recorded in the inscribed Troezen Decree found in 1959. Troezen fought at Salamis and [[s:plataea|Plataea]] and was usually a member of the [[s:peloponnesian-league|Peloponnesian League]]. It had a sanctuary of Hippolytus.
troezen.e: In the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]] Troezen changed hands among Macedonian kings and [[s:sparta|Sparta]] before joining the [[s:achaean-league|Achaean League]]. It passed under Roman control in 146 BCE and continued as a small town.
troezen.re: Greek religion; cults of Hippolytus and Poseidon

tetouan-under-al-mandri.t: Tetouan refounded by exiles from Granada under the al-Mandri family, a corsair city ruled for a time by the famous Sayyida al-Hurra.
tetouan-under-al-mandri.o: Tetouan had lain in ruins since a Castilian raid around 1400. Around 1484, Ali al-Mandri, a military leader from the [[s:emirate-of-granada|Emirate of Granada]], rebuilt the town with Andalusi refugees, with permission from the [[s:wattasid-sultanate|Wattasid Sultanate]], as a base against the Portuguese at [[e:ceuta|Ceuta]].
tetouan-under-al-mandri.r: The Andalusi elite ran Tetouan as an autonomous city, rebuilding walls and the medina in Granadan style. Corsairs operating from its river raided Spanish and Portuguese shipping and coasts, bringing captives for ransom. After al-Mandri's death his widow Sayyida al-Hurra, daughter of the founder of the [[s:emirate-of-chefchaouen|Emirate of Chefchaouen]], governed from about 1515 to 1542 and dealt directly with Portugal and [[e:spain|Spain]].
tetouan-under-al-mandri.e: Sayyida al-Hurra was deposed in 1542, and the Mandri family's influence waned as the [[s:saadi-sultanate|Saadi Sultanate]] extended its control over northern [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]] in the 1560s. The Andalusi heritage of Tetouan's medina, now a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO]] World Heritage site, remains.

territory-of-inini.t: The vast forested interior of French Guiana, governed as a separate territory from 1930 to 1946 in an attempt to develop it apart from the coast.
territory-of-inini.o: In 1930 [[e:france|France]] separated the interior of [[s:french-guiana|French Guiana]] from the coastal colony, creating the Territory of Inini. The aim was to develop the gold-rich forests and administer the indigenous and maroon peoples directly, outside the control of the coastal elected council.
territory-of-inini.r: Inini was governed directly by the governor of [[s:french-guiana|French Guiana]], with its nominal capital at Saint-Élie, a gold-mining settlement. Gold prospecting was the main economic activity, and there was little infrastructure beyond river transport. The territory covered most of French Guiana's land but held only a small population of indigenous Amerindian peoples, maroon communities and gold miners.
territory-of-inini.e: In 1946, when [[s:french-guiana|French Guiana]] became an overseas [[e:departement|department]] of [[e:france|France]], Inini was merged back into it, though the interior kept a separate administrative status until 1969. Its former area now forms the interior communes of French Guiana, home to Amerindian and maroon communities.

talcher-state.t: A princely state on the Brahmani river in Odisha, whose territory held the Talcher coalfield, today one of India's largest.
talcher-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to the late 15th century, but little is reliably known about its origins.
talcher-state.r: Talcher was a small inland state of farmland and forest, tributary to the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]] and, from 1803, one of the Orissa Tributary Mahals under British supervision. [[e:coal|Coal]] mining began there in the early 20th century. In 1938 Praja Mandal agitation against the Raja led tens of thousands of subjects to leave the state in protest.
talcher-state.e: Talcher merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948 and is now an industrial town in Angul district.

taifa-of-niebla.t: A taifa based on the walled town of Niebla on the Tinto river, ruled by the Arab Banu Yahya until Seville annexed it.
taifa-of-niebla.o: Around 1023 Ahmad ibn Yahya al-Yahsubi, of an Arab family long settled in the region, established an independent principality around Niebla, taking advantage of the weakness of the Hammudid [[e:caliphate|caliphs]] and the rivalries of the south-western [[e:taifa|taifas]].
taifa-of-niebla.r: Niebla controlled the lower Tinto valley and the mining district inland, with its red stone walls and fertile riverland. Its rulers, styled with honorifics such as Izz al-Dawla, were caught between the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]] and the [[s:taifa-of-huelva|Taifa of Huelva]], and briefly accepted [[e:seville|Seville's]] protection before resisting it.
taifa-of-niebla.e: In 1053 al-Mutadid of the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]] annexed Niebla, deposing Muhammad ibn Yahya. The town later reappeared twice as an independent [[e:taifa|taifa]], in the [[s:second-taifa-of-niebla|Second Taifa of Niebla]] and the [[s:third-taifa-of-niebla|Third Taifa of Niebla]].

territory-of-papua.t: Australia's first colonial territory, formerly British New Guinea, administered for over three decades by Sir Hubert Murray.
territory-of-papua.o: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] transferred [[s:british-new-guinea|British New Guinea]] to the new [[s:commonwealth-of-australia|Commonwealth of Australia]], and the Papua Act of 1906 renamed it the Territory of Papua, with its capital at Port Moresby. It was the first overseas territory governed by [[e:australia|Australia]], and it took over the government stations and village constable system built up under William MacGregor.
territory-of-papua.r: Hubert Murray, lieutenant governor from 1908 until his death in 1940, followed a paternalistic policy that restricted the sale of land to Europeans, relied on armed constabulary and village constables, and made punitive raids rarer. The European population remained small, and plantations, [[e:copper|copper]] and gold mining developed only modestly. Missions provided most schooling and health care. Papuans had no political rights, and the economy was poorer than that of the neighbouring [[s:territory-of-new-guinea|Territory of New Guinea]].
territory-of-papua.e: The Japanese advance on Port Moresby was stopped on the Kokoda Track in 1942 with help from Papuan carriers. Civil rule was suspended and both territories were run by a single military administration. In 1949 Papua was joined with New [[e:guinea|Guinea]] as the [[s:territory-of-papua-and-new-guinea|Territory of Papua and New Guinea]].
territory-of-papua.la: English, Hiri Motu, Papuan and Austronesian languages

twenty-fourth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The brief Saite kingdom of Tefnakht and Bakenranef, which challenged the Kushites for control of Egypt.
twenty-fourth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Tefnakht, Great Chief of the [[s:libu|Libu]] and the Ma at Sais in the western Delta, united much of the Delta and Middle [[e:egypt|Egypt]] in the 720s BCE. His advance south provoked the invasion of [[e:piye|Piye]] of the [[s:kushite-empire|Kushite Empire]] around 728 BCE, after which Tefnakht submitted but kept his power and took royal titles.
twenty-fourth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: Its kings controlled the western Delta and Memphis and drew on the wealth of Delta trade with the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]]. Bakenranef, called Bocchoris by the [[e:greeks|Greeks]], was remembered in Greek tradition as a wise lawgiver who reformed contract law. A vase with his name found in an Etruscan tomb at [[s:tarquinii|Tarquinia]] shows Saite trade links.
twenty-fourth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: Around 720 BCE the Kushite king Shabaka conquered the Delta; Manetho says he burned Bakenranef alive. The Saite family survived as local rulers and re-emerged as the [[s:twenty-sixth-dynasty-of-egypt|Twenty-sixth Dynasty of Egypt]].

tzutujil-kingdom.t: A Maya kingdom on the southern shore of Lake Atitlán, a rival of the K'iche' and Kaqchikel, conquered by Pedro de Alvarado in 1524.
tzutujil-kingdom.o: The Tz'utujil were one of the highland Maya peoples whose lineages, like those of the K'iche', claimed origins in migrations from the east. From about 1250 they established a kingdom around Lake Atitlán, with their capital at Chuitinamit, on a hill near modern [[s:spanish-jamaica|Santiago]] Atitlán.
tzutujil-kingdom.r: The kingdom was ruled by its Ajtz'ikinajay lineage and controlled the lake shores and the [[e:cacao|cacao]]-growing lands of the Pacific slope to the south. It fought repeatedly with the K'iche' and Kaqchikel kingdoms over these valuable lands. Lake fishing and highland farming also supported its people.
tzutujil-kingdom.e: In 1524 Pedro de Alvarado, aided by Kaqchikel allies, defeated the Tz'utujil in a battle by the lake, and their ruler Tepepul submitted. The kingdom became part of the [[s:captaincy-general-of-guatemala|Captaincy General of Guatemala]]. Tz'utujil is still spoken around Lake Atitlán.

tallo-kingdom.t: The Makassar kingdom joined with Gowa in a twin state, whose rulers served as chancellors and led South Sulawesi's conversion to Islam.
tallo-kingdom.o: Tallo was founded in the 15th century, according to the [[s:gowa-sultanate|Makassar]] chronicles, by a prince of Gowa who left after a succession dispute and settled near the mouth of the Tallo River, north of today's Makassar city. In the early 16th century the two kingdoms swore an alliance and came to act as one state, described in the saying 'one people, two kings'.
tallo-kingdom.r: The ruler of Tallo usually served as chancellor of Gowa. Karaeng Matoaya was the first [[s:gowa-sultanate|Makassar]] ruler to accept [[e:islam|Islam]], in 1605, and guided the expansion of the joint state. His son Karaeng Pattingalloang, famous for his learning, collected European books, maps and a globe.
tallo-kingdom.e: Tallo shared the fate of the [[s:gowa-sultanate|Gowa Sultanate]], losing power after the Treaty of Bongaya of 1667 and the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] conquest of South [[e:sulawesi|Sulawesi]] in 1906. Its name survives in a district of Makassar, where the royal tombs of Tallo still stand.

theban-eleventh-dynasty.t: The Theban kings who rose from local governors to reunite Egypt at the end of the First Intermediate Period.
theban-eleventh-dynasty.o: Around 2134 BCE the governors of the Theban [[e:nome|nome]], led by Mentuhotep I and Intef I, broke with the [[s:herakleopolitan-kingdom|Herakleopolitan Kingdom]] and claimed royal titles. [[s:thebes|Thebes]], until then a minor provincial town, became the capital of a southern kingdom stretching from Elephantine to the region of [[s:abydos|Abydos]].
theban-eleventh-dynasty.r: Intef II, who reigned for about fifty years, fought the north for Thinis and [[s:abydos|Abydos]] and expanded the kingdom. The early kings were buried in large rock-cut 'saff' tombs at el-Tarif on the west bank of [[s:thebes|Thebes]]. They promoted the war god Montu and the local god [[e:amun|Amun]], and relied on Nubian [[e:archery|archers]], some of whom settled at Gebelein.
theban-eleventh-dynasty.e: Mentuhotep II defeated Herakleopolis and reunited the country around 2055 BCE, a date often used for the start of the [[s:middle-kingdom-of-egypt|Middle Kingdom of Egypt]]. His mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari set a model for later Theban royal building.

teozacoalco.t: A Mixtec kingdom of the Mixteca Alta whose dynastic history is preserved in the Codex Zouche-Nuttall and the Map of Teozacoalco of 1580.
teozacoalco.o: Teozacoalco, Chiyo Cahnu in Mixtec, was a royal seat in the western Mixteca Alta by about 1000. Its rulers were closely related by marriage to the lords of [[s:tilantongo|Tilantongo]], the senior Mixtec house, and its first dynasty appears in the codices of this period.
teozacoalco.r: Like other Mixtec kingdoms, it was a small domain ruled by a hereditary lord and lady from a palace, drawing tribute from dependent villages. The Map of Teozacoalco, painted for the Spanish Relaciones Geográficas, lists its rulers in a genealogy of about 25 generations and helped scholars link the codices to real places and dates.
teozacoalco.e: Teozacoalco fell under Aztec tribute in the late 15th century and came under Spanish rule after 1522, its native lords continuing as caciques under colonial authority.

tripura-kingdom.t: The Manikya kingdom of the Tripuri people, one of the longest-ruling dynasties of north-east India, recorded in its own royal chronicle, the Rajmala.
tripura-kingdom.o: The Rajmala traces the dynasty through a long legendary line; the historical Manikya dynasty emerged around 1400, when Maha Manikya ruled the hills east of [[e:bengal|Bengal]]. Its kings took the title Manikya and soon controlled parts of the plains of eastern Bengal.
tripura-kingdom.r: Dhanya Manikya (r. 1490–1515) expanded the kingdom and fought the [[s:bengal-sultanate|Bengal Sultanate]]. The [[e:mughal-empire|Mughals]] later took the plains, which the Maharajas held as the zamindari of Chakla Roshnabad. The kings blended Tripuri traditions with [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] kingship and Bengali court culture. Bir Chandra Manikya (r. 1862–1896) built modern Agartala and befriended Rabindranath Tagore.
tripura-kingdom.e: Tripura became a princely state under the British. In 1949 Maharani Kanchan Prabha Devi, regent for her son, signed the merger agreement with [[e:india|India]]. Tripura became a Union territory and in 1972 a state of the [[s:republic-of-india|Republic of India]].

taifa-of-huelva.t: A small Arab-ruled taifa on the Odiel estuary, home of the Bakri family whose son became the great geographer Abu Ubayd al-Bakri.
taifa-of-huelva.o: Around 1012, during the collapse of caliphal power, the Arab family of the Banu Bakr made themselves independent in Huelva and the island town of Saltés at the mouth of the Odiel and Tinto rivers. Their founder was Abu Zayd Muhammad ibn Ayyub al-Bakri.
taifa-of-huelva.r: The [[e:taifa|taifa]] was a coastal principality living from fishing, salt and the iron industry of Saltés, which exported metalwork along the Atlantic coast. Its rulers balanced between the neighbouring [[s:taifa-of-niebla|Taifa of Niebla]] and the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]]. The family was cultured: Abu Ubayd al-Bakri, son of the last ruler, later wrote the Book of Roads and Kingdoms.
taifa-of-huelva.e: In 1051 the Abbadid ruler al-Mutadid of [[e:seville|Seville]] forced the last ruler, Abd [[e:al-aziz|al-Aziz]] al-Bakri, to give up Huelva and Saltés. The family moved to [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]], where Abu Ubayd built his scholarly career.

turk-shahis.t: A Turkic dynasty that ruled Kabul and Gandhara for over 150 years, blocking the Arab advance into the Indian subcontinent.
turk-shahis.o: Around 665 a Turkic dynasty, probably linked to the [[s:western-turkic-khaganate|Western Turkic Khaganate]] and Tokharistan, replaced the [[s:nezak-huns|Nezak Huns]] in [[e:kabul|Kabul]] and Kapisa. Its founder Barha Tegin claimed a long descent, and al-Biruni later recorded traditions of a line of sixty kings.
turk-shahis.r: The Turk Shahis ruled a largely Buddhist and [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] population from [[e:kabul|Kabul]], and later also [[s:kingdom-of-gandhara|Gandhara]], issuing coins with Bactrian and Brahmi legends. They received [[s:later-tang|Tang]] Chinese titles; Tegin Shah was recognised in the 720s. Allied with the [[s:zunbils|Zunbils]] to the south, they repeatedly fought off Arab armies from Sistan and Khurasan.
turk-shahis.e: In the early 9th century the Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliph]] [[e:al-mamun|al-Ma'mun]] forced the last Turk Shahi king to submit and convert, and soon after, around 822, the [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] minister Kallar overthrew the dynasty, founding the [[s:hindu-shahis|Hindu Shahis]].

talava.t: Latgalian principality in north-eastern Latvia whose ruler Tālivaldis allied with the German crusaders against the Estonians.
talava.o: Tālava was a Latgalian territory in what is now north-eastern [[s:republic-of-latvia|Latvia]], with its main stronghold at Beverīna. It appears in Henry of [[e:livonia|Livonia's]] chronicle in the early 13th century, when it paid tribute to Pskov and was ruled by the elder Tālivaldis.
talava.r: Tālava's rulers led a Latgalian society of farmers and warriors with hillforts. Facing raids from the Estonians of [[s:sakala|Sakala]] and [[s:ugandi|Ugandi]], Tālivaldis and his sons Rameķis and Varibulis accepted [[e:latin|Latin]] baptism around 1208 and joined the Germans and the [[s:livonian-brothers-of-the-sword|Livonian Brothers of the Sword]] in campaigns northwards.
talava.e: In 1215 raiders from [[s:sakala|Sakala]] captured Tālivaldis and roasted him to death. His sons kept a subordinate role, but in 1224 Tālava was divided between the [[e:bishop|bishop]] of Riga and the Sword Brothers. It became part of [[s:terra-mariana|Terra Mariana]], and the Latgalians merged into the Latvian people.

turpan-khanate.t: The eastern successor of the Chagatai Khanate, ruling Turpan and Hami, where Islam finally displaced the region's old Buddhist culture.
turpan-khanate.o: After [[s:moghulistan|Moghulistan]] divided in the 1460s, its eastern lands around Turpan, Aksu and [[s:kingdom-of-kucha|Kucha]] formed a separate khanate. From 1487 Yunus Khan's son [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Ahmad Khan ruled it, and Turpan became the capital of what is sometimes called Eastern [[e:moghulistan|Moghulistan]] or Uyghurstan.
turpan-khanate.r: The Turpan khans ruled the oases of Turpan, Kara-Shahr and at times Hami, controlling trade routes into [[e:china|China]]. Under [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Ahmad Khan and his son Mansur Khan they fought the Ming for Hami, and [[e:islamisation|Islamisation]] of the Turpan [[e:uyghurs|Uyghurs]] was largely completed in this period, ending a long Buddhist tradition. The khanate was linked by marriage and rivalry to the [[s:yarkent-khanate|Yarkent Khanate]].
turpan-khanate.e: The Turpan khanate was weakened by divisions and absorbed into the [[s:yarkent-khanate|Yarkent Khanate]] in the 17th century. In 1680 the [[s:dzungar-khanate|Dzungar Khanate]] conquered both, bringing the oases under [[e:oirats|Oirat]] rule.

taulantii.t: Illyrian kingdom around Epidamnus on the Albanian coast, whose king Glaukias fought Alexander the Great and raised the young Pyrrhus.
taulantii.o: The Taulantii held the coastal plain around Epidamnus (Durrës) from at least the 5th century BCE; Thucydides records them in the quarrel over Epidamnus that helped spark the [[e:peloponnesian-war|Peloponnesian War]]. By the 4th century BCE they were ruled by kings.
taulantii.r: Their kings controlled the hinterland of the Greek colonies of Epidamnus and Apollonia, trading with them and at times dominating them. In 335 BCE Glaukias joined Cleitus of Illyria against Alexander at Pelion. Glaukias later sheltered the infant Pyrrhus of Epirus and in 312 BCE seized Epidamnus.
taulantii.e: After Glaukias the Taulantian kingdom faded from view. By the later 3rd century BCE their lands lay within the [[s:illyrian-kingdom|Illyrian Kingdom]] of Agron and Teuta, and after 229 BCE much of the coast came under Roman protection.

tungri.t: People of eastern Belgium who settled the former land of the Eburones and whose town Atuatuca Tungrorum became Tongeren.
tungri.o: After Caesar destroyed the [[s:eburones|Eburones]] in 53 BCE, new groups settled the area between the Meuse and the [[e:rhine|Rhine]]. [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] says the Tungri were the first Germani to cross the Rhine, and that the name Germani spread from them to all their kin.
tungri.r: Their chief town Atuatuca Tungrorum was founded under Augustus and grew into a walled city on the road from Bavay to [[s:free-imperial-city-of-cologne|Cologne]]. Tungrian [[e:cohort|cohorts]] served across the empire, most famously on Hadrian's Wall and at Vindolanda.
tungri.e: The region suffered Frankish raids from the 3rd century, and Tongeren was rebuilt with a smaller wall. In the 4th century it became the seat of [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Servatius, whose see later moved to Maastricht and then [[s:prince-bishopric-of-liege|Liège]]. Tongeren claims to be the oldest town in [[s:kingdom-of-belgium|Belgium]].

tiberina-republic.t: A short-lived republic proclaimed in Perugia in 1798, quickly absorbed into the French-backed Roman Republic.
tiberina-republic.o: In February 1798, as French troops overthrew papal rule in [[e:rome|Rome]], patriots in [[s:commune-of-perugia|Perugia]] and the upper [[e:tiber-river|Tiber]] valley proclaimed a republic named after the river, taking over the government of Perugia and nearby Umbrian towns.
tiberina-republic.r: Known mainly from local records, the Tiberina Republic was a provisional government of local patriots under French protection. It replaced papal officials, planted liberty trees and adopted republican symbols.
tiberina-republic.e: Within weeks, in 1798, it was merged into the [[s:roman-republic-1798-1799|Roman Republic]] (1798–1799), and [[s:commune-of-perugia|Perugia]] became a [[e:departement|department]] capital of that state.

turmodigi.t: A people of the upper Arlanzón in Burgos, whose town Segisamo served as Augustus' base in the Cantabrian Wars.
turmodigi.o: The Turmodigi, or Murbogi, lived around the upper Arlanzón and Pisuerga in modern Burgos province from the later Iron Age, between the [[s:vaccaei|Vaccaei]], [[s:autrigones|Autrigones]] and [[s:cantabri|Cantabri]]. Their language was probably Celtic.
turmodigi.r: Little is known of their society. Their main settlement was Segisamo, modern Sasamón, and they farmed the northern Meseta and herded in its uplands.
turmodigi.e: In 26 BCE Augustus made Segisamo his camp for the campaign against the [[s:cantabri|Cantabri]], and the Turmodigi were integrated into [[s:hispania-tarraconensis|Hispania Tarraconensis]]. Segisamo continued as a Roman town.

taifa-of-alpuente.t: One of the smallest taifas of al-Andalus, a family-ruled mountain lordship in the hills north-west of Valencia that outlasted many larger rivals.
taifa-of-alpuente.o: Around 1009, as caliphal authority collapsed, the Banu Qasim, a family of uncertain origin settled in the Valencian uplands, made the fortress town of Alpuente the centre of their own principality under Abd Allah ibn Qasim, who took the honorific Yumn al-Dawla.
taifa-of-alpuente.r: The state covered little more than a cluster of castles and valleys in the Serranía, living from herding, dry farming and control of routes between [[e:valencia|Valencia]] and [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]]. Its survival depended on its remoteness and on careful diplomacy with [[e:toledo|Toledo]], Valencia and [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]]. Few details of its internal life are recorded.
taifa-of-alpuente.e: The [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]], who unified [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]] after 1090, absorbed Alpuente around 1106. The town later passed under [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] rule and was taken by the [[s:crown-of-aragon|Crown of Aragon]] in the 13th century.

thasos.t: North Aegean island colony of Paros that grew rich from gold mines and wine, and whose revolt in 465 BCE was crushed by Athens.
thasos.o: Colonists from [[s:paros|Paros]], among them the poet Archilochus, settled Thasos c. 680 BCE, displacing Thracian inhabitants. The Thasians soon gained a foothold on the facing Thracian mainland, with its gold and [[e:silver|silver]] mines near Mount Pangaion.
thasos.r: Thasos drew wealth from gold mines on the island and the mainland, marble quarries and wine, exported in stamped [[e:amphora|amphorae]] across the [[e:aegean|Aegean]] and [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]]. It had an oligarchic government and built strong walls with sculpted gates. The painter Polygnotus was Thasian. The island submitted to [[e:persia|Persia]] in 491 BCE and then joined the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]].
thasos.e: When [[s:athens|Athens]] challenged its mainland mines, Thasos revolted in 465 BCE and surrendered to Cimon after a two-year siege, losing its fleet and walls. It later passed under Macedonian rule, was freed by [[e:rome|Rome]] in 196 BCE and kept free status under Roman control.

taraon-state.t: One of the Chaube jagirs of Bundelkhand, held by a branch of the Brahmin family that once governed the fort of Kalinjar.
taraon-state.o: The Chaubes were [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] governors of the great fortress of Kalinjar under the Bundela rulers of [[s:panna-state|Panna]]. When the British took Kalinjar in 1812, they gave the family members small [[e:jagir|jagirs]], including Taraon, in return for its surrender.
taraon-state.r: Taraon was a minor holding of a few villages under the [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] Agency, ruled by a Chaube chief. Little else is recorded.
taraon-state.e: After independence Taraon was merged into [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] with the other [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] states and absorbed by 1950.

taifa-of-lorca.t: A minor taifa in the frontier town of Lorca, between Murcia and Almería, independent for some four decades in the 11th century.
taifa-of-lorca.o: Around 1051 local rulers made Lorca and its castle independent, breaking away from the authority exercised over the region by Almería and the [[s:taifa-of-murcia|Taifa of Murcia]] during the fragmentation of the 11th century.
taifa-of-lorca.r: Little is recorded beyond its outline. The state centred on Lorca's great hilltop fortress and the irrigated Guadalentín valley. It lay close to the Castilian stronghold of Aledo, held from 1086, which raided the surrounding lands.
taifa-of-lorca.e: Lorca fell to the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] around 1091 together with [[e:murcia|Murcia]] and Almería. It later passed to [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]] in 1244 and became a frontier town facing the [[s:emirate-of-granada|Emirate of Granada]].

tecumsehs-confederacy.t: A pan-tribal alliance led by the Shawnee brothers Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa that tried to halt American expansion and fought beside Britain in the War of 1812.
tecumsehs-confederacy.o: Tenskwatawa, known as the Prophet, preached rejection of American goods and ways and a return to Native traditions. In 1808 he and his brother Tecumseh founded Prophetstown near the junction of the Tippecanoe and Wabash rivers, drawing followers from many nations. Tecumseh argued that Native land was held in common and could not be sold by any single nation.
tecumsehs-confederacy.r: The confederacy united warriors from the Shawnee, Kickapoo, Potawatomi, Wyandot, Ho-Chunk and others under Tecumseh's leadership and his brother's religious authority. Tecumseh denounced the Treaty of Fort Wayne of 1809 and travelled south to recruit the Creek. In his absence William Henry Harrison destroyed Prophetstown after the Battle of Tippecanoe in 1811.
tecumsehs-confederacy.e: Tecumseh allied with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in the War of 1812 and helped capture Detroit, but he was killed at the Battle of the Thames in October 1813, and the confederacy collapsed. It was the last great attempt to unite Native nations east of the [[e:mississippi-river|Mississippi]] against expansion.

tarbelli.t: Aquitanian people of the Adour basin and the Landes coast, known for river gold and the hot springs of Dax.
tarbelli.o: The Tarbelli were one of the Aquitani, the peoples between the Garonne and the [[e:pyrenees|Pyrenees]] who spoke a language related to Basque. They held the lower Adour valley and the Atlantic shore around modern Dax and Bayonne. Known chiefly from Caesar, Strabo and Pliny.
tarbelli.r: Strabo describes rich gold deposits in their land, with nuggets found in shallow pits and river sands. Their hot springs at Aquae Tarbellicae (Dax) became famous under [[e:rome|Rome]]. No central capital is recorded before the Roman period.
tarbelli.e: The Tarbelli submitted to Caesar's legate Publius [[e:marcus-licinius-crassus|Crassus]] in 56 BCE after his campaign in Aquitania. Under Augustus they formed a civitas with Aquae Tarbellicae as its chief town, which later became the seat of the [[e:bishop|bishops]] of Dax.

tonk-state.t: The only Muslim-ruled state of Rajputana, created in 1817 for the Pathan freebooter Amir Khan in exchange for disbanding his army.
tonk-state.o: [[e:amir|Amir]] Khan, a Pathan soldier of fortune, led a large army in alliance with Yashwant Rao Holkar of [[s:indore-state|Indore State]] and plundered Rajputana for two decades. In 1817 he agreed to disband his troops, and the British confirmed him as Nawab of Tonk with lands granted earlier by Holkar.
tonk-state.r: Tonk was a 17-gun salute state of the Rajputana Agency made up of scattered districts. Nawab Muhammad Ali Khan was deposed in 1867 after men acting for him killed members of the family of the Thakur of Lawa. The Nawabs collected Arabic and Persian [[e:manuscript|manuscripts]], now kept in the Maulana Abul Kalam Azad Arabic Persian Research Institute at Tonk.
tonk-state.e: Tonk acceded to [[e:india|India]] and in 1948 was merged into the [[s:united-state-of-rajasthan|United State of Rajasthan]]; it is now a district of Rajasthan.

tembe-kingdom.t: A Tsonga kingdom on Delagoa Bay that traded ivory with Europeans for three centuries before its lands were split between Portugal and Britain.
tembe-kingdom.o: The Tembe dynasty ruled the southern shore of Delagoa Bay from at least the mid-16th century, when Portuguese shipwreck survivors recorded its chiefs. In the 18th century a branch, the Maputo or Mabudu, became dominant south of the bay and expanded towards the Lubombo mountains.
tembe-kingdom.r: Tembe kings drew wealth from controlling the [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] trade of Delagoa Bay, dealing with Portuguese, English, [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and Austrian merchants, and from [[e:cattle|cattle]] and farming. Under Makasana in the late 18th and early 19th centuries the kingdom was a strong regional power, but it later paid tribute to the [[s:zulu-kingdom|Zulu Kingdom]] and contended with Swazi and [[s:gaza|Gaza]] [[e:nguni|Nguni]] pressure.
tembe-kingdom.e: The 1875 MacMahon arbitration awarded Delagoa Bay to Portugal. In the 1890s the kingdom was divided along the new border, with the south (Maputaland) joining British [[s:zulu-kingdom|Zululand]] and the north conquered by Portugal in 1895.

trinh-lords.t: The hereditary military rulers of northern Vietnam who held real power behind the Le emperors for over two centuries.
trinh-lords.o: Trinh Kiem, son-in-law of the Le loyalist leader Nguyen Kim, took command of the Le restoration forces after Nguyen Kim's death in 1545 and became the real power behind the [[s:later-le-dynasty|Later Le dynasty]]. His son Trinh Tung recaptured Thang Long from the [[s:mac-dynasty|Mac dynasty]] in 1592.
trinh-lords.r: The Trinh lords governed Dang Ngoai, the northern realm Europeans called [[s:french-protectorate-of-tonkin|Tonkin]], from a palace beside the Le emperor's, controlling the army, taxes and appointments while leaving ritual to the emperor. They fought seven campaigns against the [[s:nguyen-lords|Nguyen lords]] between 1627 and 1672 without success, then focused on administration, examinations and trade with the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and English.
trinh-lords.e: Peasant revolts weakened the north in the 18th century. In 1786 the Tay Son under Nguyen Hue marched on Thang Long and defeated Trinh Khai, and the last lord, Trinh Bong, fled in 1787. Their realm passed to the [[s:tay-son-dynasty|Tay Son dynasty]].

tosa-domain.t: The Yamauchi domain on Shikoku whose lower samurai, including Sakamoto Ryoma, helped engineer the end of the shogunate in 1867.
tosa-domain.o: After Chosokabe Morichika lost Tosa for joining the western army at [[e:battle-of-sekigahara|Sekigahara]], [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] gave the province to Yamauchi Kazutoyo, who arrived in 1601 and built [[s:kingdom-of-cochin|Kochi]] castle. Former Chosokabe retainers resisted and were suppressed.
tosa-domain.r: Tosa was sharply divided between the upper [[e:samurai|samurai]], descended from Yamauchi followers, and the lower samurai and rural goshi, many of Chosokabe stock. Nonaka Kenzan's 17th-century reforms developed land and forests. In the 1860s the lord Yamauchi Toyoshige, known as Yodo, steered between [[e:shogun|shogunate]] and loyalists, while the loyalist party of Takechi Hanpeita was crushed.
tosa-domain.e: Tosa men Sakamoto Ryoma and Goto Shojiro proposed the peaceful return of power to the emperor, which the [[e:shogun|shogun]] accepted in 1867, and Tosa troops fought for the new government. It became [[s:kingdom-of-cochin|Kochi]] Prefecture in 1871, and Itagaki Taisuke later led the democratic movement from Tosa.

twenty-third-dynasty-of-egypt.t: A rival Libyan line of kings in Upper Egypt, born from the civil wars that broke up the Twenty-second Dynasty.
twenty-third-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Around 837 BCE, amid conflict in the [[s:twenty-second-dynasty-of-egypt|Twenty-second Dynasty of Egypt]], Pedubast I proclaimed himself king and was recognised at [[s:thebes|Thebes]]. Manetho linked the dynasty with [[e:tanis|Tanis]], while earlier scholars placed it at Leontopolis; many Egyptologists now see it as a mainly Theban and Upper Egyptian line, but its extent is debated.
twenty-third-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The dynasty shared power with the Bubastite kings and local Libyan chiefs, each controlling cities and temples. Osorkon III and his son Takelot III ruled as co-regents and placed family members as high priests and as God's Wife of [[e:amun|Amun]] at [[s:thebes|Thebes]]. Royal monuments are few, but Theban inscriptions record [[e:nile|Nile]] flood levels and priestly appointments by year of each king.
twenty-third-dynasty-of-egypt.e: Around 735 BCE [[s:thebes|Thebes]] passed under the [[s:kushite-empire|Kushite Empire]]. Shepenupet I, daughter of Osorkon III and God's Wife of [[e:amun|Amun]], adopted Amenirdis I, sister of the Kushite king [[e:piye|Piye]]. Rudamun's line ended as minor rulers, and Iuput II of Leontopolis submitted to Piye.

taifa-of-murviedro.t: A fleeting principality at Murviedro, the old Saguntum, held by a Valencian notable during the turmoil around El Cid's campaigns.
taifa-of-murviedro.o: After the collapse of the [[s:taifa-of-valencia|Taifa of Valencia]]'s independence and the installation of al-Qadir as a Castilian client in 1086, the Valencian notable Abu Isa ibn Labbun made himself master of the fortress town of Murviedro, the ancient [[s:saguntum|Saguntum]], north of [[e:valencia|Valencia]].
taifa-of-murviedro.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, the lordship was little more than the castle and its district. Ibn Labbun manoeuvred between al-Qadir, the [[s:taifa-of-albarracin|Taifa of Albarracín]] and El Cid, paying tribute to survive.
taifa-of-murviedro.e: By about 1092 Ibn Labbun had handed the town to the ruler of Albarracín. El Cid captured Murviedro in 1098, adding it to the [[s:lordship-of-valencia|Lordship of Valencia]], before it passed to the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]].

turco-egyptian-sudan.t: The Turkiyya, Egyptian rule over Sudan from 1821, which created Sudan's borders and capital before collapsing in the Mahdist revolt.
turco-egyptian-sudan.o: In 1820 to 1821 armies sent by [[s:egypt-under-muhammad-ali|Egypt under Muhammad Ali]], led by his son Ismail Pasha, conquered the [[s:funj-sultanate|Funj Sultanate]] and [[e:kordofan|Kordofan]], seeking gold and slaves for the army. Ismail was killed by the Ja'ali chief at Shendi in 1822, and harsh reprisals followed. Khartoum became the capital in the 1820s.
turco-egyptian-sudan.r: Governors-general ruled through Turkish, Egyptian and European officials, imposing heavy taxes. Merchants opened the White [[e:nile|Nile]] and the south to the [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trades]], with private armies such as that of [[s:zubayrs-bahr-al-ghazal|Zubayr's Bahr al-Ghazal]]. The [[s:khedivate-of-egypt|Khedivate of Egypt]] annexed [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]] in 1874 and Equatoria, and appointed Charles Gordon governor-general to suppress the slave trade.
turco-egyptian-sudan.e: From 1881 the [[e:mahdi|Mahdi]], Muhammad Ahmad, led a revolt against Egyptian rule. His forces took Khartoum in January 1885, killing Gordon, and founded the [[s:mahdist-state|Mahdist State]]. The Turkiyya left [[e:sudan|Sudan]] with its capital, much of its territory and a lasting legacy of the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]].

tomara-dynasty-of-gwalior.t: A Rajput dynasty that ruled from the fortress of Gwalior, whose king Man Singh built the Man Mandir palace and patronised dhrupad music.
tomara-dynasty-of-gwalior.o: Bir Singh Deo, a Tomara chief serving the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]], seized the fort of [[s:gwalior-state|Gwalior]] around 1394, during the confusion that followed Firuz Shah Tughluq's death and preceded [[e:timur|Timur's]] invasion. His descendants held Gwalior as an independent kingdom, at times paying tribute to the Sayyid and [[e:lodi-dynasty|Lodi]] sultans of [[e:delhi|Delhi]].
tomara-dynasty-of-gwalior.r: Dungarendra Singh had the colossal Jain rock-cut statues carved into the cliffs of [[s:gwalior-state|Gwalior]] fort. Man Singh Tomar, the most famous ruler, built the Man Mandir palace with its blue tile work and sponsored music; the dhrupad style and the singer tradition later associated with Tansen developed at his court. His queen Mrignayani is remembered in legend.
tomara-dynasty-of-gwalior.e: [[e:ibrahim-lodi|Ibrahim Lodi]] of the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] besieged [[s:gwalior-state|Gwalior]] and forced Vikramaditya Tomar to surrender in 1523. Vikramaditya later died fighting for Ibrahim at the [[e:first-battle-of-panipat|First Battle of Panipat]] in 1526. Gwalior passed to the [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]].

talpur-dynasty.t: A Baloch dynasty of mirs who ruled Sindh from Hyderabad, Khairpur and Mirpur until the British conquest of 1843.
talpur-dynasty.o: The Talpurs were Baloch tribal chiefs who served as commanders of the [[s:kalhora-dynasty|Kalhora dynasty]]. After the Kalhoras killed several Talpur leaders, Mir Fateh Ali Khan Talpur defeated the last Kalhora ruler at the Battle of Halani in 1783 and took control of Sindh, receiving recognition from the [[s:durrani-empire|Durrani Empire]].
talpur-dynasty.r: The Talpur mirs shared power among related branches, ruling from Hyderabad, [[s:khairpur-state|Khairpur]] and Mirpur Khas as a family confederation. They maintained Sindh's Persian court culture and Baloch tribal military system, and built tombs and forts. Their territory controlled the lower [[e:indus|Indus]], which [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] wanted for trade and for access to [[s:islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-2021-present|Afghanistan]].
talpur-dynasty.e: The British forced treaties on the mirs, used Sindh during the First Anglo-Afghan War and then provoked war. Charles Napier defeated the Talpurs at Miani and Dubbo in 1843, annexing Sindh to the [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Presidency]]. The [[s:khairpur-state|Khairpur]] branch survived as a princely state until 1955.

tsushima-fuchu-domain.t: The island domain of the So family, Japan's sole intermediary with Joseon Korea through the Edo period.
tsushima-fuchu-domain.o: The So family had ruled Tsushima, between Kyushu and [[e:korea|Korea]], since the 13th century and depended on trade with Korea. After the Japanese invasions of Korea in the 1590s, So Yoshitoshi worked to restore relations, and [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] confirmed his domain in 1600.
tsushima-fuchu-domain.r: To secure peace the So forged diplomatic letters between the [[e:shogun|shogun]] and the Korean king, which led to the Korean embassy of 1607; the forgery was exposed in the Yanagawa affair of 1635 but the So kept their role. They staffed the [[e:japan|Japan]] House at Busan, monopolised trade in Korean ginseng, [[e:rice|rice]] and Chinese [[e:silk|silk]], and escorted the Korean embassies to Edo.
tsushima-fuchu-domain.e: In 1861 a Russian warship occupied part of the island until British pressure forced it out. After abolition in 1871 the domain became Izuhara Prefecture and was later joined to [[e:nagasaki|Nagasaki]] Prefecture, and Korean relations passed to the Meiji foreign ministry.

tarcondimotid-cilicia.t: The Tarcondimotid kingdom, a Roman client state in the Amanus mountains of eastern Cilicia, loyal to Mark Antony.
tarcondimotid-cilicia.o: Tarcondimotus, a local ruler in the Amanus mountains of eastern [[e:cilicia|Cilicia]], supported [[e:pompey|Pompey]] when [[e:rome|Rome]] reorganised the region in 64 BCE and was recognised as dynast. He later took the title king, ruling from Hierapolis-Castabala.
tarcondimotid-cilicia.r: The kingdom controlled the passes between [[e:cilicia|Cilicia]] and [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] and the plain around Castabala. Tarcondimotus I called himself Philantonios, friend of Antony, and supplied ships and troops to his patrons. Coins with his portrait and Greek titles survive.
tarcondimotid-cilicia.e: Tarcondimotus I died fighting for Antony in 31 BCE. Augustus later restored his son Tarcondimotus II Philopator, whose death in 17 CE led [[e:rome|Rome]] to absorb the kingdom into its provinces.

tyras.t: A Greek colony at the mouth of the Dniester whose site, later the fortress of Akkerman, was inhabited for more than two thousand years.
tyras.o: Settlers from [[s:miletus|Miletus]] founded Tyras around 600 BCE on the right bank of the Dniester estuary, at modern Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi. The town took its name from the river, which the [[e:greeks|Greeks]] called Tyras, and is sometimes linked with an earlier settlement called Ophiusa.
tyras.r: Tyras was a small self-governing polis run by magistrates and a council on the usual Greek model. It lived by trading wine, [[e:olive-oil|olive oil]] and fine pottery to the peoples of the hinterland in return for grain, fish, hides and slaves, and it minted its own coins. Its neighbours were in turn [[e:scythians|Scythians]], [[s:getae|Getae]] and [[s:sarmatians|Sarmatians]].
tyras.e: The [[s:getae|Getae]] of Burebista sacked the town around 50 BCE. It recovered under Roman protection from the 1st century CE, with a Roman garrison and links to the province of Moesia Inferior. Gothic raids in the 3rd century and the arrival of the [[e:huns|Huns]] ended the ancient city, though the site was later rebuilt as Moncastro and Akkerman.

tlatelolco.t: The twin city of Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, home to the greatest market of the Americas, independent until 1473.
tlatelolco.o: Tlatelolco was founded in 1337, according to [[e:mexica|Mexica]] chronicles, by a group that split from the founders of [[e:tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] and settled on an adjacent island. Its first ruler, Cuacuauhpitzahuac, was a son of [[e:tezozomoc|Tezozomoc]] of the [[s:tepanec-empire|Tepanec Empire]], under whose protection it grew.
tlatelolco.r: Tlatelolco had its own tlatoani and a great temple. Its market, described by [[e:bernal-diaz-del-castillo|Bernal Díaz del Castillo]], drew some 60,000 people a day, trading food, cloth, obsidian, feathers and slaves. Its merchants ([[e:pochteca|pochteca]]) carried trade across [[e:mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]]. Relations with [[e:tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] were close but competitive.
tlatelolco.e: In 1473 [[e:axayacatl|Axayacatl]] of [[e:tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] defeated Tlatelolco and killed its ruler Moquihuix, and the city was annexed by the [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]] under a military governor. In 1521 it saw the last Aztec stand against [[e:hernan-cortes|Cortés]]. Its site is now the Plaza of the Three Cultures in [[e:mexico-city|Mexico City]].

turones.t: Gallic people of the middle Loire whose Roman town Caesarodunum became Tours.
turones.o: The Turones lived along the Loire around modern Tours, between the [[s:carnutes|Carnutes]], the [[s:andecavi|Andecavi]] and the [[s:bituriges-cubi|Bituriges Cubi]]. Caesar mentions them among the peoples where he quartered legions and among those who joined the revolt of 52 BCE.
turones.r: Little is known of their society beyond their oppida and coinage.
turones.e: Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their chief town was Caesarodunum, later called Civitas Turonorum, from which comes Tours. In the 4th century it became the see of Saint Martin of Tours, and his shrine made it one of the great pilgrimage centres of Gaul.

thespiae.t: Boeotian city below Mount Helicon, whose seven hundred citizens stood with the Spartans at Thermopylae and which honoured Eros and the Muses.
thespiae.o: Thespiae lay in the plain of southern Boeotia below Mount Helicon. It developed in the early Iron Age and became one of the larger Boeotian cities, often resisting the domination of [[s:thebes|Thebes]]. Its territory included the Valley of the Muses and the port of Creusis.
thespiae.r: Thespiae's chief cult honoured Eros, whose statue by Praxiteles later drew visitors, and it held the Mouseia festival for the Muses. In 480 BCE seven hundred Thespians under Demophilus fought and died at [[e:battle-of-thermopylae|Thermopylae]], and the [[e:persians|Persians]] burned the city. Thespiae joined the [[s:boeotian-league|Boeotian League]] but was frequently at odds with [[s:thebes|Thebes]].
thespiae.e: [[s:thebes|Thebes]] pulled down its walls in 423 BCE and destroyed it c. 373 BCE. Rebuilt under Macedonian protection, it continued as a cultural centre and passed under [[e:rome|Rome]] in 146 BCE.
thespiae.re: Greek religion; cults of Eros and the Muses

territory-of-the-comoros.t: The French overseas territory of the Comoro Islands, whose split vote on independence left Mayotte French.
territory-of-the-comoros.o: The Comoro Islands had been attached to [[s:french-madagascar|French Madagascar]] since 1912. In 1946 [[e:france|France]] made them a separate overseas territory, the Territoire des Comores, with its own elected assembly and deputies in the French parliament, and with Dzaoudzi on [[s:colony-of-mayotte-and-dependencies|Mayotte]] as the administrative capital.
territory-of-the-comoros.r: The islands' economy rested on vanilla, [[e:cloves|cloves]], copra and ylang-ylang essential oil, largely controlled by French companies and local elites. Internal autonomy was granted in 1961 under Said Mohamed Cheikh. The capital was moved from Dzaoudzi to Moroni on Grande Comore in the 1960s, a decision resented on [[s:colony-of-mayotte-and-dependencies|Mayotte]].
territory-of-the-comoros.e: In the 1974 referendum three islands voted for independence while [[s:colony-of-mayotte-and-dependencies|Mayotte]] voted to stay French. Ahmed Abdallah declared independence on 6 July 1975, but [[e:france|France]] kept Mayotte, which the Comoros still claim.

turkestan-assr.t: The first Soviet republic in Central Asia, created from Russian Turkestan and divided into the national republics in 1924.
turkestan-assr.o: After the Tashkent Soviet took power in late 1917 and crushed the [[s:kokand-autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]], the Turkestan Soviet Republic was proclaimed in April 1918 within the [[s:russian-sfsr|Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic]], covering the former [[s:turkestan-governorate-general|Turkestan Governorate-General]]. Cut off by civil war fronts until 1919, it was at first dominated by Russian settlers.
turkestan-assr.r: [[e:moscow|Moscow's]] Turkestan Commission, sent in 1919, curbed settler chauvinism and brought Muslim communists into government, including Turar Ryskulov. The republic fought the Basmachi revolts in [[s:principality-of-ferghana|Ferghana]] and famine, and introduced land reform. It governed from Tashkent, with the Bukharan and Khorezm republics as neighbours.
turkestan-assr.e: In the national delimitation of 1924 the republic was dissolved and its territory split among the [[s:uzbek-ssr|Uzbek SSR]], the [[s:turkmen-ssr|Turkmen SSR]], the [[s:kirghiz-assr|Kara-Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast]], the [[s:tajik-assr|Tajik ASSR]] and the [[s:kazakh-assr|Kazakh ASSR]]. This drew the outlines of today's Central Asian states.

transcaspian-government.t: An anti-Bolshevik government of railway workers and Socialist Revolutionaries in Ashgabat, remembered for the execution of the 26 Baku Commissars.
transcaspian-government.o: In July 1918 railway workers and Socialist Revolutionaries in Ashgabat overthrew the local Soviet authorities of the [[s:turkestan-assr|Turkestan ASSR]], forming the Transcaspian Provisional Government under Fyodor Funtikov. Facing Red forces from Tashkent, it appealed for help to the British in [[e:persia|Persia]].
transcaspian-government.r: The government controlled the Trans-Caspian railway from Krasnovodsk towards [[e:merv|Merv]], relying on [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] and Russian volunteers and a small British force under General Wilfrid Malleson. In September 1918 its men shot the 26 [[e:baku|Baku]] Commissars in the desert east of Krasnovodsk, an event that became a major Soviet symbol of British intervention.
transcaspian-government.e: After the British withdrew in 1919, the Red Army advanced along the railway, taking Ashgabat in July 1919 and Krasnovodsk in February 1920. Transcaspia returned to the [[s:turkestan-assr|Turkestan ASSR]] and later became the [[s:turkmen-ssr|Turkmen SSR]].

twenty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The kings of Tanis who ruled northern Egypt after the New Kingdom, sharing the country with the priests of Amun at Thebes.
twenty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.o: On the death of [[e:ramesses-xi|Ramesses XI]] around 1077 BCE, [[e:smendes|Smendes]], who had governed the north from the Delta, became king and founded the Twenty-first Dynasty. The capital moved to [[e:tanis|Tanis]] in the north-eastern Delta, built largely from monuments carried from the abandoned Ramesside capital Pi-Ramesses.
twenty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The Tanite kings ruled Lower and Middle [[e:egypt|Egypt]], while the [[s:theocracy-of-amun-at-thebes|Theocracy of Amun at Thebes]] governed the south with family ties to them. [[e:tanis|Tanis]] was laid out as a northern [[s:thebes|Thebes]] with a great temple of [[e:amun|Amun]]. The intact royal tombs found there by Pierre Montet in 1939 to 1940 include the [[e:silver|silver]] coffin and gold mask of Psusennes I. Siamun campaigned in [[s:philistine-pentapolis|Philistia]], and Osorkon the Elder was a Libyan.
twenty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.e: Around 943 BCE Sheshonq I, a Libyan chief of the [[s:meshwesh|Meshwesh]] and relative by marriage of the last king, Psusennes II, succeeded peacefully and founded the [[s:twenty-second-dynasty-of-egypt|Twenty-second Dynasty of Egypt]].

tervingi.t: Gothic people north of the lower Danube whose flight from the Huns in 376 led to the Roman disaster at Adrianople.
tervingi.o: The Tervingi are first named in 291 as a branch of the Goths living between the [[e:danube|Danube]] and the Dniester, in former Roman [[e:dacia|Dacia]] and [[s:principality-of-moldavia|Moldavia]]. They emerged from the Gothic peoples who had raided the empire through the 3rd century and settled after [[e:rome|Rome]] abandoned Dacia around 271.
tervingi.r: They were ruled by tribal leaders under an overall judge (iudex), the best known being Athanaric. A treaty with Constantine in 332 made them Roman allies and opened trade. [[e:christianity|Christianity]] spread among them through Ulfilas, who translated the Bible into Gothic, and Athanaric persecuted Christians in 369–372. [[e:valens|Valens]] fought them in 367–369.
tervingi.e: In 376 the [[e:huns|Huns]] attacked, and a large group under Fritigern was admitted across the [[e:danube|Danube]]. Roman mistreatment led to war, and in 378 they destroyed [[e:valens|Valens's]] army at Adrianople. They later formed the core of the [[e:visigoths|Visigoths]].

tercia-pars-regni.t: The ducatus, a third of the Hungarian kingdom ruled by princes of the Árpád dynasty, which fuelled civil wars until abolished by Coloman.
tercia-pars-regni.o: In 1048 King Andrew I granted a third of the [[s:kingdom-of-hungary-1000-1301|Kingdom of Hungary]] (1000-1301) to his brother Béla, as a ducatus, or duchy. It covered two blocks: one around Nyitra (Nitra) in the north-west and one around Bihar in the east.
tercia-pars-regni.r: The duke held royal revenues, counties and castles in his third, struck his own coins and kept his own retinue. The arrangement made the duke heir presumptive, but it repeatedly led to war: Béla took the throne from Andrew in 1060, and Géza and Ladislaus fought King [[e:solomon|Solomon]] in the 1070s.
tercia-pars-regni.e: King Coloman ended the arrangement, taking the duchy from his brother Álmos in 1107. The territory returned to the crown, and Álmos was later blinded with his son Béla.

teutonic-order-mergentheim.t: The Teutonic Order's headquarters at Mergentheim, from which, after losing Prussia in 1525, it governed its scattered lands for nearly three centuries.
teutonic-order-mergentheim.o: When Grand Master Albert secularised [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1525, the order's German master, Walter von Cronberg, who resided at Mergentheim in Franconia, was made administrator of the grand mastership in 1527, and his successors combined both offices as Hoch- und Deutschmeister. Mergentheim became the order's seat and the capital of its territories within the empire.
teutonic-order-mergentheim.r: The grand master ranked as a prince of the empire and ruled the district around Mergentheim as well as [[e:commandery|commanderies]] grouped into bailiwicks across [[e:germany|Germany]], [[e:austria|Austria]] and beyond. The knights, nobles bound by vows, served as officers in imperial armies against the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]]. From the late 16th century the office usually went to [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] archdukes or Wittelsbach princes, and Mergentheim castle was rebuilt in Baroque style.
teutonic-order-mergentheim.e: [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] dissolved the order in the states of the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]] in 1809, and Württemberg annexed Mergentheim, suppressing a local uprising. The order survived in [[e:austria|Austria]] and since 1929 has continued as a clerical order with its seat in [[e:vienna|Vienna]].

thessalian-league.t: Federation of the cities of Thessaly, famous for its cavalry, which elected a war leader called the tagos and was later dominated by Macedon.
thessalian-league.o: The plains of Thessaly were ruled by landowning families such as the Aleuadae of [[s:larissa|Larissa]]. By the 6th century BCE the cities formed a league with the neighbouring perioikoi peoples. Aleuas the Red was credited with organising Thessaly into four districts, each supplying cavalry and [[e:hoplite|hoplites]].
thessalian-league.r: In wartime the league elected a tagos as commander. Thessalian cavalry was the best in [[e:greece|Greece]], and the economy rested on grain and horses worked by serfs called penestai. The Thessalians sided with [[e:persia|Persia]] in 480 BCE. Jason of [[s:tyranny-of-pherae|Pherae]], elected tagos c. 374 BCE, briefly made Thessaly a great power before his murder in 370 BCE.
thessalian-league.e: Philip II was made archon of the league in the 340s BCE, and Macedonian kings held the post thereafter. [[e:rome|Rome]] restored a Thessalian League centred on [[s:larissa|Larissa]] in 196 BCE, and it continued under Roman control from 146 BCE.

tricasses.t: Small Gallic people of the upper Seine whose Roman town Augustobona became Troyes.
tricasses.o: The Tricasses are not mentioned by Caesar and were probably dependents of the [[s:senones|Senones]] in his time. Pliny and Ptolemy record them as a separate people on the Seine in [[s:county-of-champagne|Champagne]].
tricasses.r: Nothing is known of their pre-Roman institutions.
tricasses.e: Under [[e:rome|Rome]] they formed a civitas with Augustobona as its chief town, later called Trecae after the people, the origin of Troyes. [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Lupus of Troyes is said to have negotiated with Attila in 451, and the city became capital of the [[s:county-of-champagne|County of Champagne]].

tulunid-emirate.t: The first autonomous dynasty of Islamic Egypt, founded by Ahmad ibn Tulun, builder of Cairo's great mosque.
tulunid-emirate.o: Ahmad ibn Tulun, son of a Turkish slave soldier at the Abbasid court in [[e:samarra|Samarra]], was sent to [[e:egypt|Egypt]] as deputy governor in 868. He took control of the province's finances, built his own army of Turkish and African slave soldiers and, while still recognising the [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]], made Egypt effectively independent. In 878 he occupied [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]].
tulunid-emirate.r: Ibn Tulun founded a new capital, al-Qata'i, north of [[e:fustat|Fustat]], with a palace, hospital and the great Mosque of Ibn Tulun, completed in 879 and still standing. [[e:egypt|Egypt's]] revenue now stayed largely in the country, funding irrigation and building. His son Khumarawayh made a treaty with the [[e:caliphate|caliph]] in 886 and married his daughter Qatr al-Nada to al-Mu'tadid with a famously lavish dowry.
tulunid-emirate.e: Extravagance and the murder of Khumarawayh in 896 left the dynasty weak. In 905 an Abbasid army under Muhammad ibn Sulayman retook [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and razed al-Qata'i, except for the mosque.

taifa-of-mertola.t: A tiny taifa on the Guadiana at Mértola, an old river port in southern Portugal, independent for little more than a decade.
taifa-of-mertola.o: Around 1033 a local leader, known as Ibn Tayfur, made Mértola and its district independent, in the period when the small principalities of the south-west were breaking away from both the Hammudids and the [[s:taifa-of-badajoz|Taifa of Badajoz]].
taifa-of-mertola.r: Known only from brief references in Arabic chronicles, the state consisted of the hilltop town and its castle above the Guadiana, the highest navigable point for river traffic from the Atlantic, with [[e:copper|copper]] and grain trade.
taifa-of-mertola.e: Around 1044 al-Mutadid of the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]] annexed Mértola. A century later it became the base of the [[e:sufism|Sufi]] rebel Ibn Qasi, as the [[s:second-taifa-of-mertola|Second Taifa of Mértola]].

third-taifa-of-valencia.t: The last Muslim kingdom of Valencia under Zayyan ibn Mardanish, which fell to James I of Aragon in 1238.
third-taifa-of-valencia.o: In 1229 Zayyan ibn Mardanish, a descendant of the Wolf King of the [[s:second-taifa-of-murcia|Second Taifa of Murcia]], overthrew the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] governor of [[e:valencia|Valencia]], Abu Zayd. Abu Zayd fled to James I of [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]], later converting to [[e:christianity|Christianity]] and helping his campaigns.
third-taifa-of-valencia.r: Zayyan ruled the city and the irrigated [[e:huerta|huerta]] with its [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] and [[e:silk|silk]], seeking help from the [[s:hafsid-sultanate|Hafsids]] of [[e:tunis|Tunis]]. His position was weak: he faced Ibn Hud's rival power in [[e:murcia|Murcia]] and the steady advance of Aragonese forces, which won at the Puig in 1237.
third-taifa-of-valencia.e: After a siege, Zayyan surrendered [[e:valencia|Valencia]] to James I on 28 September 1238, and the Muslim population was allowed to leave. The city became the capital of the [[s:kingdom-of-valencia|Kingdom of Valencia]]. Zayyan withdrew to Dénia and later [[e:murcia|Murcia]].

territory-of-western-samoa.t: New Zealand's rule over the former German Samoa, marked by a deadly influenza epidemic and the Mau protests, which ended in 1962 as the first independent Pacific island nation.
territory-of-western-samoa.o: [[s:new-zealand|New Zealand]] troops occupied [[s:german-samoa|German Samoa]] in August 1914, at [[e:britain|Britain's]] request, and governed it under military rule for the rest of the war. Afterwards the [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] granted [[e:new-zealand|New Zealand]] a mandate over the territory, governed from 1920 by a civil administrator at Apia.
territory-of-western-samoa.r: In 1918 the ship Talune brought influenza that killed about a fifth of the population, while [[s:american-samoa|American Samoa]] escaped through quarantine. Resentment fed the Mau movement of non-cooperation, led by the merchant Olaf Frederick Nelson and Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III. On 28 December 1929, Black Saturday, [[s:new-zealand|New Zealand]] police fired on a Mau procession in Apia, killing Tamasese and others. The territory became a [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] trust territory in 1946.
territory-of-western-samoa.e: Self-government advanced in the 1950s under Prime Minister Fiamē Mataʻafa. Western Samoa became independent on 1 January 1962, the first Pacific island state to do so, and was renamed Samoa in 1997. [[s:new-zealand|New Zealand]] formally apologised for its colonial wrongs in 2002.
