tahirid-dynasty.t: The first hereditary governors of Khurasan under the Abbasids, founded by the general who won al-Ma'mun his throne.
tahirid-dynasty.o: Tahir ibn Husayn, a Persian general of [[e:khorasan|Khurasani]] origin, defeated the [[e:caliphate|caliph]] al-Amin's armies in the civil war of 811 to 813 and secured the throne for [[e:al-mamun|al-Ma'mun]]. In 821 al-Ma'mun appointed him governor of Khurasan. Tahir dropped the caliph's name from the [[e:khutba|Friday prayer]] shortly before his death in 822, but his family was confirmed in office.
tahirid-dynasty.r: The Tahirids ruled Khurasan from [[e:nishapur|Nishapur]] as loyal but autonomous governors, sending tribute to [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] while another branch held the police command of Baghdad itself. Abdallah ibn Tahir (828 to 845) was known for justice, protection of peasants and regulation of the [[e:qanat|qanat]] irrigation system. The family were Arabic-speaking patrons of poetry and [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] scholarship, while campaigning against [[e:kharijites|Kharijites]] and frontier peoples.
tahirid-dynasty.e: Under Muhammad ibn Tahir the dynasty weakened, and in 873 Ya'qub ibn al-Layth of the [[s:saffarid-dynasty|Saffarid dynasty]] seized [[e:nishapur|Nishapur]]. Tahirids remained prominent in [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] into the early 10th century, and Khurasan later passed to the [[s:samanid-empire|Samanid Empire]].

taifa-of-ronda.t: A Berber taifa centred on the gorge-top town of Ronda, ruled by the Banu Ifran until its annexation by the Abbadids of Seville.
taifa-of-ronda.o: Around 1015 Abu Nur Hilal ibn Abi Qurra of the [[s:banu-ifran-emirate|Banu Ifran]], a [[e:zanata-berbers|Zanata]] [[e:berbers|Berber]] clan, made himself independent in Ronda and the surrounding Serranía, first as a governor for the Hammudids and then in his own name.
taifa-of-ronda.r: Ronda's position above the Tajo gorge made it nearly impregnable, and the state controlled routes between the coast and the Guadalquivir valley. Its rulers were often at war with [[e:seville|Seville]], and court intrigue was frequent: Abu Nur was briefly overthrown and later restored.
taifa-of-ronda.e: In 1065 al-Mutadid of the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]] annexed Ronda, ending Ifranid rule. The town later served the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]], the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]] and the [[s:emirate-of-granada|Emirate of Granada]] before falling to [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]] in 1485.
ru: Abu Nur Hilal ibn Abi Qurra

turkmenistan.t: A gas-rich desert state on the Caspian, one of the world's most closed countries, shaped by the personality cult of Saparmurat Niyazov.
turkmenistan.o: The [[s:turkmen-ssr|Turkmen SSR]] declared independence on 27 October 1991 under its Communist Party leader Saparmurat Niyazov, who became president of the new state and in 1999 was made president for life.
turkmenistan.r: Niyazov styled himself Turkmenbashi, 'leader of the [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]]', and created an elaborate personality cult, with golden statues and his book Ruhnama required reading. He renamed months after himself and his mother. The country declared permanent neutrality, recognised by the UN in 1995. Its economy rests on enormous natural gas reserves, exported mainly to [[e:china|China]], and on [[e:cotton|cotton]], while political opposition and independent media are banned.
turkmenistan.e: After Niyazov's death in 2006 Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow became president, building his own cult. In 2022 his son Serdar Berdimuhamedow succeeded him, while Gurbanguly kept great influence as chairman of the people's council.

thanadevli-state.t: A minor Kathi chiefship of the Kathiawar peninsula, one of many small shareholder estates in the Sorath and Gohelwad country.
thanadevli-state.o: Thana Devli was one of the small Kathiawar holdings held by a Kathi family, the clan that gave the peninsula its name. It took shape as a separate estate by around 1600, though its early history is known mainly from local tradition.
thanadevli-state.r: Like many Kathi estates, it was held by co-sharers of the ruling family. It paid tribute to the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads]] of [[s:baroda-state|Baroda]] and to [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh]], and after 1807 came under British supervision in the Kathiawar Agency. Little else is recorded.
thanadevli-state.e: The estate merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960.

triballi.t: Powerful Thracian people of the Morava and Iskar valleys who killed an Odrysian king, wounded Philip II and defied Alexander the Great.
triballi.o: The Triballi held the plains south of the [[e:danube|Danube]] between the Morava and Iskar rivers, in modern eastern [[s:serbia|Serbia]] and north-western [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]], by the 5th century BCE. Greek historians treat them as one of the largest Thracian peoples, independent of the [[s:odrysian-kingdom|Odrysian Kingdom]].
triballi.r: Ruled by kings and war leaders, they were feared raiders. In 424 BCE the Odrysian king Sitalces died fighting them, and in 376 BCE they attacked [[s:abdera-800|Abdera]] on the [[e:aegean|Aegean]]. In 339 BCE they ambushed Philip II returning from [[s:scythia|Scythia]], wounding him and seizing his booty. In 335 BCE Alexander defeated them, and their king Syrmus took refuge on the [[e:danube|Danube]] island of Peuce before submitting.
triballi.e: Defeats by the [[s:autariatae|Autariatae]] and later the Celtic [[s:scordisci|Scordisci]] weakened them. [[e:rome|Rome]] conquered the region when [[e:marcus-licinius-crassus|Marcus Licinius Crassus]] campaigned in 29 BCE, and their land became part of Moesia.

tazes.t: A small Maya province of north-eastern Yucatán, known only from brief mentions in Spanish colonial records.
tazes.o: Tazes (Taz) was one of the territories into which northern Yucatán split after the fall of the [[s:league-of-mayapan|League of Mayapan]] around 1441. It lay in the north-east of the peninsula, near the provinces of [[s:cupul|Cupul]] and [[s:ecab|Ecab]].
tazes.r: Known only from a few colonial sources, Tazes seems to have been a group of towns without a strong central ruler. Its people, like their neighbours, farmed [[e:maize|maize]] and lived in dispersed towns under local batabs.
tazes.e: Tazes came under Spanish control during the conquest of eastern Yucatán in the 1540s and was absorbed into the [[s:province-of-yucatan|Province of Yucatán]].

taifa-of-menorca.t: An autonomous Muslim island state that survived for half a century as a tributary of Aragon after the Christian conquest of Majorca.
taifa-of-menorca.o: After James I of [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]] took Majorca in 1229, the Muslim leaders of Menorca agreed in 1231, by the Treaty of Capdepera, to recognise him as overlord and pay tribute, while keeping their own government, law and religion. The island was known in Arabic as Manurqa.
taifa-of-menorca.r: The island was ruled by a ra'is from Madina Manurqa, the later Ciutadella. Abu Uthman Said ibn Hakam (ruled 1234-1282), a scholar and poet, gathered a library and kept the island prosperous through farming, livestock and trade with [[e:north-africa|North Africa]] while paying tribute to [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]].
taifa-of-menorca.e: In January 1287 Alfonso III of [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]] invaded, accusing the island of aiding the [[s:hafsid-sultanate|Hafsid Sultanate]]. Most inhabitants were enslaved or expelled, and Menorca was resettled by Catalans as part of the [[s:kingdom-of-majorca|Kingdom of Majorca]].

tajik-ssr.t: The Soviet republic of the Tajiks, the poorest in the Soviet Union, whose capital Stalinabad grew into modern Dushanbe.
tajik-ssr.o: In October 1929 the [[s:tajik-assr|Tajik ASSR]] was separated from the [[s:uzbek-ssr|Uzbek SSR]] and upgraded to a union republic, the Tajik SSR, with the addition of the Khujand district. The capital Dushanbe was named Stalinabad from 1929 to 1961.
tajik-ssr.r: The republic was reshaped by collectivisation and forced resettlement of mountain populations to the [[e:cotton|cotton]] fields of the south. The Vakhsh valley was irrigated, and huge projects such as the Nurek dam on the Vakhsh and the Tursunzoda aluminium smelter followed. Tajik literature flourished under writers such as Sadriddin Ayni, while the Pamirs formed the Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Oblast. Leaders were mostly drawn from the northern Khujand region.
tajik-ssr.e: Riots in Dushanbe in 1990 foreshadowed instability. The republic declared independence on 9 September 1991 and became [[s:tajikistan|Tajikistan]], soon plunging into civil war.

totonac-state-of-cempoala.t: The chief city of the Totonacs on the Gulf Coast of Veracruz, whose ruler became the first indigenous ally of Hernán Cortés in 1519.
totonac-state-of-cempoala.o: The [[e:totonacs|Totonacs]] dominated central Veracruz in the Postclassic period, and Cempoala (Zempoala) became their principal city from around 1200, after the decline of [[s:el-tajin|El Tajín]]. It lay on a fertile coastal plain near the Actopan river.
totonac-state-of-cempoala.r: Cempoala was a large city of walled ceremonial precincts with temples built of river stones and stucco, surrounded by irrigated fields and gardens. It was ruled by a lord whom Spanish chroniclers called the 'Fat Cacique'. In the mid-15th century the Totonac region came under the [[s:aztec-empire|Aztec Empire]], which demanded heavy tribute.
totonac-state-of-cempoala.e: In 1519 [[e:hernan-cortes|Cortés]] landed nearby and persuaded Cempoala to rebel against Aztec tax collectors; its warriors joined his march inland. In 1520 Cortés defeated Pánfilo de Narváez at Cempoala. Epidemics soon devastated the city, which was largely deserted by the late 16th century.

taifa-of-lerida.t: A Hudid taifa at Lleida on the Segre, a frontier state facing the Catalan counties that at times rivalled its parent state, Zaragoza.
taifa-of-lerida.o: Lleida belonged to the Upper March governed from [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]]. Its governor Sulayman ibn Hud ruled Lleida for years before he took Zaragoza in 1039 and founded the Hudid dynasty; on his death in 1046 his son Yusuf al-Muzaffar ruled it as an independent kingdom, fighting his brother al-Muqtadir of the [[s:taifa-of-zaragoza|Taifa of Zaragoza]].
taifa-of-lerida.r: The [[e:taifa|taifa]] controlled the fertile Segre valley and bordered the [[s:county-of-barcelona|County of Barcelona]] and the [[s:county-of-urgell|County of Urgell]], to whom it paid tribute. Under al-Mundhir (1081-1090) it was joined with Tortosa and Dénia, and he allied with Barcelona against his brother al-Mutaman of [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]], whose commander El Cid defeated them at Almenar in 1082.
taifa-of-lerida.e: Lleida passed under Almoravid control around 1110. In 1149 Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona and Ermengol VI of Urgell captured the city, adding it to what became the [[s:principality-of-catalonia|Principality of Catalonia]].

tikal.t: One of the most powerful Classic Maya kingdoms, Mutal, whose temples rise above the Petén forest and whose long rivalry with Calakmul shaped Maya politics.
tikal.o: Tikal was occupied from about 800 BCE and grew into a major centre in the Late Preclassic. Its royal dynasty, later counted back to the founder Yax Ehb Xook, is traditionally dated to about 90 CE, and the North Acropolis became its royal burial ground.
tikal.r: In 378 CE Sihyaj K'ahk', linked with [[s:teotihuacan|Teotihuacan]], arrived and installed a new king, after which Tikal dominated much of the central Petén. Its rivalry with the [[s:kingdom-of-kaan|Kingdom of Kaan]] led to defeat by [[s:caracol|Caracol]] in 562 and a long hiatus. Jasaw Chan K'awiil I defeated Calakmul in 695, opening a revival marked by the great twin-pyramid complexes and Temples I to VI.
tikal.e: Tikal's last dated monument was raised in 869, and the city was largely abandoned by about 900 during the Classic Maya collapse. It became a national park in 1955 and a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1979.

turkestan-governorate-general.t: The Russian colonial government of Central Asia, ruled from Tashkent, which turned the region's oases into a cotton economy.
turkestan-governorate-general.o: After Russian forces took Tashkent in 1865, the Turkestan Governorate-General was created in 1867 under General Konstantin von Kaufmann. It expanded through the conquest of [[e:samarkand|Samarkand]] in 1868, the [[s:khanate-of-kokand|Khanate of Kokand]] in 1876 and the [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] lands after the storming of Geok Tepe in 1881.
turkestan-governorate-general.r: The governor-general held wide military and civil powers, with the [[s:emirate-of-bukhara|Emirate of Bukhara]] and the [[s:khanate-of-khiva|Khanate of Khiva]] left as [[e:protectorate|protectorates]]. [[e:russia|Russia]] built the Trans-Caspian and Orenburg-Tashkent railways and promoted American [[e:cotton|cotton]], which became the region's main crop. Muslim courts and customs were mostly left in place, but Russian settlers took land on the steppe. The Jadid movement campaigned for educational reform.
turkestan-governorate-general.e: A revolt in 1916 against wartime labour conscription was brutally suppressed. After the Russian Revolution of 1917 the Tashkent Soviet seized power, and the region became the [[s:turkestan-assr|Turkestan ASSR]] in 1918.

tunip.t: Tunip, a Syrian city of the Orontes valley caught between Egypt, Mitanni and the Hittites in the Late Bronze Age.
tunip.o: Tunip lay in the Orontes region of western [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]]; its site is uncertain. It appears in the 15th century BCE among the cities that resisted [[e:thutmose-iii|Thutmose III]] of the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]], as an ally of [[s:kadesh|Kadesh]] and the [[s:mitanni-empire|Mitanni Empire]].
tunip.r: Little is known of its government, though a council of citizens appears to have shared power. In the [[e:amarna-letters|Amarna letters]], the people of Tunip wrote to the [[e:pharaoh|pharaoh]] begging him to restore the son of their former ruler and protect them from Aziru of the [[s:kingdom-of-amurru|Kingdom of Amurru]].
tunip.e: Tunip passed under Hittite control in the 14th century BCE. [[e:ramesses-ii|Ramesses II]] attacked it during his Syrian wars, and it fades from the record in the 13th century BCE.

third-dominican-republic.t: The Dominican state from 1924 to 1965, dominated for three decades by the brutal dictatorship of Rafael Trujillo.
third-dominican-republic.o: The [[s:military-government-of-santo-domingo|Military Government of Santo Domingo]] ended in 1924 with the election of Horacio Vásquez. His attempt to extend his term weakened his government, and in 1930 Rafael Trujillo, commander of the US-trained army, took power in a coup and won a fraudulent election.
third-dominican-republic.r: Trujillo ruled directly or through puppet presidents until 1961, controlling the economy through family monopolies, including much of the [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] industry. Santo Domingo was renamed Ciudad Trujillo in 1936. In October 1937 his troops massacred thousands of Haitians along the border, the Parsley Massacre. He paid off the foreign debt and built roads and ports, while the secret police tortured and murdered opponents, including the Mirabal sisters in 1960.
third-dominican-republic.e: Trujillo was assassinated on 30 May 1961. Juan Bosch won the 1962 election but was overthrown in 1963. In April 1965 a civil war between constitutionalists and the military led to US intervention, and elections in 1966 began the present [[s:dominican-republic|Dominican Republic]].

tadmekka.t: A Berber caravan town in Mali's Adrar des Ifoghas, home to the oldest Arabic inscriptions in West Africa.
tadmekka.o: Tadmekka, at the site of Essouk in the [[s:emirate-of-adrar|Adrar]] des Ifoghas of northern [[e:mali|Mali]], grew from the 9th century as a market on the trans-Saharan routes linking the [[e:niger-bend|Niger bend]] with [[s:sultanate-of-ouargla|Ouargla]], Ghadames and [[e:kairouan|Kairouan]]. Its inhabitants were [[e:berbers|Berbers]], and Ibadi merchants were among its first Muslim traders.
tadmekka.r: The 11th-century geographer al-Bakri described Tadmekka as a fine town whose name meant 'resembling [[e:mecca|Mecca]]', ruled by [[e:berbers|Berber]] chiefs, with merchants who used unstamped pure gold as currency. Excavations have found clay coin moulds for gold dinars, and Arabic inscriptions on nearby rocks, dated 1011 and 1013, are the oldest known in [[e:west-africa|West Africa]].
tadmekka.e: Tadmekka declined as trade shifted towards [[e:timbuktu|Timbuktu]] and [[e:gao|Gao]] and the [[s:mali-empire|Mali Empire]] extended its influence. By the late 14th century the town was largely abandoned, and its people dispersed among the [[e:tuareg|Tuareg]] of the [[s:emirate-of-adrar|Adrar]].

travunia.t: Small Slavic principality around Trebinje in eastern Herzegovina, ruled by local lords under Serbian, Byzantine and Dukljan overlords.
travunia.o: Travunia formed in the 7th to 9th centuries among [[e:serbs|Serbs]] settled in the hinterland of Dubrovnik. Constantine VII records that its ruler Krajina, son of Beloje, married the daughter of the Serbian prince Vlastimir in the 9th century, tying it to the [[s:principality-of-serbia-early-medieval|Principality of Serbia (early medieval)]].
travunia.r: Ruled by hereditary župans from Trebinje, it had towns such as Risan and controlled routes from the coast into the interior. It was usually dependent on a larger neighbour: [[s:serbia|Serbia]], [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], and from the 11th century [[s:duklja|Duklja]], whose rulers often installed relatives there.
travunia.e: Grand Župan Stefan Nemanja of the [[s:grand-principality-of-serbia|Grand Principality of Serbia]] annexed Travunia, with [[s:duklja|Duklja]], around 1186. It remained part of the Serbian lands, later passing to Bosnia, and its centre Trebinje is now in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

turkmen-ssr.t: The Soviet republic of the Turkmen, a desert land of gas fields and cotton built around the Karakum Canal.
turkmen-ssr.o: The [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] SSR was created in October 1924 in the national delimitation of Soviet [[e:central-asia|Central Asia]], from the Transcaspian region of the [[s:turkestan-assr|Turkestan ASSR]] and Turkmen districts of the Bukharan and Khorezm republics. Its capital was Poltoratsk, renamed Ashgabat in 1927.
turkmen-ssr.r: Soviet rule settled nomadic and semi-nomadic [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] tribes, collectivised farming and fought Basmachi resistance led by Junaid Khan into the 1930s. In 1948 an earthquake destroyed Ashgabat, killing tens of thousands. The Karakum Canal, begun in the 1950s, carried water from the [[e:oxus|Amu Darya]] for [[e:cotton|cotton]], and natural gas became a major export. Turkmen was written in a [[e:latin|Latin]] alphabet from 1928 and in Cyrillic from 1940.
turkmen-ssr.e: Saparmurat Niyazov, first secretary from 1985, led the republic to independence on 27 October 1991, when it became [[s:turkmenistan|Turkmenistan]].

tarkhan-dynasty.t: A Mongol-descended dynasty that ruled lower Sindh from Thatta between the Arghuns and the Mughal conquest.
tarkhan-dynasty.o: Mirza Isa Tarkhan, an officer of the [[s:arghun-dynasty|Arghun dynasty]] descended from a Mongol military family, seized Thatta in 1554 as Arghun authority collapsed. After Shah Husain Arghun's death he became master of lower Sindh, ruling from Thatta in the [[e:indus|Indus]] delta.
tarkhan-dynasty.r: The Tarkhans ruled a prosperous delta region with the port of Lahari Bandar, trading with [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]], the [[e:persian-gulf|Persian Gulf]] and the Portuguese. The Portuguese sacked Thatta in 1555 after a dispute. Mirza Isa and his successors built tombs at the Makli necropolis, adding Persian-style monuments to the earlier Samma tombs.
tarkhan-dynasty.e: Mirza Jani Beg Tarkhan was defeated by [[e:akbar|Akbar's]] general Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan and submitted in 1591. Sindh became part of the [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]], though Tarkhan descendants served as governors for a time.

travancore-cochin.t: The union of the princely states of Travancore and Cochin, an Indian state from 1949 to 1956 that became the core of Kerala.
travancore-cochin.o: On 1 July 1949 the kingdoms of [[s:travancore|Travancore]] and Cochin were merged into the United State of Travancore and Cochin, with its capital at Thiruvananthapuram. The Maharaja of Travancore, Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma, became Rajpramukh.
travancore-cochin.r: Travancore-Cochin became a Part B state in 1950. Its politics were lively and unstable, with Congress ministries, coalitions and a strong Communist movement. The state had [[e:india|India's]] highest literacy rate and a large Christian population, and its economy rested on coconut, [[e:rubber|rubber]], [[e:spice-trade|spices]] and coir.
travancore-cochin.e: Under the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 the Tamil-speaking southern taluks went to Madras State, and Malabar was added from Madras, forming the new state of Kerala on 1 November 1956.

triarchy-of-negroponte.t: Crusader lordship on Euboea, split among three Lombard lords under the growing shadow of Venice, which eventually took over the whole island.
triarchy-of-negroponte.o: After the [[e:fourth-crusade|Fourth Crusade]], Boniface of Montferrat granted Euboea in 1205 to Jacques d'Avesnes and then to [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] nobles from [[s:commune-of-verona|Verona]], notably Ravano dalle Carceri. In 1209 Ravano recognised Venetian overlordship. After his death in 1216 the island was divided into three parts, the terzieri, each held by a lord called a triarch.
triarchy-of-negroponte.r: The triarchs, of families such as the dalle Carceri and Ghisi, were [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]] but relied on [[e:venice|Venice]], which held quarters and a bailo in the town of Negroponte ([[s:chalcis|Chalcis]]) and controlled its trade. Greek peasants worked the land under [[e:latin|Latin]] lords. The renegade knight Licario, serving [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], recaptured much of the island in the 1270s.
triarchy-of-negroponte.e: Threatened by the Catalans of the [[s:duchy-of-athens|Duchy of Athens]] and the Turks, the triarchs ceded more and more to [[e:venice|Venice]]. By 1390 Venice ruled the whole island directly as [[s:venetian-negroponte|Venetian Negroponte]].

tripolitanian-republic.t: Often called the first republic in the Arab world, proclaimed by Tripolitanian leaders in 1918 to resist Italian rule.
tripolitanian-republic.o: After the Ottoman defeat in the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]], Tripolitanian notables met at Msallata in November 1918 and proclaimed a republic, exploiting the fact that [[s:italian-libya|Italian Libya]] controlled only the coast. Its leadership was a council including Sulayman al-Baruni, [[e:ramadan|Ramadan]] al-Suwayhili of Misrata, Ahmad al-Murayyid and Abd al-Nabi Bilkhayr.
tripolitanian-republic.r: The republic sought international recognition but received none. In 1919 [[e:italy|Italy]] issued a statute granting Tripolitanians citizenship and an elected parliament, briefly easing tension. Rivalries among the leaders, between Arab and [[e:berbers|Berber]] groups and between regions undermined unity; al-Suwayhili was killed in 1920 during internal fighting.
tripolitanian-republic.e: In 1922 Tripolitanian leaders offered the [[e:emirate|emirate]] to Idris of the [[s:senussi-order|Senussi Order]] to unite resistance, but Fascist [[e:italy|Italy]] launched its reconquest the same year, and the republic collapsed.

third-taifa-of-niebla.t: The last independent Muslim state of western al-Andalus, ruled by Ibn Mahfuz from Niebla until Alfonso X took it in 1262.
third-taifa-of-niebla.o: Around 1234, as Ibn Hud's power faded, Shuayb ibn Muhammad ibn Mahfuz established himself in Niebla and the surrounding district as an independent ruler. After [[e:ferdinand-iii-of-castile|Ferdinand III]] took [[e:seville|Seville]] in 1248, he accepted Castilian overlordship and paid tribute.
third-taifa-of-niebla.r: The small realm covered Niebla, Huelva and the lower Guadiana region, protected by Niebla's massive walls. As a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:crown-of-castile|Crown of Castile]], Ibn Mahfuz kept internal autonomy, but his isolation between Castilian [[e:seville|Seville]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-portugal|Kingdom of Portugal]] left him little room to manoeuvre.
third-taifa-of-niebla.e: In 1262 Alfonso X besieged Niebla for several months, and Ibn Mahfuz surrendered in exchange for lands and income in [[e:seville|Seville]]. The territory became part of [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]].

taifa-of-denia.t: A maritime taifa that ruled the Balearic Islands and raided Sardinia, founded by the freedman Mujahid al-Amiri on the Valencian coast.
taifa-of-denia.o: Mujahid al-Amiri, a freedman of the Amirid household, seized Dénia around 1010 during the collapse of the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]]. He soon added the [[e:balearic-islands|Balearic Islands]] and briefly set up a puppet [[e:caliphate|caliph]], al-Muaiti, to give his rule legitimacy.
taifa-of-denia.r: Dénia was a naval power. In 1015-1016 Mujahid's fleet invaded [[e:sardinia|Sardinia]] before being driven out by Pisa and [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]]. The port traded across the western [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]], and the court supported Quranic scholarship: Abu Amr al-Dani, the leading authority on [[e:quran|Quran]] recitation, worked there. Under Ali Iqbal al-Dawla the state kept close ties with [[e:egypt|Egypt]].
taifa-of-denia.e: In 1076 al-Muqtadir of the [[s:taifa-of-zaragoza|Taifa of Zaragoza]] annexed Dénia, while the Balearics broke away under their governor as the [[s:taifa-of-majorca|Taifa of Majorca]]. Dénia later fell to the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] and in 1244 to the [[s:crown-of-aragon|Crown of Aragon]].

tricastini.t: Gallic people of the Rhône valley near Montélimar through whose land Hannibal marched towards the Alps in 218 BCE.
tricastini.o: The Tricastini lived east of the Rhône in the modern Drôme, around Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux. Livy names them on [[e:hannibal|Hannibal's]] route after he crossed the Rhône in 218 BCE.
tricastini.r: Almost nothing is known of their society. Their position between the [[s:cavares|Cavares]] and the [[s:vocontii|Vocontii]] placed them on the routes from the Rhône into the [[e:alps|Alps]].
tricastini.e: After the Roman conquest of 121 BCE they became part of Gallia Narbonensis. Their town was refounded as Augusta Tricastinorum, the origin of Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux, and the name lives on in the Tricastin district.

tigray.t: The northern Ethiopian province whose lords dominated the empire during the Era of the Princes, from Ras Mikael Sehul to Dejazmach Wube.
tigray.o: In the mid-18th century, as the Gondar emperors lost power, [[e:ras|Ras]] Mikael Sehul built up a strong regional state in Tigray, the old heartland of [[e:aksumite-empire|Aksum]], controlling the trade route to [[e:massawa|Massawa]]. By 1748 he was effectively ruler of the province, and in 1769 he had Emperor Iyoas killed and made himself master of the court.
tigray.r: Tigray remained formally part of the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]] but its lords acted as independent princes, with seats at [[e:battle-of-adwa|Adwa]] and Antalo. They profited from firearms imported through [[e:massawa|Massawa]] and from the [[e:salt-trade|salt trade]]. [[e:ras|Ras]] Wolde Selassie, who received the British envoy Henry Salt, and Dejazmach Sabagadis continued the tradition of Tigrayan power at Gondar.
tigray.e: In 1855 Kassa Hailu defeated Wube Haile Maryam, lord of Tigray and Semien, at the Battle of Deresge and was crowned [[e:tewodros-ii|Tewodros II]], ending the Era of Princes. Tigray remained a powerful province, and its lord Kassa Mercha later became Yohannes IV.

taifa-of-tortosa.t: A taifa at the mouth of the Ebro ruled by former Slavic palace officials, prized for its port and shipyards before Zaragoza swallowed it.
taifa-of-tortosa.o: When the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]] collapsed in civil war after 1009, the saqaliba ([[e:freedmen|freedmen]] of European origin) of the Amirid household seized several eastern towns. At Tortosa the freedman Labib al-Amiri took power, reportedly for a time also sharing in the government of [[e:valencia|Valencia]] with Mubarak and Muzaffar.
taifa-of-tortosa.r: Tortosa lived from the [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]] trade, [[e:timber|timber]] from its hinterland and the shipyards that had built caliphal fleets. Its rulers, all [[e:freedmen|freedmen]], lacked dynastic legitimacy and leaned on stronger neighbours such as Dénia and [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]], and on payments to the Counts of Barcelona. Successive governors included Muqatil, Yali and Nabil.
taifa-of-tortosa.e: Around 1060 the Hudid ruler al-Muqtadir of [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]] annexed Tortosa, ending its independence. The city stayed Muslim until Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona took it in 1148, after which it became a key port of [[s:principality-of-catalonia|Catalonia]].

termessos.t: Termessos, a fortified Pisidian city high in the Taurus mountains above Antalya, which Alexander the Great chose not to attack.
termessos.o: Termessos was built at over 1,000 metres on a mountain north-west of modern Antalya, traditionally by the Solymi, an Anatolian people said to have fought the hero Bellerophon. Its site guarded a pass between Pamphylia and the Pisidian highlands.
termessos.r: The city was governed by its own council and assembly and was famous for its fierce independence. In 333 BCE Alexander of the [[s:macedonian-empire|Macedonian Empire]] tried to force the pass but gave up the siege. Termessos later fought its neighbours and became a friend of [[e:rome|Rome]].
termessos.e: In 71 BCE [[e:rome|Rome]] granted Termessos the status of free ally by law, keeping its self-government. It remained an autonomous city within the Roman world and was abandoned after an earthquake in late antiquity.

thurii.t: Panhellenic colony founded under Athenian sponsorship near ruined Sybaris in 444 BCE, linked with Herodotus and Protagoras.
thurii.o: After several attempts by Sybarite survivors to refound their city, [[s:athens|Athens]] under Pericles organised a new colony open to settlers from all [[e:greece|Greece]]. Thurii was founded in 444 or 443 BCE near the old site, with a street plan attributed to Hippodamus and laws attributed to Protagoras. The historian [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] is said to have joined it.
thurii.r: The settlers soon quarrelled; the descendants of Sybarites claimed privileges and were expelled, and the citizen body was organised in ten tribes by origin. Thurii prospered from the Sybarite plain and fought [[s:taras|Taras]] over [[s:siris|Siris]], a dispute settled by the joint foundation of [[s:perinthus|Heraclea]] in 433 BCE. Lucanian pressure grew, and in 389 BCE they crushed a Thurian army near Laus.
thurii.e: Threatened again by the [[s:lucanians|Lucanians]], Thurii appealed to [[e:rome|Rome]], which placed a garrison there in 282 BCE; the move provoked [[s:taras|Taras]] and led to the war with Pyrrhus. Thurii later suffered in the Hannibalic War, and in 193 BCE Rome founded the [[e:latin|Latin]] colony of Copia on the site.

tibet-1912-1951.t: Tibet under the Dalai Lamas' government in its decades of de facto independence, between the fall of the Qing and the arrival of the People's Liberation Army.
tibet-1912-1951.o: After the [[s:qing-empire|Qing Empire]] collapsed, Tibetan forces expelled the Chinese garrison from Lhasa in 1912, and the Thirteenth [[e:dalai-lama|Dalai Lama]] returned from exile in [[e:india|India]] in early 1913, issuing a proclamation that Tibetans have since read as a declaration of independence. The government of the [[s:ganden-phodrang|Ganden Phodrang]] continued in Lhasa.
tibet-1912-1951.r: At the Simla Convention of 1914 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and Tibet agreed a border (the McMahon Line), but [[e:china|China]] refused to ratify the convention. The Thirteenth [[e:dalai-lama|Dalai Lama]] built a modern army, introduced stamps, currency and a short-lived English school, but powerful monasteries resisted reform. After his death in 1933 regents such as Reting Rinpoche ruled, and the Fourteenth Dalai Lama was enthroned in 1940.
tibet-1912-1951.e: In October 1950 the People's Liberation Army defeated the Tibetan army at Chamdo. In May 1951 Tibetan delegates in [[e:beijing|Beijing]] signed the Seventeen Point Agreement, and Chinese troops entered Lhasa that autumn. Tibet became part of the [[s:peoples-republic-of-china|People's Republic of China]], though its status remains disputed.

taifa-of-almeria.t: A wealthy port taifa famous for its silk, whose poet-king al-Mutasim ibn Sumadih made Almería a centre of Andalusi culture.
taifa-of-almeria.o: Almería had become the main naval base of the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]]. After its fall, the Amirid freedman Khayran seized the city around 1013, followed by another freedman, Zuhayr, who was killed in 1038. After a period under [[e:valencia|Valencia]], the Arab Tujibid family of the Banu Sumadih took power in 1041 under Man ibn Sumadih.
taifa-of-almeria.r: Almería prospered as the busiest port of [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]], trading with [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and the [[e:maghreb|Maghreb]] and producing fine [[e:silk|silks]] and brocades on thousands of looms. Al-Mutasim (1052-1091) enlarged the great Alcazaba and gathered poets and scholars at his court, while paying tribute to [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]] and quarrelling with the [[s:taifa-of-granada|Taifa of Granada]].
taifa-of-almeria.e: Al-Mutasim died in 1091 as the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] besieged the city, and his son fled to [[e:north-africa|North Africa]]. Almería became an Almoravid province, briefly broke away as the [[s:second-taifa-of-almeria|Second Taifa of Almería]] in 1145, and then fell to [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]] in 1147.

thirtieth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The last native Egyptian dynasty, whose temple-building kings held off Persia until Nectanebo II's defeat in 343 BCE.
thirtieth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Nectanebo I, a general from Sebennytos in the Delta, seized power from the [[s:twenty-ninth-dynasty-of-egypt|Twenty-ninth Dynasty of Egypt]] in 380 BCE. In 373 BCE he repelled a large Persian and Greek invasion led by Pharnabazus and Iphicrates, helped by the [[e:nile|Nile]] flood.
thirtieth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The Sebennytic kings were among the greatest temple builders in Egyptian history, with works at Philae, [[e:karnak|Karnak]], Edfu and the great Isis temple at Behbeit el-Hagar. They funded Greek [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] through temple revenues and taxes on trade at Naukratis. [[s:teos|Teos]] invaded Phoenicia with the Spartan king Agesilaus but was overthrown by his nephew Nectanebo II, who ruled for about eighteen years and promoted animal cults.
thirtieth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: In 343 BCE [[e:artaxerxes-iii|Artaxerxes III]] defeated Nectanebo II at Pelusium. The king fled to [[e:upper-egypt|Upper Egypt]] and probably [[e:nubia|Nubia]], and the country became the [[s:thirty-first-dynasty-of-egypt|Thirty-first Dynasty of Egypt]] under [[e:persia|Persia]]. Nectanebo II was the last native [[e:pharaoh|pharaoh]], later turned into [[e:alexander-the-great|Alexander the Great's]] father in the Alexander Romance.

thanesar-state.t: A Sikh chiefship at the ancient pilgrimage town of Thanesar, annexed by the British when its line ended in 1850.
thanesar-state.o: After the [[e:sikhism|Sikhs]] captured Sirhind in 1763, Sikh [[e:sardar|sardars]] divided the surrounding country, and a Sikh family established itself at Thanesar, the old town beside the sacred tanks of Kurukshetra.
thanesar-state.r: Thanesar came under British protection with the other Cis-[[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]] states in 1809. It was a small chiefship, and its history under the British is thinly recorded.
thanesar-state.e: The British took over Thanesar in 1850 when the ruling line failed, and it became part of a British district. The town is now in Kurukshetra district of Haryana.

taifa-of-silves.t: A taifa in the western Algarve ruled by the Banu Muzayn from Silves, then a rich river port and later a city of poets under Seville.
taifa-of-silves.o: Around 1027 Muhammad ibn Muzayn, from a local Arab family, took control of Silves on the Arade river. The town had grown into the chief city of the Algarve, and the family ruled it as an independent principality amid the confusion following the fall of the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]].
taifa-of-silves.r: Silves, with its red sandstone castle and navigable river, traded in figs, dried fruit and [[e:timber|timber]] and was known for its pure Arabic speech and poetry. The Banu Muzayn ruled a small territory and had to fend off the expanding [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]] and the neighbouring [[s:taifa-of-santa-maria-del-algarve|Taifa of Santa María del Algarve]].
taifa-of-silves.e: In 1063 al-Mutadid of [[e:seville|Seville]] annexed Silves and made his son al-Mutamid governor, with the poet Ibn Ammar at his side. The city later became the [[s:second-taifa-of-silves|Second Taifa of Silves]] in 1144.

tai-federation.t: A French-backed autonomous federation of Tai peoples in north-western Vietnam, led by Deo Van Long and ended by the fall of Dien Bien Phu.
tai-federation.o: The Sip [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] Chau Tai, 'twelve Tai lands', of the Black River region had long been ruled by Tai chiefly families such as the Deo of Lai Chau. In 1948 [[e:france|France]] formally created the Tai Federation under Deo Van Long, who had backed the French against the [[e:viet-minh|Viet Minh]], as part of its strategy of ethnic autonomous zones.
tai-federation.r: The federation was governed from Lai Chau by Deo Van Long with Tai, Hmong and other upland chiefs, under French military protection, and fielded Tai battalions alongside French units. It was nominally attached to Bao Dai's [[s:state-of-vietnam|State of Vietnam]] from 1950. Opium was an important part of the local economy and of French financing in the region.
tai-federation.e: [[e:viet-minh|Viet Minh]] offensives overran much of the area in 1952 to 1953, and Lai Chau was evacuated before the battle of [[e:battle-of-dien-bien-phu|Dien Bien Phu]] in 1954. The [[s:republic-of-geneva|Geneva]] Accords gave the region to [[s:democratic-republic-of-vietnam|North Vietnam]], which created the Tay Bac Autonomous Region; Deo Van Long went into exile in [[e:france|France]].

transpadane-republic.t: A French-sponsored republic in Lombardy, created after Napoleon's conquest of Milan in 1796 and the first of the Italian sister republics.
transpadane-republic.o: After defeating the Austrians at [[e:lodi-dynasty|Lodi]] in May 1796, [[e:napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte]] entered [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]] and ended Austrian rule in the Duchy of [[e:milan|Milan]]. The French set up an administration of [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] Jacobins and moderates, and in November 1796 [[e:lombardy|Lombardy]] north of the Po was organised as the Transpadane Republic.
transpadane-republic.r: The republic was governed under French military control, with local administrations in [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]] and the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] cities. It paid heavy war contributions and saw church and noble property seized and artworks shipped to [[e:paris|Paris]], but also had a lively political press and debate about Italian unity. [[e:milan|Milan's]] patriots organised a competition in 1796 on the best form of free government for [[e:italy|Italy]].
transpadane-republic.e: In June and July 1797 [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] merged the Transpadane Republic with the [[s:cispadane-republic|Cispadane Republic]] and other territories to form the [[s:cisalpine-republic|Cisalpine Republic]], with [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]] as capital.

thaba-nchu.t: The Barolong chiefdom of Moroka at Thaba Nchu, an ally of the Voortrekkers that survived as an enclave until 1884.
thaba-nchu.o: In 1833 the Barolong boo Seleka under Moroka II, together with Wesleyan missionaries, moved from Platberg on the Vaal to the mountain of Thaba Nchu, on land obtained from the Basotho. Moroka's claim to have bought it was later disputed by Moshoeshoe of the [[s:basotho-kingdom|Basotho Kingdom]].
thaba-nchu.r: The Barolong were Tswana-speaking farmers and herders with a strong Methodist mission. Moroka gave food, oxen and refuge to Voortrekker parties after their defeat by the [[e:ndebele-kingdom|Ndebele]] at Vegkop in 1836, and Thaba Nchu stayed allied to the [[e:boers|Boers]]. It remained a self-governing enclave inside the [[s:orange-free-state|Orange Free State]], whose government recognised its independence.
thaba-nchu.e: After Moroka's death in 1880 his sons fought over the succession. The Free State used the turmoil to annex Thaba Nchu in 1884, though part of the land was later incorporated into the Bophuthatswana homeland.

taifa-of-moron.t: A Berber principality around Morón de la Frontera, one of the small hill-town states between Seville and Ronda that the Abbadids absorbed.
taifa-of-moron.o: Around 1013 the Banu Dammar, a [[e:berbers|Berber]] clan whose soldiers had served the Córdoban [[e:caliphate|caliphs]], took control of Morón and its district in the countryside south-east of [[e:seville|Seville]] under Nuh ibn Abi Tuziri al-Dammari.
taifa-of-moron.r: Morón was a modest state built around a castle, olive groves and grain land. Its rulers allied with the Hammudids and the other [[e:berbers|Berber]] [[e:taifa|taifas]], such as the [[s:taifa-of-carmona|Taifa of Carmona]] and the [[s:taifa-of-ronda|Taifa of Ronda]], against the expanding Arab dynasty of [[e:seville|Seville]]. Little is known of its administration.
taifa-of-moron.e: In 1066 al-Mutadid of the [[s:taifa-of-seville|Taifa of Seville]] annexed Morón, reportedly after luring [[e:berbers|Berber]] rulers into a trap. The town remained Muslim until the Castilian conquest in the 13th century.

teos.t: Ionian port city, home of the poet Anacreon, whose citizens fled Persian conquest to found Abdera and which later hosted the guild of Dionysiac artists.
teos.o: Teos lay on an isthmus south-west of [[s:smyrna|Smyrna]] and was settled by Ionians, with Boeotian and Athenian elements according to tradition, c. 1000 BCE. It joined the [[s:ionian-league|Ionian League]], and Thales is said to have proposed Teos as the capital of a united [[e:ionia|Ionia]] because of its central position.
teos.r: Teos lived from trade and two harbours. When the Persian general Harpagus attacked c. 545 BCE, many citizens sailed away and founded [[s:abdera|Abdera]] in Thrace. Anacreon, the lyric poet, was born there. The 'Teian curses', public inscriptions of c. 470 BCE, threatened anyone who harmed the grain supply or plotted tyranny. Teos sent 17 ships to Lade in 494 BCE.
teos.e: Under the Hellenistic kings Teos built Hermogenes's great temple of Dionysus and became the seat of the Ionian-Hellespontine [[e:guild|guild]] of Dionysiac artists. It passed into Roman [[e:asia|Asia]] after 133 BCE.
